signals.title: Missing sanity check when reading from JSON files
signals.text: ### Company or project name None ### Describe the improvement When reading from a large file in JSONEachRow format, sanity checks are missing. If a file is in fact a single JSON, the parser will keep parsing it until it runs out of memory. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Clickhouse local 26.5.1.882 ### How to reproduce Spin up a machine with sufficiently low memory (8GB) and run: ``` SELECT randomString(7) AS field FROM numbers(1000000000) INTO OUTFILE 'part.json.zstd' TRUNCATE FORMAT JSON SELECT DISTINCT field FROM file('part.json.zstd', 'JSONEachRow') LIMIT 10 ``` **Actual behavior**: The process is killed due to OOM on a 12GB machine. **Expected behavior**: Same as for inserts. ``` CREATE TABLE random_strings ( field String ) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO random_strings FROM INFILE 'part.json.zstd' FORMAT JSONEachRow; INSERT INTO random_strings FROM INFILE 'part.json.zstd' FORMAT JSONEachRow Query id: 0b6cf121-c418-46b5-b5ff-af0674242b3d Ok. Received exception: Code: 117. DB::Exception: Size of JSON object at position 104857600 is extremely large. Expected not greater than 10485760 bytes, but current is 104857611 bytes per row. Increase the value setting 'min_chunk_bytes_for_parallel_parsing' or check your data manually, most likely JSON is malformed: (in file/uri /part.json.zstd): While executing ParallelParsingBlockInputFormat: While executing File: data for INSERT was parsed from file. (INCORRECT_DATA) (version 26.5.1.882 (official build)) ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_ <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #107669 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1432` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: `AggregatingStep` and `MergingAggregatedStep` don't serialize `serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte` into the query plan
signals.text: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/b849a6c2d9c8d3e4f6a6372c3c80b611f777036b/src/Processors/QueryPlan/AggregatingStep.cpp#L965-L996 `serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte` is declared as a query plan serialization setting (default 1) and read on deserialization (AggregatingStep.cpp line 1135, MergingAggregatedStep.cpp line 318), but neither `AggregatingStep::serializeSettings` nor `MergingAggregatedStep::serializeSettings` writes it. Every other `Aggregator::Params` field they carry is written (`min_hit_rate_to_use_consecutive_keys_optimization`, two-level thresholds, `enable_producing_buckets_out_of_order_in_aggregation`, ...), this one is read-only. So with `serialize_query_plan = 1`, a plan built with `serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte = 0` round-trips as 1: the node executing the deserialized plan aggregates with the trailing zero byte while the initiator runs without it. The setting exists exactly to keep the string serialization format consistent across a cluster of incompatible versions, silently dropping it on the wire defeats that. Since 25.12. Fix: add `settings[QueryPlanSerializationSetting::serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte] = params.serialize_string_with_zero_byte;` to both `serializeSettings` (AggregatingStep.cpp line 965, MergingAggregatedStep.cpp line 194). Caused by: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/90880 <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #112131 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1435` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Uninterruptible CPU-bound function evaluation over a large value
signals.text: ## Summary Expensive scalar functions (like `replaceRegexpAll`) are un-interruptible while running on single large value (e.g. long string). `KILL QUERY`, `max_execution_time`, and `OvercommitTracker` pressure is ineffective because there is no place to check for them. When the arguments are constant, the call additionally runs during **query analysis / planning** (`ActionsDAG::tryFoldFunctionToConstant` → `IExecutableFunction::executeImplDryRun`), *before* the execution pipeline exists — so it is outside the cancellation/time-limit machinery entirely. This affects many functions, demonstrated below with `replaceRegexpAll`. Observed hanging ~16 min (963 s) on a single query in a stress run, tripping the `Hung check failed, possible deadlock found` detector. ## Reproducer ```sql SELECT length(replaceRegexpAll(repeat(repeat('1', 1000000), 4), '[0-9]{1,3}', 'x')); ``` Both the input (`repeat(repeat('1', 1000000), 4)` — 4M characters) and the pattern are constant, so the call is folded during analysis. (The AST fuzzer generated this from `04496_jit_regexp_no_quadratic.sql`.) ## Evidence (from CI) `Stress test (amd_tsan)`, sha `85359752060b481071afb23e26f93273904878e4` (v26.8.1). Processlist at hung-check time: - `elapsed: 963.28`, `is_cancelled: 1` (cancellation requested, ignored), `peak_memory_usage: ~2.15 GiB`. - `QueryAnalysisMicroseconds: 5890110`, `QueryPlanBuildMicroseconds: 5237410` — essentially all time is in analysis/planning, not execution. - Hung thread stack (top frames): ``` re2::DFA::AnalyzeSearch / re2::DFA::Search → RE2::Match DB::ReplaceRegexpImpl<…NameReplaceRegexpAll>::processString (src/Functions/ReplaceRegexpImpl.h:175) DB::FunctionStringReplace<…>::executeImpl DB::IExecutableFunction::defaultImplementationForConstantArguments DB::IFunction::executeImplDryRun DB::ActionsDAG::tryFoldFunctionToConstant DB::PlannerActionsVisitorImpl::visitImpl → DB::buildExpressionAnalysisResult DB::Planner::buildPlanForQueryNode DB::InterpreterSelectQueryAnalyzer::getQueryPlan ``` ## Root cause and scope **The core issue: no interrupt point inside per-value evaluation.** `ReplaceRegexpImpl::processString` has no cancellation/deadline check. So one call over a single large value is atomic — nothing external can stop it until it returns. Additionally (perhaps not relevant to the issue) constant folding means this all happens in `ActionsDAG::tryFoldFunctionToConstant` which has no interrupt machinery at all (so `max_execution_time`, `KILL QUERY`, and `OvercommitTracker` can't do anything anyway). Execution phase polls for cancellation in between blocks, so the issue still persists there since the problem is a single large input. Some similar situations are already handled: - Oversized generators have hard caps: `repeat` (`max_repeat_times = 1'000'000`, `max_string_size = 1<<30`), `arrayWithConstant` (`max_array_size_in_columns_bytes = 1e9`, throws `TOO_LARGE_ARRAY_SIZE`), `range` (`function_range_max_elements_in_block`). - Allocation-bound work is caught by memory tracking → `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`. The uncovered quadrant is **compute-bound work over a large-but-legal value**: our 4 MB input is well under `repeat`'s 1 GiB cap, and the RE2 DFA burns CPU without allocating, so neither guard fires. Other functions with the same potential issue include the regex/search family (`replaceRegexp*`, `extractAll`, `countMatches`, `match`/`multiMatch*`, `like`/`ilike`), `*LevenshteinDistance*`/`editDistance` (genuinely O(n·m)), UTF-8/ICU transforms, and array functions (`arraySort`, `arrayDistinct`, `arrayIntersect`, lambda `arrayMap`/`arrayFilter`) over a big-but-legal array. ## Why it matters The defect defeats the server's load-shedding/recovery mechanisms, which is the dangerous part under concurrency: - `max_execution_time`, `KILL QUERY`, and `OvercommitTracker`'s "please stop and free memory" request are all ignored while the call runs. - Client timeout + retry naturally produces multiple identical queries, and client disconnect doesn't interrupt the call, so stuck evaluations accumulate, each holding a request thread and memory. - As memory approaches the cap, `OvercommitTracker` fires but cannot reclaim from the uninterruptible holders, so it kills innocent, interruptible queries (`Code: 241`) while the real holders persist — a memory-pinned state the server cannot recover from without a restart. Graceful shutdown then also waits on those threads (this is why the stress hung-check tripped). Magnitude note: the 963 s figure is inflated by TSan (~5–15×) and RE2 DFA-cache thrashing under the stress config's memory pressure (the test is literally `04496_jit_regexp_no_quadratic`). In a normal build the same query is slow-but-finite; the reliability concern is the uninterruptibility/limit-bypass, not the exact duration. ## Suggested fix direction (suggested by AI) Per-function checkpoints alone don't scale (whack-a-mole across dozens of functions). Prioritize the centralized levers: 1. **Govern constant-folding centrally.** `tryFoldFunctionToConstant` is a single choke point and always a size-1 call — give the dry-run a deadline (from `max_execution_time` / `max_estimated_execution_time`), a cancellation hook, and/or an input-size cap. This bounds the planning-phase amplifier for *every* function at once, with no per-row-loop reasoning needed. 2. **One cheap, shared, strided interrupt check** for the worst compute-bound per-element loops (e.g. `processString` and peers). Cost is negligible if done right: a relaxed atomic-flag load + `unlikely` branch, strided (every N iterations / N bytes, e.g. `if ((++counter & 0x3FFF) == 0)`) so it stays out of the innermost hot path and can't inhibit vectorization. Ideally driven by the existing real-time query-profiler signal (already fires ~1/s) setting a thread-local flag, so there is no new hot-path timing logic. (Caveat: this helps when the loop iterates during the hang — true for `replaceRegexpAll`'s incremental matching; a function whose long pole is one monolithic library call needs input bounding or a library-level deadline instead.) 3. The existing generator size caps + memory tracking already cover the oversized-generator and allocation-bound sub-classes — no need to re-solve those. ## Related - Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/47272 — "Allow cancelling queries in the middle of blocking operations." Same goal (queries must honor cancellation) but scoped to blocking *syscalls* (signal → `EINTR`) and explicitly *not* about `max_execution_time`. It does not address CPU-bound evaluation loops or the constant-folding/analysis phase, so this is a distinct case; a sufficiently general interrupt-flag framework could serve both if the project chooses to unify them. - Surfaced via the generic `Hung check failed, possible deadlock found` bucket (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107941), which matches by test name only and does not track this specific cause. - CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110449&sha=85359752060b481071afb23e26f93273904878e4&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_tsan%29

signals.title: Row policy on the shard-local table is bypassed with `serialize_query_plan = 1` on a non-local replica
signals.text: 🕵 **Describe the bug** With `serialize_query_plan = 1`, a read shipped to a non-local replica of a `Distributed` table bypasses the row policy defined on the shard-local table: the receiving server deserializes an already-built read plan, so it never applies its own row policies. With `serialize_query_plan = 0` (text shipping) the same query is filtered correctly. This matters because defining the policy on the underlying local table is the documented way to filter reads that go through a `Distributed` table (`docs/en/sql-reference/statements/create/row-policy.md`), so the workaround silently returns unfiltered rows in this mode. **How to reproduce** Version: 26.8.1.1 (reproduced on `master`, commit `bde560d7b00`). Server config: a cluster `self` with one replica pointing back at the server itself, and `<process_query_plan_packet>1</process_query_plan_packet>`. ```sql CREATE TABLE rp_leaf (x UInt32, y UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY x; INSERT INTO rp_leaf SELECT number, number FROM numbers(10); CREATE TABLE rp_dist AS rp_leaf ENGINE = Distributed('self', currentDatabase(), rp_leaf); CREATE ROW POLICY rp_l ON rp_leaf FOR SELECT USING y < 5 TO CURRENT_USER; SELECT count() FROM rp_dist SETTINGS prefer_localhost_replica = 0, serialize_query_plan = 0; -- 5, correct SELECT count() FROM rp_dist SETTINGS prefer_localhost_replica = 0, serialize_query_plan = 1; -- 10, policy skipped SELECT count() FROM rp_leaf; -- 5, correct ``` **Expected behavior** Both remote reads return `5`. Either the shipped plan carries the filter, or the receiving server re-applies its local row policies to the deserialized plan, or plan shipping is refused when the shard-local table has a row policy that applies (fail close). **Additional context** Two stateless tests already pin `serialize_query_plan = 0` for exactly this reason: - `tests/queries/0_stateless/04498_row_policy_role_scope_interserver.sh` - `tests/queries/0_stateless/04652_nested_merge_prewhere_type_mismatch.sql` (added by https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112326) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112326
signals.author: alexey-milovidov

signals.title: Inconsistent AST formatting: `BACKUP ... SETTINGS <name> = DEFAULT` cannot be parsed back
signals.text: 🕵 **Describe what's wrong** `BACKUP` / `RESTORE` accept `SETTINGS <name> = DEFAULT`, but only when it is the *first* item of the `SETTINGS` list. The formatter then reorders the list so that `<name> = DEFAULT` becomes the *last* item, and the printed query can no longer be parsed back. On a build with the formatting-consistency check enabled (`BuzzHouse`, fuzzers) this raises the logical error `Inconsistent AST formatting`. The reason is that `ParserBackupQuery::parseSettings` uses `ParserSetQuery::parseNameValuePair`, which does not understand `= DEFAULT`. When the *first* item is `<name> = DEFAULT`, the whole `ParserBackupQuery::parseSettings` fails, `pos` is restored, and the trailing `SETTINGS` clause is instead parsed by `ParserQueryWithOutput` via `ParserSetQuery(true)` — which does understand `= DEFAULT` and stores the name in `ASTSetQuery::default_settings`, printed *after* all the regular changes. Re-parsing that output now succeeds for the first setting inside `ParserBackupQuery::parseSettings` and then chokes on `, <name> = DEFAULT`. **How to reproduce** Pure formatter, no table or disk needed (`clickhouse local`): ```sql -- `DEFAULT` last: cannot be parsed at all SELECT formatQuerySingleLine($$BACKUP TABLE t TO Disk('d', 'b') SETTINGS max_final_threads = 14, foo = DEFAULT$$); -- Code: 62. DB::Exception: Syntax error: failed at position 79 (end of query) ... (SYNTAX_ERROR) -- `DEFAULT` first: parses, but is reordered to the end, so the output is not re-parseable SELECT formatQuerySingleLine($$BACKUP TABLE t TO Disk('d', 'b') SETTINGS foo = DEFAULT, max_final_threads = 14$$); -- BACKUP TABLE t TO Disk('d', 'b') SETTINGS max_final_threads = 14, foo = DEFAULT ``` Feeding the second output back in reproduces the first error, which is exactly the `Inconsistent AST formatting` round-trip failure. **Where it was seen in CI** `BuzzHouse (amd_debug)`, STID `1941-1bfa`, on an unrelated pull request: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=96886&sha=357db6092241ff3db624aeb778ec4b830f9b74a6&name_0=PR&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_debug%29 The fuzzer-generated query was: ```sql BACKUP FROM SNAPSHOT File('/var/lib/clickhouse/user_files/backup22.zip') TO Disk('local_disk', 'backup91') SETTINGS ..., iceberg_snapshot_id = DEFAULT, iceberg_timestamp_ms = DEFAULT ``` Note that this is not specific to the `iceberg_*` settings — any setting name behaves the same way, and `RESTORE` is affected too. **Expected behavior** Either `ParserBackupQuery::parseSettings` should accept `<name> = DEFAULT` in any position (note that `ASTSetQuery::default_settings` currently holds a single name, so several `= DEFAULT` items in one clause need a decision too), or `BACKUP`/`RESTORE` should reject `= DEFAULT` outright. In both cases the format/parse round-trip must be stable. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110223 (a different manifestation of the same `Inconsistent AST formatting` class)

signals.title: Query planner stuck for hours in bloom_filter index analysis when WHERE references a large scalar subquery Map, query cannot be killed
signals.text: **Describe the unexpected behaviour** A SELECT whose WHERE clause references a large Map built by scalar subqueries (a few hundred thousand keys) can get stuck for hours inside query plan optimization, specifically in bloom_filter skip index condition building, on a partitioned table that has a bloom_filter index. Because the query never leaves planning: * max_execution_time fires and marks the query cancelled (system.processes shows is_cancelled = 1) but nothing in the planning path checks the flag, so it keeps running * KILL QUERY does nothing * no QueryStart row ever shows up in system.query_log * one HTTPHandler thread sits at 100% CPU until the server is restarted, which is the only way to clear it We first hit this in production with a machine generated analytics query that had max_execution_time = 300. It ran for 9.2 hours at full core before we noticed the box running hot. Every occurrence leaks a thread permanently. **How to reproduce** Reproduces on the official Docker images 26.4.3.37 and 26.7.1.1315, single node, default config. ```sql CREATE DATABASE wedge_repro; CREATE TABLE wedge_repro.t_ok ( ts DateTime, s LowCardinality(String), ip String, b UInt64, INDEX ix ip TYPE bloom_filter GRANULARITY 4 ) ENGINE = MergeTree PARTITION BY toYYYYMMDD(ts) ORDER BY (s, ts); CREATE TABLE wedge_repro.t_hang AS wedge_repro.t_ok; -- 8 daily partitions, ip is high cardinality (roughly unique per row) INSERT INTO wedge_repro.t_ok SELECT toDateTime('2026-01-01 00:00:00') + (number % 691200), 'proxy', concat(toString(10 + intHash64(number) % 200), '.', toString(intDiv(intHash64(number), 200) % 256), '.', toString(intDiv(intHash64(number), 51200) % 256), '.', toString(intDiv(intHash64(number), 13107200) % 250)), if(number % 10 = 0, 0, (number * 2654435761) % 1000000 + 1) FROM numbers(5000); INSERT INTO wedge_repro.t_hang SELECT toDateTime('2026-01-01 00:00:00') + (number % 691200), 'proxy', concat(toString(10 + intHash64(number) % 200), '.', toString(intDiv(intHash64(number), 200) % 256), '.', toString(intDiv(intHash64(number), 51200) % 256), '.', toString(intDiv(intHash64(number), 13107200) % 250)), if(number % 10 = 0, 0, (number * 2654435761) % 1000000 + 1) FROM numbers(400000); ``` This is a per group median/MAD outlier query. Against t_ok (about 5k distinct keys) it completes in about 0.5s: ```sql WITH (SELECT mapFromArrays(groupArray(k), groupArray(v)) FROM (SELECT toString(ip) AS k, toFloat64(quantile(0.5)(b)) AS v FROM wedge_repro.t_ok GROUP BY k)) AS med, (SELECT mapFromArrays(groupArray(k), groupArray(v)) FROM (SELECT toString(ip) AS k, toFloat64(quantile(0.5)(abs(b - med[k]))) AS v FROM wedge_repro.t_ok GROUP BY k)) AS mad SELECT count() FROM wedge_repro.t_ok WHERE s = 'proxy' AND if(abs(b - med[toString(ip)]) > 3 * mad[toString(ip)] * 1.4826, 1, 0) = 1 SETTINGS max_execution_time = 300; ``` The identical query against t_hang (about 400k distinct keys) never returns: ```sql WITH (SELECT mapFromArrays(groupArray(k), groupArray(v)) FROM (SELECT toString(ip) AS k, toFloat64(quantile(0.5)(b)) AS v FROM wedge_repro.t_hang GROUP BY k)) AS med, (SELECT mapFromArrays(groupArray(k), groupArray(v)) FROM (SELECT toString(ip) AS k, toFloat64(quantile(0.5)(abs(b - med[k]))) AS v FROM wedge_repro.t_hang GROUP BY k)) AS mad SELECT count() FROM wedge_repro.t_hang WHERE s = 'proxy' AND if(abs(b - med[toString(ip)]) > 3 * mad[toString(ip)] * 1.4826, 1, 0) = 1 SETTINGS max_execution_time = 300; ``` The scalar subqueries themselves evaluate in a few seconds, the hang starts after that. Leaving it for 6+ minutes produces no timeout error despite max_execution_time = 300: ```sql SELECT query_id, elapsed, is_cancelled FROM system.processes; -- elapsed climbs past 300 with is_cancelled = 1 and never stops SELECT count() FROM system.query_log WHERE query_id = '<id>'; -- 0, QueryStart is never written (it is logged after planning) ``` KILL QUERY on the id has no effect either. Only a server restart clears the thread. Variations we tried, each changing one thing from the hanging case: | variant | result | |---|---| | ~5k keys (t_ok above) | 0.5s | | no bloom_filter index | completes, about 1 min | | SETTINGS use_skip_indexes = 0 | completes | | unpartitioned table (single part), same 400k keys | planning finishes in tens of seconds, then executes | | 5 parts, ~50k keys | tens of seconds | | 5 parts, ~400k keys, 1 bloom index | hangs, hours or more | So the cost looks roughly like map size times number of parts times whatever the per candidate matching does per entry, and at realistic sizes it might as well be infinite. There is no cancellation point anywhere in that phase. Note the timeout does work during the scalar subquery evaluation itself (with a low max_execution_time the query dies there and returns TIMEOUT_EXCEEDED normally), it is specifically the index analysis afterwards that cannot be interrupted. **Error message and/or stacktrace** No error is ever produced. Stack of the spinning thread captured via system.stack_trace during the original incident on 26.4.3.37: ``` fmt::v12::detail::copy_noinline / parse_format_string / vformat_to DB::tryMatchJSONSubcolumnToIndex(...) DB::tryMatchNodeToJSONIndex(DB::RPNBuilderTreeNode const&, std::vector<std::string> const&, std::string const&) DB::tryMatchNodeToJSONIndex(DB::RPNBuilderTreeNode const&, DB::Block const&, std::string const&) DB::MergeTreeIndexConditionBloomFilter::traverseTreeEquals(...) DB::MergeTreeIndexConditionBloomFilter::traverseFunction(...) DB::RPNBuilder<DB::MergeTreeIndexConditionBloomFilter::RPNElement>::traverseTree(...) DB::RPNBuilder<DB::MergeTreeIndexConditionBloomFilter::RPNElement>::traverseTree(...) DB::RPNBuilder<DB::MergeTreeIndexConditionBloomFilter::RPNElement>::RPNBuilder(...) DB::MergeTreeIndexBloomFilter::createIndexCondition(...) DB::ReadFromMergeTree::buildIndexes(...) DB::ReadFromMergeTree::applyFilters(...) DB::SourceStepWithFilterBase::applyFilters() DB::QueryPlanOptimizations::optimizePrimaryKeyConditionAndLimit(...) DB::QueryPlanOptimizations::optimizeTreeSecondPass(...) DB::QueryPlan::optimize(...) DB::QueryPlan::buildQueryPipeline(...) DB::InterpreterSelectQueryAnalyzer::buildQueryPipeline() DB::InterpreterSelectQueryAnalyzer::execute() DB::executeQueryImpl(...) DB::executeQuery(...) DB::HTTPHandler::processQuery(...) DB::HTTPHandler::handleRequest(...) DB::HTTPServerConnection::run() ``` The top of the stack differs between snapshots (the fmt frames come and go), so it is progressing through an enormous amount of work rather than deadlocked on a lock. The table in the original incident also had a JSON column, hence the tryMatchJSONSubcolumnToIndex frames. A JSON column is not required, the plain columns table above hangs the same way. **Expected behavior** Two separate issues really: 1. Index condition analysis should not do per part work proportional to the size of a folded scalar constant. The map here is on the value side of an arithmetic expression, it can never help prune a bloom filter, so ideally the matcher would give up on large constants immediately. 2. Plan optimization should check the cancellation flag somewhere. Even if the analysis stays slow, max_execution_time and KILL QUERY should be able to stop it. As it stands, any pathological planning case turns into a permanently leaked thread at 100% CPU, and the only fix is restarting the server. This part seems worth fixing regardless of point 1. Workaround for anyone else hitting this: SETTINGS use_skip_indexes = 0 makes the query complete with identical results. **Additional context** The triggering queries are machine generated (per group median/MAD baselines attached via scalar subquery maps, which we use instead of window functions to avoid buffering whole partitions). We can share the full 33 frame symbolized stack, the original 190 column schema, and timings if useful. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #113289 - Backported to: `26.7.4.40`, `26.5.7.47` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Custom-key parallel replicas over a Merge table with a Distributed child: children are offloaded to a finalized stage (CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE, logical error in GroupingAggregatedTransform)
signals.text: 🕵 Reading a `Merge` table (or the `merge` table function) with custom-key parallel replicas (`parallel_replicas_mode = 'custom_key_sampling'` or `'custom_key_range'`) fails with an exception when the common processing stage of the children is `WithMergeableState` — for example, when one of the underlying tables is a `Distributed` table. ```sql CREATE TABLE t_mrg_ck_1 (k UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k AS SELECT number FROM numbers(100000); CREATE TABLE t_mrg_ck_2 (k UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k AS SELECT number FROM numbers(100000); CREATE TABLE t_mrg_ck_3 (k UInt64) ENGINE = Distributed('test_shard_localhost', currentDatabase(), 't_mrg_ck_1'); SET enable_parallel_replicas = 1, max_parallel_replicas = 3, cluster_for_parallel_replicas = 'test_cluster_one_shard_three_replicas_localhost', parallel_replicas_for_non_replicated_merge_tree = 1, parallel_replicas_mode = 'custom_key_sampling', parallel_replicas_custom_key = 'k'; SELECT count() FROM merge(currentDatabase(), '^t_mrg_ck_'); ``` ``` Code: 70. DB::Exception: Conversion from UInt64 to AggregateFunction(count) is not supported: while converting source column `count()` to destination column `count()`: Child table: default.t_mrg_ck_1. (CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE) ``` Depending on the aggregate function, it instead trips an assertion in the pipeline — an exception in debug and sanitizer builds (found by the AST fuzzer, STID `3970-479a`): ```sql SELECT 47, quantileExactInclusive(visibleWidth(['1', '2'])) IGNORE NULLS FROM merge(currentDatabase(), '^t_mrg_ck_') GROUP BY ALL LIMIT 973; ``` ``` Logical error: 'Chunk should have AggregatedChunkInfo/ChunkInfoWithAllocatedBytes in GroupingAggregatedTransform.'. ``` **Root cause.** The `Distributed` child reports `WithMergeableState` from its `getQueryProcessingStage`, so `StorageMerge::getQueryProcessingStage` sets the common stage of all children to `WithMergeableState`, and `ReadFromMerge::createPlanForTable` plans each `MergeTree` child through an interpreter with `SelectQueryOptions(WithMergeableState)`. Inside that child interpreter, the custom-key branch of `PlannerJoinTree` (`src/Planner/PlannerJoinTree.cpp`, the `canUseParallelReplicasCustomKey` block) offloads the child query to the replicas at the hard-coded stage `WithMergeableStateAfterAggregationAndLimit`, ignoring the requested `to_stage`. The child plan therefore produces finalized rows (post-aggregation, post-`LIMIT`) where the parent `ReadFromMerge` pipeline expects partial aggregation states: `convertAndFilterSourceStream` throws `CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE` when the finalized type differs from the state type, and when the types coincide structurally, the chunks without `AggregatedChunkInfo` reach `GroupingAggregatedTransform` and trip the assertion. Only the analyzer path is affected (`enable_analyzer = 0` returns correct results). Reproduced on current master (verified on a binary with no unrelated changes); found by the targeted AST fuzzer on https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110972 (which is unrelated: the failure reproduces without `parallel_replicas_allow_merge_tables`, a setting that does not exist on master), report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110972&sha=ac0a584ce316ace31f4dbc16b38e1262a2344751&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%2C%20old_compatibility%29 The custom-key offload should be skipped when the requested `to_stage` is below `WithMergeableStateAfterAggregationAndLimit`: a plan that must stop at a partial stage cannot accept a finalized remote read. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110972 <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #113742 - Backported to: `26.7.4.29`, `26.5.7.52` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Logical error: Block structure mismatch in deserialization of query plan `Window` step for `AggregateFunction` state (distributed plan)
signals.text: The targeted AST fuzzer catches a `LOGICAL_ERROR` (exception, `abortOnFailedAssertion` in debug builds) when a serialized distributed query plan containing a `Window` step with an aggregate-function state column is deserialized: ``` Logical error: 'Block structure mismatch in deserialization of query plan Window step stream: different types: theilsUArgMaxState(__table2.n, __table2.n, toUInt32OrDefault('fe80::1'_String)) OVER (ORDER BY __table2.n ASC NULLS LAST ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 7 PRECEDING) AggregateFunction(theilsUArgMax, UInt32, UInt32, UInt32) AggregateFunction(size = 0) theilsUArgMaxState(...) AggregateFunction(theilsUArgMax, UInt32, UInt32, UInt32) AggregateFunction(size = 0)'. ``` Failed query: ```sql SELECT __table1.n AS n, round(__table1.tu, NULL) AS `round(tu, 2)` FROM view( SELECT theilsUArgMaxState(n, n, toUInt32OrDefault('fe80::1')) OVER (ORDER BY n ASC NULLS LAST ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 7 PRECEDING) AS tu, n FROM t_window_crosstab__fuzz_3 ) AS __table1 ``` The exception is thrown from `checkBlockStructure` in `QueryPlan::deserialize` (`src/Processors/QueryPlan/Serialization.cpp`), called from `DB::deserializeQueryPlan` in `src/QueryPipeline/DistributedPlanExecutor.cpp` — i.e. the header restored after deserializing the `Window` step does not match the serialized one for the `AggregateFunction` state column (the two printed types render identically, so the mismatch is likely in a non-printed property of the `AggregateFunction` data type, e.g. the version — see the shared-mutable-state issues around aggregate function type versioning). The same failure signature (STID 0993-290c) fired on several unrelated PRs, so it is not specific to any of them: - https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113759&sha=63097ab62e02b91246c7d065e5ea7edd593b742a&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%29 (PR https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113759, 2026-08-08) - PR https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110102 — AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted, old_compatibility), 2026-08-08 - PR https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/82980 — Stress test (amd_asan_ubsan), 2026-08-05 - PR https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111941 — AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted), 2026-07-26 <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #114020 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1452` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Inconsistent AST formatting: `view((SELECT ...))` in table-function arguments loses subquery parentheses and cannot be parsed back (STID: 1941-1bfa)
signals.text: 🕵 Found by `AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted, old_compatibility)` on an unrelated PR (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/91993, which only touches hex encoding): [CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=91993&sha=eae3a3cbbfb5d81bed061634d53c701167dce04a&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%2C%20old_compatibility%29). The fuzzer produced a query containing `view((SELECT ...))` as an argument of a comparison function nested inside `file(...)` table-function arguments. Formatting the AST drops the parentheses around the `view` subquery argument (`view((SELECT ...))` → `view(SELECT ...)`), and the formatted text cannot be parsed back, so the format-consistency check fails with a logical error (`abortOnFailedAssertion` in the debug build): ``` Logical error: 'Inconsistent AST formatting: the query: DESCRIBE TABLE file(concat(xor(if(indexHint(and(greaterOrEquals(alias5764._time, toLowCardinality(toNullable(1048575)) + number), lessOrEquals(alias5764._time, view((SELECT toUInt16OrDefault(65536, equals(minus(materialize(NULL, arrayElement(b)), greater(lowCardinalityIndices('\\\\', toLowCardinality(NULL)), -1)), toInt8OrZero(2147483646)))))))), a <= toInt256OrDefault(-2147483647), materialize(isNullable(NULL))), and(b >= 257, 1.1754943508222875e-38 > b)), currentDatabase(), toFixedString(toNullable('_04513.orc'), assumeNotNull(256)))) SAMPLE 100 / 5 SETTINGS input_format_orc_use_fast_decoder = 0 cannot parse query back from DESCRIBE TABLE file(concat(xor(if(indexHint(and(greaterOrEquals(alias5764._time, toLowCardinality(toNullable(1048575)) + number), lessOrEquals(alias5764._time, view(SELECT toUInt16OrDefault(65536, equals(minus(materialize(NULL, arrayElement(b)), greater(lowCardinalityIndices('\\\\', toLowCardinality(NULL)), -1)), toInt8OrZero(2147483646))))))), a <= toInt256OrDefault(-2147483647), materialize(isNullable(NULL))), and(b >= 257, 1.1754943508222875e-38 > b)), currentDatabase(), toFixedString(toNullable('_04513.orc'), assumeNotNull(256)))) SAMPLE 100 / 5 SETTINGS input_format_orc_use_fast_decoder = 0'. ``` The two texts differ only in the parentheses around the `view` subquery: the original has `view((SELECT ...))`, the re-formatted text has `view(SELECT ...)`. On a recent master-based **release** build (`clickhouse local`) the asymmetry is observable in the opposite direction — the parenthesized form is the one that does not parse inside table-function arguments: ```sql -- parses fine (special `view` handling in expression context): SELECT lessOrEquals(t, view((SELECT 1))); -- parses fine (unparenthesized subquery): SELECT * FROM file(if(indexHint(lessOrEquals(t, view(SELECT 1))), 'a', 'b')); -- SYNTAX_ERROR (parenthesized subquery inside table-function arguments): SELECT * FROM file(if(indexHint(lessOrEquals(t, view((SELECT 1)))), 'a', 'b')); ``` So whether `view((SELECT ...))` / `view(SELECT ...)` parses depends on context (plain expression vs. table-function argument) and on build/compatibility configuration, while the formatter always emits the unparenthesized form. Either the parser should accept both forms in all contexts where `view` is accepted at all, or the formatter should print the form that is guaranteed to parse back in the surrounding context. Previous distinct manifestations of this dedup bucket (STID: 1941-1bfa) were fixed individually: #109501 (back-quoted numeric type name, fixed by #109720), #106850, #106358, #100131. This `view` parenthesization case is a new one. CIDB shows this check failing on 5 unrelated PRs in the last 30 days (112921, 110886, 113533, 91993, 111061) and never on master — expected, since the AST fuzzer only runs per-PR with random queries. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #114658 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1436` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Physical column shadowing `_part`: `SELECT count() ... WHERE isNull(_part > 0)` throws NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK
signals.text: **Describe what's wrong** On a table that has a **physical column named `_part`** (shadowing the virtual column), an aggregate query whose `WHERE` wraps that column in `isNull(...)` fails with `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK`, at default settings. The same predicate works in a plain `SELECT *`, and the same query works when the column does not shadow a virtual. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on current master, `26.8.1.1061` (official build). 20/20 deterministic. **How to reproduce** ```sql CREATE TABLE t_part_shadow (_part UInt32, x UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO t_part_shadow VALUES (1, 100), (2, 200), (3, 300); SELECT count() FROM t_part_shadow WHERE isNull(_part > 0); -- throws ``` ``` Code: 10. DB::Exception: Not found column _part in block. There are only columns: _partition_id, _part_uuid, _part_data_version, _disk_name. (NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK) ``` No settings required — plain defaults over HTTP and native client, old and new analyzer both throw. **Expected behavior** `0` — `_part` here is the user's `UInt32` column (`_part > 0` is never NULL), which is what `SELECT count() FROM t_part_shadow WHERE isNull(toNullable(_part) > 0)` and `SELECT * FROM t_part_shadow WHERE isNull(_part > 0)` correctly return. **Additional context — scope probed** - `SELECT * ... WHERE isNull(_part > 0)` **works**; `SELECT count()`, `EXPLAIN SELECT count()`, and the `PREWHERE` form all **throw** — the trigger is the read that needs no physical columns, where the filter becomes a candidate for part-level evaluation over virtual columns. - The exception's block dump (`_partition_id, _part_uuid, _part_data_version, _disk_name`) is the virtuals-only filter block: `getHeaderWithVirtualsForFilter` correctly *skips* virtuals shadowed by physical columns (`if (columns.contains(name)) continue;` in `MergeTreeData`), but the predicate analysis still classifies the `isNull(_part > 0)` conjunct as evaluable over virtuals, so `filterPartsByVirtualColumns` evaluates it on a block that (correctly) has no `_part`. - Un-wrapped comparisons on the shadowed column work: `WHERE _part = 2`, `WHERE (_part = 2) AND (_part > 0)` are fine; `isNull(...)` / `IS NULL` composition is what reaches the broken path. `NOT (_part > 0)` and `(_part > 0) = 1` also work. - Shadowing `_partition_id` instead does not trigger it. - The existing test `04201_virtual_column_override_where_filter.sql` pins the simple-predicate forms of this exact shadowing scenario; the `isNull` composition is the gap. Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signals.title: query_plan_join_swap_table changes the result of ANY INNER JOIN with OR-ed ON conditions (deterministic, max_threads = 1)
signals.text: ### Describe the bug The planner's automatic build-side swap (`query_plan_join_swap_table`, default `auto`) changes the result of an `ANY INNER JOIN` with **OR-ed conditions** in `ON`. On identical single-part tables, single-threaded, the swapped plan deterministically returns **6 rows** and the unswapped plan **3 rows** — the swapped output is a strict superset. `EXPLAIN actions = 1` shows both plans keep `Type: inner | Strictness: any | Algorithm: HashJoin` while the table read order flips, so the `ANY` deduplication is applied to opposite sides. With a single equality condition (no `OR`) both plans agree, so the multi-disjunct key path is the trigger. ### How to reproduce ```sql CREATE TABLE l (a Int32, b Int32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a; CREATE TABLE r (a Int32, b Int32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a; INSERT INTO l SELECT number % 8, number % 3 FROM numbers(12); INSERT INTO r SELECT number % 5, number % 8 FROM numbers(12); SELECT * FROM l ANY JOIN r ON l.b = r.b OR l.a = r.a ORDER BY ALL SETTINGS max_threads = 1, query_plan_join_swap_table = 'true'; -- 6 rows SELECT * FROM l ANY JOIN r ON l.b = r.b OR l.a = r.a ORDER BY ALL SETTINGS max_threads = 1, query_plan_join_swap_table = 'false'; -- 3 rows ``` Outputs, stable across 20/20 runs per arm (`clickhouse local`, one part per table, `max_threads = 1`): ``` -- swap 'true' (and the default 'auto', which swaps here): 0 0 0 0 0 2 0 2 1 1 1 1 2 2 2 7 3 0 3 3 4 1 4 4 -- swap 'false': 0 0 0 0 0 2 0 2 1 1 1 1 ``` Whatever row choice `ANY` is permitted to make per key, the two plans do not even agree on the **number** of emitted rows, and the divergence is controlled purely by a performance plan setting. Note also that both outputs emit only a small subset of the left keys that have matches (for example `l = (2, 1)` matches `r = (4, 1)` via `b` but is emitted by neither plan), so the intended `ANY` + `OR` semantics may be off in both plans — the deterministic swap-controlled difference is the unambiguous part. ### Affected versions Reproduced on master 26.8.1.1068 and on 26.7. Not bisected. ### Related Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112640 (the `ANY LEFT JOIN` + `OR` face of the swap: racy under `max_threads > 1`; this `INNER` face is deterministic and single-threaded) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111645 Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signals.title: Settings profile with a Map setting (`http_response_headers`) does not survive a serialization round trip
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Describe the unexpected behaviour An access entity with a Map-valued setting — e.g. a settings profile with `http_response_headers` — is serialized into a form that ClickHouse's own parser cannot read back. The stored entity becomes permanently unloadable. ### How to reproduce ```sql -- A string literal is the only accepted way to write a Map setting in a profile -- (map literals {...}, array literals [...], and map(...) are all rejected here): CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE test_profile SETTINGS http_response_headers = '{''Content-Type'':''application/json'', ''Access-Control-Allow-Origin'':''*''}' CONST; SHOW CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE test_profile; -- CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE `test_profile` SETTINGS http_response_headers = [('Content-Type', 'application/json'), ('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*')] CONST -- Feeding the emitted statement back — which is exactly what DiskAccessStorage and -- ReplicatedAccessStorage store and re-parse via deserializeAccessEntity: CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE test_profile2 SETTINGS http_response_headers = [('Content-Type', 'application/json'), ('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*')] CONST; -- Code: 62. DB::Exception: Syntax error: failed at position 72 ([): -- Expected one of: literal, NULL, NULL, number, Bool, TRUE, FALSE, string literal, end of query ``` No value of the setting round-trips — even an empty map serializes as `[] CONST`, which is rejected the same way. ### Root cause The write path and the read path disagree: - Write: `SettingsProfileElement` (`src/Access/SettingsProfileElement.cpp`) casts the value to the setting's native type (`Map`), and the AST formats the Field as a literal, producing an array-of-tuples literal `[('k', 'v'), ...]`. - Read: `ParserSettingsProfileElement` (`src/Parsers/Access/ParserSettingsProfileElement.cpp`) parses the value with a scalar-only literal parser. Unlike the query-level `SETTINGS` clause parser, it was never extended to accept collection literals (cf. #75065, where the query-level parser expects `literal or map, ..., OpeningCurlyBrace`). So `serializeAccessEntity` → `deserializeAccessEntity` fails for any user/role/profile whose profile elements contain a collection-valued setting (`http_response_headers`, `additional_table_filters`, ...). > *Generated by [Nerve](https://github.com/ClickHouse/nerve)*

signals.title: Heap-use-after-free: Parquet v3 prefetcher reads and writes through a `ReadBuffer` freed by `IInputFormat::onFinish`
signals.text: 🕵️ ## Describe what's wrong `ParquetV3BlockInputFormat` does not override `resetReadBuffer()`, so `IInputFormat::onFinish()` frees the format's owned `ReadBuffer` while the Parquet `Prefetcher`'s IO tasks are still reading through it on the prefetch thread pool. The tasks then dereference freed memory. ASan on a plain `clickhouse local` run of the reproducer below (master, 26.8.1.1310): ``` ==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x7112bd001800 WRITE of size 1048576 at 0x7112bd001800 thread T9 (ParquetPrefetch) #3 in DB::ReadBuffer::next() src/IO/ReadBuffer.cpp:113:15 #5 in DB::ReadBuffer::read(char*, unsigned long) src/IO/ReadBuffer.h:169:37 #6 in DB::Parquet::Prefetcher::readSync(...) src/Processors/Formats/Impl/Parquet/Prefetcher.cpp:113:29 #7 in DB::Parquet::Prefetcher::runTask(...) src/Processors/Formats/Impl/Parquet/Prefetcher.cpp:540:13 #8 in DB::Parquet::Prefetcher::scheduleTask(...)::$_0::operator()() src/Processors/Formats/Impl/Parquet/Prefetcher.cpp:435 #15 in DB::ThreadPoolCallbackRunnerFast::threadFunction() src/Common/threadPoolCallbackRunner.cpp:225:13 ``` It is a **1 MiB write into freed heap**, so this is memory corruption, not only a bad read. The same defect was hit independently by the `La Casa Del Dolor (arm_asan_ubsan)` CI job, where the report is a read and carries the full free/allocation stacks: ``` ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0xfcdd2aec39c0 READ of size 8 at 0xfcdd2aec39c0 thread T423 (ThreadPool) #0 in DB::Parquet::Prefetcher::readSync(...) Prefetcher.cpp:110:21 <- reader->setReadUntilEnd() #1 in DB::Parquet::Prefetcher::runTask(...) Prefetcher.cpp:523:13 #2 in DB::Parquet::Prefetcher::scheduleTask(...)::$_0::operator()() Prefetcher.cpp:424:17 #9 in DB::ThreadPoolCallbackRunnerFast::threadFunction() threadPoolCallbackRunner.cpp:225:13 0xfcdd2aec39c0 is located 0 bytes inside of 272-byte region freed by thread T468 (ThreadPool) here: #1 in std::default_delete<DB::ReadBuffer>::operator()(DB::ReadBuffer*) #7 in std::vector<std::unique_ptr<DB::ReadBuffer>>::~vector() #8 in DB::ISource::work() src/Processors/ISource.cpp:140:13 ... #18 in DB::IPolygonDictionary::loadData() src/Dictionaries/PolygonDictionary.cpp:337:8 previously allocated by thread T468 (ThreadPool) here: #2 in DB::FileDictionarySource::loadAll() src/Dictionaries/FileDictionarySource.cpp:60:19 ``` `ISource.cpp:140` is the `onFinish()` call inside the `catch (...)` handler, and the freed 272-byte region is the `ReadBufferFromFile` that `FileDictionarySource::loadAll` handed to the format via `addBuffer`. ## How to reproduce Reproduces on master (26.8.1.1310) with the official `build_amd_asan_ubsan` binary, **8 out of 10 runs, with no ThreadFuzzer and no unusual settings**. Under ThreadFuzzer it hit on the first run. Run Fiddle: https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/06f26a34-d286-40a1-85f5-7d3e952d47b8 On a release build this prints only the load error and exits 53: `Code: 53. CAST AS Array can only be performed between same-dimensional Array ... While executing ParquetV3BlockInputFormat. (TYPE_MISMATCH)` — the 1 MiB write into freed memory is silent. On an ASan build the process dies with the report above instead (5/5 runs of exactly the commands above; 8/10 in an earlier variant, so it is a race, but a very wide one). The polygon dictionary is only a convenient way to make the pipeline throw mid-read while owning its `ReadBuffer` — the defect is in the format, not in the dictionary. ## Root cause `Prefetcher` protects only *its own* lifetime. `scheduleTask` captures the shutdown handle and each task takes `std::shared_lock(*_shutdown, std::try_to_lock)`; `~Prefetcher` calls `shutdown->shutdown()` (`ShutdownHelper`, `src/Common/threadPoolCallbackRunner.h:507`), which blocks until every in-flight task has released. As its own comment says, "`this` is safe to access as long as `shutdown_lock` is held". But `Prefetcher::reader` points at a `ReadBuffer` owned by `IInputFormat::owned_buffers`, an unrelated lifetime that the handshake does not cover: - `IInputFormat::onFinish()` -> `resetReadBuffer()` -> `resetOwnedBuffers()` -> `owned_buffers.clear()` - `ParquetV3BlockInputFormat` overrides `resetParser()` and `onCancel()`, but **not `resetReadBuffer()`**. `resetParser()` happens to be safe only because it destroys the reader *before* delegating to the base. `resetReadBuffer()` has no such ordering, so the buffer dies while the `ReadManager` -> `Reader` -> `Prefetcher` chain is still alive with tasks running. Three routes reach it: `onFinish()` from the `catch (...)` in `ISource::work()` (the one above), `onFinish()` on the normal completion path (`ISource.cpp:133`) with speculative prefetches still outstanding, and `IInputFormat::setReadBuffer` when a format is reused across files. ## Suggested fix Mirror what `resetParser()` already does, so `~Prefetcher` drains the IO tasks before the base frees the buffer: ```cpp void ParquetV3BlockInputFormat::resetReadBuffer() { /// ~Prefetcher waits for in-flight IO tasks, which read through the buffer that /// IInputFormat::resetReadBuffer() is about to free. { std::lock_guard lock(reader_mutex); reader.reset(); } IInputFormat::resetReadBuffer(); } ``` ## Additional context Distinct from #109678 / #112573. That was a data race on `AsynchronousBoundedReadBuffer::prefetch_future` consumed by concurrent `readBigAt` (the `RandomRead` branch, `Prefetcher.cpp:102`). This one is a lifetime bug in the `SeekAndRead` branch, which already holds `read_mutex` — locking cannot help once the object is freed — and the freed buffer here is a plain `ReadBufferFromFile`, so `AsynchronousBoundedReadBuffer` is not involved at all. The binary used above already contains #112573 (merged into 26.8.1.1240). Found by this Dolor run: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=94148&sha=a2ef409981fc77a168eaf8cc68d7ddf67c9fadec&name_0=PR&name_1=La+Casa+Del+Dolor+%28arm_asan_ubsan%29 <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #114668 - Backported to: `26.7.4.42` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Push dynamic TopN thresholds into MergeTree reads for ORDER BY ... LIMIT (2-3x on ClickBench Q24/Q26)
signals.text: **Use case.** `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` over a sorted-by-something-else table with a narrow projection, e.g. ClickBench Q24/Q26: ```sql SELECT SearchPhrase FROM hits WHERE SearchPhrase <> '' ORDER BY EventTime LIMIT 10; SELECT SearchPhrase FROM hits WHERE SearchPhrase <> '' ORDER BY EventTime, SearchPhrase LIMIT 10; ``` The original build of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 implemented a **dynamic TopN threshold pushdown** (`Push TopN threshold to MergeTreeSource`, commit `2e2f594308f4`, plus `Better query condition cache: make TopN dynamic filters deterministic and reusable`, gated by `max_limit_to_push_down_topn_predicate = 100`): while the partial-sort transform maintains the current top-`n`, the running n-th-best value of the `ORDER BY` key is pushed down into the `MergeTree` read as a dynamic threshold, so granules whose key range cannot beat the current top-`n` are skipped instead of read, decompressed, and sorted. This mechanism was dropped during the upstreaming of that PR (the scaffolding was removed from the branch; the surviving `RewriteOrderByLimitPass` is a different, row-offset-based approach — it is off by default and measures performance-neutral on ClickBench when enabled). Master's lazy materialization (`query_plan_optimize_lazy_materialization`) covers the wide-`SELECT *` case (Q23), but does not prune reads for narrow projections: every granule passing the `WHERE` is still fully processed. Measured on identical single-part ClickBench data (hot, interleaved runs, 96-core aarch64), original bench-opt build (25.9.1.1) vs master `405e218ff`: Q24 0.009 s vs 0.013 s, Q26 0.008 s vs 0.013 s (1.2–1.3x with times this small). The gap is much larger on the official `c7a.metal-48xl` numbers: Q24 0.014 s vs 0.046 s, Q26 0.014 s vs 0.044 s (**2–3x**). A related consideration from the original design: the dynamic filter interacts with the query condition cache, so the thresholds need to be deterministic/reusable (or excluded from the cache key) — the original branch had a follow-up commit specifically making the TopN dynamic filters deterministic for that reason. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944#issuecomment-5280709772

signals.title: `OPTIMIZE TABLE` on DeltaLake/Paimon/Hudi object-storage tables silently succeeds as a no-op instead of throwing `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`
signals.text: **Describe the unexpected behaviour** `OPTIMIZE TABLE` on an object-storage table whose lake type does not implement compaction — `DeltaLakeLocal`/`DeltaLake`, `Paimon*`, `Hudi`, and plain object-storage engines — returns Ok and does nothing: no files rewritten, no new `_delta_log` commit, no error, nothing in the log. Every other engine that does not support OPTIMIZE throws `Code: 48. Method optimize is not supported by storage <name>` (`Memory`, `Join`, `Distributed`, ...), and Iceberg — the one lake type that does implement compaction — validates its gate loudly (`Code: 36. ... Enable 'allow_experimental_iceberg_compaction' setting to call optimize for iceberg tables`). So within the same `StorageObjectStorage` class, `OPTIMIZE TABLE iceberg_table` either compacts or tells you why not, while `OPTIMIZE TABLE delta_table` silently succeeds as a no-op — a user running it reasonably assumes compaction happened. **How to reproduce** Master `26.8.1.1375`, via `clickhouse local` (the Delta log is bootstrapped by hand with the same pattern as the `04628_delta_lake_partition_special_values` stateless test, because ClickHouse cannot initialize a Delta transaction log itself): ```bash mkdir -p delta/_delta_log cat > delta/_delta_log/00000000000000000000.json <<'EOF' {"protocol":{"minReaderVersion":1,"minWriterVersion":2}} {"metaData":{"id":"optimize-noop-repro","format":{"provider":"parquet","options":{}},"schemaString":"{\"type\":\"struct\",\"fields\":[{\"name\":\"k\",\"type\":\"long\",\"nullable\":true,\"metadata\":{}},{\"name\":\"v\",\"type\":\"long\",\"nullable\":true,\"metadata\":{}}]}","partitionColumns":[],"configuration":{},"createdTime":1700000000000}} EOF for i in 1 2 3; do clickhouse local -q "INSERT INTO FUNCTION deltaLakeLocal('$PWD/delta') SELECT number + $i*100 AS k, number AS v FROM numbers(10) SETTINGS allow_experimental_delta_lake_writes = 1" done ls delta/*.parquet | wc -l # 3 ls delta/_delta_log/*.json | wc -l # 4 clickhouse local -q "CREATE TABLE td ENGINE = DeltaLakeLocal('$PWD/delta'); OPTIMIZE TABLE td; SELECT 'OPTIMIZE returned Ok'" ls delta/*.parquet | wc -l # still 3 — nothing happened ls delta/_delta_log/*.json | wc -l # still 4 — no commit was written ``` The contrast on the same binary: ```sql CREATE TABLE tm (x UInt8) ENGINE = Memory; OPTIMIZE TABLE tm; -- Code: 48. DB::Exception: Method optimize is not supported by storage Memory. (NOT_IMPLEMENTED) ``` ```sql -- Iceberg (the one lake with OPTIMIZE support) refuses loudly without its gate: OPTIMIZE TABLE iceberg_table; -- Code: 36. DB::Exception: Enable 'allow_experimental_iceberg_compaction' setting to call optimize for iceberg tables. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) ``` **Mechanism** The base `IStorage::optimize` throws `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` (`src/Storages/IStorage.cpp:261`), which is what makes every non-supporting engine loud. `StorageObjectStorage::optimize` (`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorage.cpp:727`) overrides it to `return configuration->optimize(...)`, whose default implementations return `false` (`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorageConfiguration.h:285`, `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/IDataLakeMetadata.h:138`) — and `InterpreterOptimizeQuery::execute` discards the returned `bool` (`src/Interpreters/InterpreterOptimizeQuery.cpp`, the `table->optimize(...)` call). So the "nothing was optimized" signal exists but is dropped. The override was introduced with the Iceberg compaction work (`IcebergMetadata::optimize` is the only lake implementation), and the silent success for the other lake types looks like collateral rather than a decision. **Expected behavior** When `configuration->optimize` returns `false`, `StorageObjectStorage::optimize` should throw like the `IStorage` default (`NOT_IMPLEMENTED`, or a hint in the Iceberg gate style), so `OPTIMIZE TABLE` never reports success while doing nothing. Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signals.title: S3Queue `after_processing='move'` silently destroys a consumed file on a basename collision (default `move_preserve_path=false`)
signals.text: ### Company or project name _(quality/durability testing)_ ### Describe what's wrong With `after_processing = 'move'` and an `after_processing_move_prefix` set, S3Queue relocates each consumed object to `<move_prefix>/<basename>`, because `after_processing_move_preserve_path` defaults to `false`. When two consumed objects share a basename under different source prefixes — e.g. `data/a/part.csv` and `data/b/part.csv`, both matched by a glob like `data/*/part.csv` — they both resolve to the **same** destination key `<move_prefix>/part.csv`. The move is a per-object copy-then-delete (`ObjectStorageQueuePostProcessor::moveWithinBucket`): `copyObject(src -> dst)` followed by `removeObjectIfExists(src)`. So the second object's `copyObject` **overwrites** the first at the destination, and both source objects are then deleted. An S3 overwrite is not an error, so no exception is raised, nothing is logged, and `ObjectStorageQueueMovedObjects` counts both moves as successful. Net effect: one consumed file's content is permanently destroyed — gone from the source, overwritten at the destination — while the queue reports both files moved. The `move` action exists specifically to *retain* consumed files (audit, replay, or relocating them out of the ingest prefix), so this silently violates the very guarantee the feature provides, and it happens with the default settings. Same-basename objects across prefixes are common in practice (e.g. partitioned exports `date=2026-01-01/part.csv`, `date=2026-01-02/part.csv`). ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce - ClickHouse version 26.8 (also present in current master). - Object storage layout — two files that share the basename `part.csv` under different prefixes, with distinct content: - `s3://<bucket>/data/a/part.csv` → rows `0..9` - `s3://<bucket>/data/b/part.csv` → rows `100..109` ```sql CREATE TABLE dst (id UInt64, val UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; CREATE TABLE q (id UInt64, val UInt64) ENGINE = S3Queue('https://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/data/*/part.csv', '<key>', '<secret>', 'CSV') SETTINGS mode = 'unordered', keeper_path = '/clickhouse/s3q_move_demo', after_processing = 'move', after_processing_move_prefix = 'archive'; -- after_processing_move_preserve_path defaults to false CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv TO dst AS SELECT id, val FROM q; ``` After both files are consumed: ```sql SELECT count(), uniqExact(id) FROM dst; -- 20, 20 → both files were ingested/acked ``` List the bucket: ``` archive/part.csv <- ONE object (only one file's content survives) data/a/part.csv, data/b/part.csv <- both GONE (deleted after the move) ``` One consumed file's bytes are destroyed. Setting `after_processing_move_preserve_path = 1` avoids it — the archive then keeps both `archive/data/a/part.csv` and `archive/data/b/part.csv`. ### Expected behavior Every object retained by `after_processing = 'move'` should survive exactly once. A destination-key collision under the default `after_processing_move_preserve_path = false` should not silently overwrite-and-delete a consumed file. Reasonable options: default `preserve_path` to `true`, fail the move loudly on a collision, or skip an existing destination — but not destroy data without any error or log line. ### Error message and/or stacktrace None — the loss is silent. `ObjectStorageQueueMovedObjects` reports both objects moved even though only one survives at the destination. ### Additional context Related to the `after_processing = 'delete'` silent-leftover behaviour in #114801 and the re-ingestion duplication in #114421; this is the `move`-leg sibling, but here the consequence is data loss (a destroyed file) rather than leftover or duplicated objects. Source (current master): `applyMovePrefixIfPresent` builds the destination as `move_prefix / fileName(remote_path)` when `preserve_path` is false, and `moveWithinBucket` does `copyObject` then `removeObjectIfExists` per object, swallowing per-object failures — in `src/Storages/ObjectStorageQueue/ObjectStorageQueuePostProcessor.cpp`.

signals.title: Iceberg writer serializes day/hour partition transforms as non-canonical `days`/`hours`, breaking external readers (pyiceberg: UnknownTransform)
signals.text: **Describe what's wrong** The Iceberg writer serializes the `day` and `hour` partition transforms under the non-canonical plural names `days` / `hours` in the table metadata. The [Iceberg spec](https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#partition-transforms) defines the transform names as `year`, `month`, `day`, `hour` (singular), and that is what other writers emit. Spec-following readers do not recognize the plural forms: pyiceberg 0.10.0 parses them as `UnknownTransform(transform='days')`, so a ClickHouse-written time-partitioned Iceberg table silently loses its partition information (and with it partition pruning) in external readers. The writer is also internally inconsistent: the *sort order* serialization path maps the same functions to the canonical singular names (`{"toRelativeDayNum", "day"}, {"toRelativeHourNum", "hour"}` in `parseFunction`, `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Iceberg/Utils.cpp`), while the *partition spec* path emits the plural (`getPartitionField` writes `"days"` / `"hours"`, same file). `year` and `month` are emitted correctly in both paths. ClickHouse's own reader is lenient (`parseTransformAndArgument` accepts `day`, `date`, `days`, `dates`, …), so the bug is invisible in ClickHouse-only round-trips — it only breaks interoperability, which is the main reason to write Iceberg metadata in the first place. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on master 26.8.1.1375, on every write. **How to reproduce** ```bash clickhouse local --path . --query " CREATE TABLE t (k Int64, ts DateTime) ENGINE = IcebergLocal('\$PWD/ice/', 'Parquet') PARTITION BY (toRelativeDayNum(ts)) SETTINGS allow_insert_into_iceberg = 1; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, toDateTime('2026-01-01 00:00:00') + number * 3600 FROM numbers(100) SETTINGS allow_insert_into_iceberg = 1; " grep -ho '"transform" : "[^"]*"' ice/metadata/*.json | sort -u ``` **Expected behavior** ``` "transform" : "day" ``` **Actual behavior** ``` "transform" : "days" ``` And through pyiceberg 0.10.0: ```python from pyiceberg.table import StaticTable t = StaticTable.from_metadata('ice/metadata/<latest>.metadata.json') print([repr(f.transform) for f in t.spec().fields]) # ["UnknownTransform(transform='days')"] ``` `PARTITION BY (toRelativeHourNum(ts))` produces `"transform" : "hours"` with the same result. `toYearNumSinceEpoch` / `toMonthNumSinceEpoch` correctly produce `year` / `month`. Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signals.title: Iceberg writer declares `timestamp` (without zone) in metadata but writes Parquet with `isAdjustedToUTC=true` — CH-written tables with DateTime are unreadable by pyiceberg
signals.text: **Describe what's wrong** When ClickHouse writes an Iceberg table containing a `DateTime` or `DateTime64` column, the table metadata and the data files contradict each other: - the Iceberg schema declares the column as `timestamp` — which the [spec](https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#primitive-types) defines as *microsecond precision **without** timezone*, and whose required [Parquet mapping](https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#parquet) is `timestamp(isAdjustedToUTC=false, unit=MICROS)`; - the Parquet data files are written with `isAdjustedToUTC=true` (`timestamp[us, tz=UTC]`). Spec-following readers refuse the combination. pyiceberg 0.10.0 fails the scan of every ClickHouse-written Iceberg table that contains a timestamp column: ``` ValueError: Unsupported schema projection from timestamp[us, tz=UTC] to timestamp[us] ``` Either consistent choice would fix interoperability: declare `timestamptz` in the Iceberg schema (arguably the right mapping for `DateTime`, which is epoch-based instant semantics), or write the Parquet files with `isAdjustedToUTC=false`. ClickHouse's own reader accepts its own output, so the bug is invisible in ClickHouse-only round-trips. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on master 26.8.1.1375, on every write. Same behavior for `DateTime` and `DateTime64(6)`. **How to reproduce** ```bash clickhouse local --path . --query " CREATE TABLE t (k Int64, ts DateTime) ENGINE = IcebergLocal('\$PWD/ice/', 'Parquet') SETTINGS allow_insert_into_iceberg = 1; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, toDateTime('2026-01-01 00:00:00') + number * 3600 FROM numbers(50) SETTINGS allow_insert_into_iceberg = 1; " grep -ho '"type" : "timestamp[^"]*"' ice/metadata/*.json | sort -u python3 - <<'PY' import glob import pyarrow.parquet as pq from pyiceberg.table import StaticTable print(pq.read_schema(sorted(glob.glob('ice/data/**/*.parquet', recursive=True))[0]).field('ts').type) t = StaticTable.from_metadata(sorted(glob.glob('ice/metadata/*.metadata.json'))[-1]) t.scan().to_arrow() PY ``` **Expected behavior** Metadata and data files agree — either `timestamptz` + `isAdjustedToUTC=true`, or `timestamp` + `isAdjustedToUTC=false` — and external readers can scan the table. **Actual behavior** ``` "type" : "timestamp" timestamp[us, tz=UTC] ValueError: Unsupported schema projection from timestamp[us, tz=UTC] to timestamp[us] ``` Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114848 (the same writer also serializes day/hour partition transform names non-canonically; both were found probing writer output against external readers). Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signals.title: [CI crash] ThreadGroupSwitcher possibly causing memory tracking issues
signals.text: <details><summary>Stack trace details</summary> The sipHash64(st.trace_full) is 11757953060920895701 The trace is from the master or release branch: True The query for CIDB to compare the trace with the known one: ```sql WITH ( SELECT groupArrayDistinct(cleanStackTrace(trace_full) AS trace) FROM default.stack_traces WHERE sipHash64(trace) IN (11757953060920895701, {ANOTHER_TRACE_HASH}) -- FIXME: replace with the known hash ) AS traces, 1.97 AS alpha, stack_frame_weights AS ( WITH ( SELECT count() FROM default.stack_traces FINAL ) AS total, 2.0 AS beta, 3.7 AS gamma SELECT arrayJoin(cleanStackTrace(trace_full)) AS frame, countDistinct(trace_full) AS count, log(total / count) AS IDF, sigmoid(beta * (IDF - gamma)) AS weight FROM default.stack_traces FINAL GROUP BY frame ), (SELECT groupArray(weight) AS w, groupArray(frame) AS f FROM stack_frame_weights) AS weights, (trace -> arrayMap((_frame, pos) -> (pow(pos, -alpha) * arrayFirst(w, f -> (f = _frame), weights.w, weights.f)), trace, arrayEnumerate(trace))) AS get_trace_weights, (arr -> arrayStringConcat(arr, '\n')) AS joinArr SELECT arraySimilarity(traces[1], traces[2], get_trace_weights(traces[1]) signals.title: RFC: Runtime filter transport in DQE
signals.text: Right now a join runtime filter is local to its fragment: the build side creates it and only the `__applyFilter` sites in the same fragment ever see it. So when the probe side is a fact table scan in another stage, we shuffle the whole scan output even though the filter would have killed most of it. I want to ship the filter instead: each build task sends its partial over the exchange layer, the probe-side fragments merge the partials and apply the union, and the pruning happens before the shuffle rather than after. A few things I consider non-negotiable: - fail open: rows pass unfiltered until the merged filter shows up, and a filter that never arrives (or half-arrives) can't change the result - only inclusion filters can travel, an exclusion filter built from a subset of the keys drops rows it shouldn't - wire cost stays bounded by the configured static filter size even when the cardinality estimates are garbage - don't ship at all unless the estimated build key set is small next to the receiving scan None of this is new. It's the Bloomjoin from R* ([Mackert & Lohman, VLDB 1986](https://dblp.org/rec/conf/vldb/MackertL86.html)): ship a hashed bit vector instead of doing a semi-join, in their measurements it beat everything else. The modern take is predicate transfer ([Yang et al., CIDR 2024](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2024/papers/p22-yang.pdf)), which extends the same trick to the whole join graph.

signals.title: Table referenced in a subquery inside a CONSTRAINT is not a loading dependency, so the server does not start after it is dropped
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong A table referenced from a subquery inside a `CONSTRAINT` is evaluated while the dependent table is being attached, but it is not registered as a *loading* dependency. Nothing prevents dropping it, and after that the server does not start: attaching the dependent table throws `UNKNOWN_TABLE` and metadata loading fails. `DDLLoadingDependencyVisitor` only visits `ASTFunction`, `ASTFunctionWithKeyValueArguments` and `ASTStorage`, so a table in the `FROM` of a subquery is never seen, and `DDLLoadingDependencyVisitor::extractTableNameFromArgument` returns early for an `ASTSubquery` argument with the comment "Do not add tables from the subquery into dependencies, because `CREATE` will succeed anyway". `CREATE` does succeed - it is `ATTACH` on startup that does not. The *referential* graph does know about the table, because `DDLDependencyVisitor` visits `ASTTableExpression`, so `check_referential_table_dependencies = 1` rejects the `DROP`. But that setting is off by default, and it is the loading graph that both the default `check_table_dependencies` check and the `DROP DATABASE` drop order (added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97057) rely on. So the same-database `DROP DATABASE` hazard from https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/87369 is still open for this kind of dependency, and here even a plain `DROP TABLE` is enough. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes, reproduced on `26.8.1.1` (master). ### How to reproduce ``` $ clickhouse local --path /tmp/dep_repro --multiquery -q " CREATE DATABASE db ENGINE = Atomic; CREATE TABLE db.t1 (id UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); CREATE TABLE db.t2 (conversation UInt64, CONSTRAINT c CHECK (SELECT id FROM db.t1 LIMIT 15) IN (conversation)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); SELECT name, loading_dependencies_table FROM system.tables WHERE database = 'db'; DROP TABLE db.t1; " t1 [] t2 ['conversation'] ``` Note that `db.t1` is missing from the loading dependencies of `db.t2` (`conversation` is there because `expr IN table` is read as a table reference), and that `DROP TABLE db.t1` succeeds. Loading the same metadata again - the equivalent of a server restart - fails: ``` $ clickhouse local --path /tmp/dep_repro -q "SELECT count() FROM db.t2" Code: 722. DB::Exception: Waited job failed: Code: 695. DB::Exception: Load job 'load table db.t2' failed: Code: 60. DB::Exception: Table db.t1 does not exist. Maybe you meant db.t2?: While processing (SELECT id FROM db.t1 LIMIT 15) AS _subquery1: While processing ((SELECT id FROM db.t1 LIMIT 15) AS _subquery1) IN (default.conversation): Cannot attach table `db`.`t2` from metadata file store/48b/48b87126-75b1-456b-bc55-8d9154a478e2/t2.sql from query ATTACH TABLE db.t2 UUID '7a3f7ac0-6b40-4608-88a9-33b49c638b73' (`conversation` UInt64, CONSTRAINT c CHECK (SELECT id FROM db.t1 LIMIT 15) IN (default.conversation)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple() SETTINGS index_granularity = 8192. (UNKNOWN_TABLE),. (ASYNC_LOAD_WAIT_FAILED) ``` With `DROP TABLE db.t1 SETTINGS check_referential_table_dependencies = 1` the drop is rejected as expected: ``` Code: 630. DB::Exception: Cannot drop or rename db.t1 (...), because some tables depend on it: db.t2. (HAVE_DEPENDENT_OBJECTS) ``` ### Expected behavior A table referenced in a subquery inside a constraint should be a loading dependency of the table that carries the constraint, so that dropping it is rejected by the default `check_table_dependencies` check, and so that `DROP DATABASE` drops the dependent first. ### Error message and/or stacktrace Seen in CI as a `Cannot start clickhouse-server` stress failure on 2026-07-22, `Stress test (amd_msan)`: ``` <Error> Application: Caught exception while loading metadata: Code: 722. DB::Exception: Waited job failed: Code: 695. DB::Exception: Load job 'load table test_1.t2__fuzz_19' failed: Code: 60. DB::Exception: Table test_1.t1 does not exist. Maybe you meant test_1.t2?: While processing (SELECT id FROM test_1.t1 LIMIT 15) AS _subquery3: While processing ((SELECT id FROM test_1.t1 LIMIT 15) AS _subquery3) IN (test_1.conversation): Cannot attach table `test_1`.`t2__fuzz_19` from metadata file store/db9/db9c3db2-fdb6-4494-8b03-9223ac2a3a1b/t2__fuzz_19.sql from query ATTACH TABLE test_1.t2__fuzz_19 UUID '13942a08-5df1-4805-affc-adfc86c726a4' (`conversation` UInt64, CONSTRAINT constraint_conversation CHECK (SELECT id FROM test_1.t1 LIMIT 15) IN (test_1.conversation)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple() ... ``` CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110231&sha=4de836223549fd5224ca017b8c1a28e344ce38e9&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_msan%29 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110231 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/87369 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97057 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/102506

signals.title: Assorted ideas to slightly improve JOINs
signals.text: Only ideas that are rather easy to implement. 1. Add `IColumn::shrinkToFit` method. It will remove overallocation of columns and save memory (for hash join) up to 2x. Use this method in `HashJoin` unconditionally. 2. For CROSS JOIN (nested loops): compress blocks in memory if there is large amount of data. Uncompress while joining (repeatedly for every iteration of the outer loop). The implementation is very easy after #20168. 3. For CROSS JOIN (nested loops): write blocks to tmp directory in Native format (similar to external sorting and external aggregation) if there is large amount of data. Read many times while joining. 4. Compress blocks for hash join in memory. While joining, maintain LRU cache of uncompressed blocks. Can work good if JOIN is skewed, otherwise questionable. 5. If the amount of data is large, serialize all records on disk in `RowBinary` format and keep offsets in hash table (we will have 8 bytes per record + key size + hash table overhead instead of keeping all data). While joining, do batch reads with AIO and also maintain small LRU hash table in memory. The performance can be decent (1 million IOPS on modern SSD). 6. If the amount of data is large, replace HashJoin to SSDCacheDictionary (the performance of SSDCacheDictionary assumed to be decent). 7. Represent the data structure for right hand side of JOIN or IN as a table for key-value requests. When doing distributed JOIN, instead of usual (broadcast or shuffle) algorithms, do lookup requests over network. Right hand side of distributed JOIN can be represented as a special kind of distributed table with local cache of lookup results. Applicability is limited but can be good for some scenarios: large rhs table but small subset of keys are JOINed. 8. For INNER and RIGHT JOIN try to use the set of keys of rhs table as an index for lhs table, similar to IN.

signals.title: Handling `max_authentication_methods_per_user` setting for multiple ssh keys in user authentication
signals.text: The new setting `max_authentication_methods_per_user` was introduced in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/65277. It is possible to specify multiple SSH keys for user authentication as a single method: ```sql IDENTIFIED WITH ssh_key BY KEY 'public_key' TYPE 'ssh-rsa', KEY 'another_public_key' TYPE 'ssh-ed25519', KEY 'another_public_key' TYPE 'ssh-dsa' ``` The example above is treated as one authentication method, but in reality, it involves three separate keys. Using the new multi-authentication method syntax, it can be rewritten as: ```sql IDENTIFIED WITH ssh_key BY KEY 'public_key' TYPE 'ssh-rsa', ssh_key BY KEY 'another_public_key' TYPE 'ssh-ed25519', ssh_key BY KEY 'another_public_key' TYPE 'ssh-dsa' ``` While functionally equivalent, the second option considered as three separate authentication merhods. Question: Should this behavior remain as it is, or should there be adjustments to handle this scenario? Possible options include: 1. Introducing a breaking change that requires a new syntax (e.g., enforced use of the BY keyword). 2. When checking if the limit has exceeded, account for the list of ssh keys that can be used for authentication. 3. Refactoring the parser to treat the first syntax as multi-authentication rather than a single method with multiple keys. 4. Leaving the current behavior unchanged. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #111181 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1445` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->
