signals.title: Do not inject random ORDER BY into queries planned to an intermediate stage
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110188 With `inject_random_order_for_select_without_order_by = 1`, `InjectRandomOrderIfNoOrderByPass` wrapped every top-level query into `SELECT * FROM (...) ORDER BY rand()`, including queries that are planned only up to an intermediate stage. For a `Merge` table with a `Distributed` child, the other children are planned to `WithMergeableState`; the wrapper made such a child plan complete its aggregation, so blocks without `AggregatedChunkInfo` reached `MergingAggregatedTransform`, and the query failed with a logical error (exception) `Chunk info was not set for chunk in MergingAggregatedTransform`. Now the injection pass is only added when the query is processed to stage `Complete`, so intermediate-stage plans (`Merge`/`Distributed` children) are left untouched, while the injection still applies to the user-facing query. Minimal reproducer (found by BuzzHouse on [this report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110188&sha=cdc23648d36878b136bf2c8d87ee9b0a29651412&name_0=PR&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29), unrelated to that PR's changes — it reproduces on master): ```sql CREATE TABLE t_local (x UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY x; INSERT INTO t_local SELECT number FROM numbers(100); CREATE TABLE t_dist (x UInt64) ENGINE = Distributed('test_shard_localhost', currentDatabase(), 't_local'); SET inject_random_order_for_select_without_order_by = 1; SELECT count() FROM merge(currentDatabase(), '^t_(local|dist)$'); -- LOGICAL_ERROR before this fix ``` ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a logical error (exception) `Chunk info was not set for chunk in MergingAggregatedTransform` when the setting `inject_random_order_for_select_without_order_by` is enabled and an aggregation query reads from a `Merge` table containing a `Distributed` child: the random `ORDER BY rand()` wrapper is no longer injected into queries planned only up to an intermediate stage. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1453` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->
signals.author: alexey-milovidov

signals.title: Fix quadratic JSON subcolumn skip-index matching over a large dotted constant
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113003 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a query plan optimization stall when a `WHERE` clause contains a large string constant with many dots and the table carries a `bloom_filter`, `tokenbf_v1`, `ngrambf_v1` or `text` skip index. Matching a filter column name against `JSONAllPaths(...)` index columns enumerated every dot split of the name, which made skip-index condition building quadratic in the constant's length. Closes #113003. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113003 **What breaks.** A `SELECT` whose `WHERE` contains a large dotted string constant, over a table with a skip index, spends unbounded time in query plan optimization. The reporter measured 9.2 hours at 100% of one core with `max_execution_time = 300` set, on 26.4.3.37 and 26.7.1.1315. Nothing on that path observes cancellation, so `max_execution_time` fires and `KILL QUERY` is inert, no `QueryStart` row is written, and the handler thread is leaked until restart. Workaround was `SETTINGS use_skip_indexes = 0`. **Root cause.** `tryMatchJSONSubcolumnToIndex` reads a filter column name as `<json_column>.<path>`. Not knowing where the split is, it enumerated every dot split of the name and per split formatted a lookup key and scanned the index columns. The name embeds a folded constant verbatim (`position('a.a.a...', s)`), so its length is user-controlled, giving O(length^2). **The change.** Scan the index columns instead: keep entries shaped `JSONAllPaths(X)` and test each `X` against the name by prefix-plus-dot. Cost no longer depends on the name. Selection is deliberately unchanged (shortest matching `X`, ties to the first entry), which reproduces what walking dot positions left to right did. This is not `bloom_filter`-specific: `tokenbf_v1`, `ngrambf_v1` and `text` reach the same helper, so all four are fixed at once. **Validation.** The reporter's repro goes from 42.7s to 0.16s on a debug build. All 80 existing `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` cases in `04024_json_skip_index_*` pass unchanged; 3 new cases pin the previously untested ambiguous case where two index columns match one name. The new cost test asserts allocated bytes rather than wall clock, and was verified to fail on the pre-fix binary. The cancellation gap is real and separate; it ships as a follow-up. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Backported to: `26.7.4.40`, `26.5.7.47` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Introduce zk leader metrics to Keeper mntr
signals.text: Adds leader-only Keeper `mntr` metrics: - `zk_leader_uptime` - `zk_sum_election_time` - `zk_cnt_election_time` - `zk_sum_leader_unavailable_time` - `zk_cnt_leader_unavailable_time` `zk_leader_uptime` starts at NuRaft `BecomeLeader`. The cumulative election and leader-unavailability metrics sample `isLeaderAlive` once per `heart_beat_interval_ms`; election completion is recorded at `BecomeLeader`, while leader-unavailability completes when polling observes a live local leader. `srst` resets all four cumulative values. The intended alternative was exact NuRaft lifecycle callbacks: an election-start callback before pre-vote or vote, plus a leader-ready callback for leader-unavailability completion. That requires changing vendored NuRaft and an upstream contribution, whose merge timeline could delay these Keeper monitoring metrics. This PR therefore delivers the metrics now through existing NuRaft state, while documenting the sampling limitation: boundaries can differ by up to one heartbeat interval and short no-leader windows can be missed. Also added keeper-only metrics - `KeeperLastLeaderElectionTime` - `KeeperLastLeaderUnavailableTime` ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Introduce emulated ZooKeeper metrics in Keeper `mntr` command: `zk_leader_uptime`, `zk_sum_election_time`, `zk_cnt_election_time`, `zk_sum_leader_unavailable_time`, `zk_cnt_leader_unavailable_time`; Also introduce related leader-oriented metrics for Keeper only: `KeeperLastLeaderElectionTime`, `KeeperLastLeaderUnavailableTime`
signals.author: UberDever

signals.title: Write wide integers in Parquet as Decimal
signals.text: Previously UInt128/UInt256/Int128/Int256 were written as `FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY`, but as little-endian. Since little-endian is not lexicographically sortable, there were no statistics and no way to prune row groups and pages. This was not intentional, but rather an accidental artifact from when Parquet serialization was first introduced in ClickHouse. However, we cannot just change the endianness and break existing code/data. Here instead we switch to `DECIMAL` encoding in Parquet, which is big-endian. This enables row group and page pruning for querying for queries that use filtering on wide integer columns. The encoding is a little bit akward with 17 or 33 bytes per integer, but it enables other data consumers to have a correct data interpretation hint. Since the new data cannot be read by older versions, this new serialization mode is behind `output_format_parquet_wide_integer_as_decimal` setting, which defaults to `0` to preserver backward compatibility. The new version can still read old data (but not the other way around). <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add opt-in Parquet serialization of UInt128/UInt256/Int128/Int256 as DECIMAL to enable row group and page pruning.

signals.title: Fix division by zero in `ReadFromMergeTree` when `StorageMerge` truncates the number of streams
signals.text: The `AST fuzzer (amd_debug)` crashed the server with `Integer divide by zero` on ```sql SELECT id FROM merge(currentDatabase(), '^t$') ORDER BY id DESC SETTINGS max_streams_to_max_threads_ratio = 1073741824, max_threads = 4 ``` The planner computes `max_streams = max_threads * max_streams_to_max_threads_ratio = 2^32`, which passes the existing overflow check (it only rejects values that do not fit into `size_t`). `ReadFromMerge::createPlanForTable` then passed `UInt32(streams_num)` to `storage->read`, truncating `2^32` to `0`. The child `ReadFromMergeTree` divides by the requested number of streams in `spreadMarkRangesAmongStreamsWithOrder` (`(info.sum_marks - 1) / num_streams`), so debug and sanitizer builds crash with SIGFPE (release builds happen to eliminate the dead division, since its only use is in a loop that runs zero times). `IStorage::read` takes `size_t num_streams`, so the cast was a pointless leftover — this change removes it and adds a regression test that crashes debug builds without the fix. Additionally (per review), `StorageMerge` multiplied the requested number of streams by `max_streams_multiplier_for_merge_tables` (clamped to the number of selected tables) with unchecked `Float64` -> `size_t` casts, while the planner only bounds-checks `max_threads * max_streams_to_max_threads_ratio`. Both multiplications now go through a shared helper that throws `PARAMETER_OUT_OF_BOUND` (like the planner check) when the product does not fit into `size_t`, with a second regression test. Also (per review), `spreadMarkRangesAmongStreams` and `spreadMarkRangesAmongStreamsWithOrder` clamp an unnecessarily large number of streams down to the amount of data, but the check itself computed `num_streams * min_marks_for_concurrent_read`, which wraps around for huge stream counts. The clamp was then skipped and the ordered path went on to `split_parts_and_ranges.reserve(num_streams)`, throwing `std::length_error` in every build — reachable both directly on a `MergeTree` table and, now that the stream count is no longer truncated, through a `Merge` table. The comparison now uses a division, which is equivalent (`min_marks_for_concurrent_read` is always at least one) and cannot overflow, with a third regression test. Also (per review, and confirmed by the AST fuzzer on this PR), a streaming read (`FROM ... STREAM`) bypasses the `spreadMarkRanges*` helpers entirely: `groupPartitionsByStreams` created one `MergeTreeCommitOrderSequentialSource` per requested stream with no clamp, so a huge `max_threads * max_streams_to_max_threads_ratio` product threw `std::length_error` from `pipes.reserve` (or would exhaust memory for merely absurd values). Since a streaming read has no marks by which the stream count could be clamped, such values are now rejected with `PARAMETER_OUT_OF_BOUND`, with a fourth regression test. The cap is 65536: a source costs about 35 KB (measured on a sanitizer build: a single streaming read over a one-row table peaks at 669 MB / 1026 MB / 4030 MB of RSS for 1000 / 10000 / 100000 streams, over a 557 MB baseline), so the million that the limit on the number of threads in `MergeTreeReadPool` uses would still allocate tens of gigabytes before the query could fail, which is exactly what the check is there to prevent. The number of useful streaming sources is bounded by the number of cores, so 65536 leaves several orders of magnitude of headroom. Found by the AST fuzzer on an unrelated PR: [CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113010&sha=59507af89c33f62942e855b50b3e66704cbcf2e9&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%29) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113010 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a crash (arithmetic exception in debug and sanitizer builds) when reading from a `Merge` table with a very large `max_streams_to_max_threads_ratio`: the number of streams was truncated to 32 bits, so multiples of `2^32` became zero. Also, throw an exception instead of undefined behavior when the product of the number of streams and `max_streams_multiplier_for_merge_tables` exceeds the range of `size_t`, fix a `std::length_error` when reading a `MergeTree` table with a huge `max_streams_to_max_threads_ratio`, and reject huge stream counts on streaming reads (`FROM ... STREAM`) instead of trying to create a source per stream.
signals.author: alexey-milovidov

signals.title: Push tuple element predicates into Parquet and ORC subcolumn reads
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112575 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Filter pushdown now works for `Tuple` subcolumns in Parquet and ORC files. A predicate such as `WHERE tup.1 = 555555` over `file()`, `s3()` or `url()` now prunes row groups and row index strides using the tuple element's own statistics instead of reading the whole file. ### Description Closes: #112575 Three independent defects, all needed for the reported query to prune. Parquet's reader itself was fine. **The analyzer never produced a subcolumn.** `StorageFile`/`StorageURL`/`StorageObjectStorage` return `false` from `supportsOptimizationToSubcolumns`, so `tupleElement(tup, 1)` was never rewritten to `tup.1`; the pass also accepted only `TableNode`, skipping table functions. That blanket `false` keeps #106147 fixed (`NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK` on `.null` in PREWHERE), so rather than flipping it this adds a narrow `supportsOptimizationToTupleElementSubcolumns` virtual defaulting to the existing one, with a `{Tuple, tupleElement}`-only allow-list. `04303_object_storage_prewhere_isnotnull_subcolumn` passes unmodified. Source identity also moves to the table-expression node: every `file()` resolves to the same `_table_function.file` ID, so two such sources shared a key. Accepting table functions generally also makes `format()`, `values()` and `view()` eligible for the other transformers; those storages already answer `supportsSubcolumns()`, so the default covers them. **ORC's search argument builder resolved top-level names only,** so any dotted name emitted `YES_NO_NULL` while the read path in the same file resolved them recursively. Resolving recursively also reaches the flattened-`Nested` descent, which rewrites the type it is given, so the builder keeps the key's own type: an array-typed predicate over a flattened `Nested` leaf is not pushed, since scalar element statistics cannot decide it. **ORC built its KeyCondition from the reader header,** which carries only the parent column, so the predicate degraded to `unknown`. ORC now passes `initKeyConditionOnce` a local copy extended with the tuple element paths the filter references; `FormatFilterInfo`, the Parquet call site and the reader header are untouched. Admission requires a named tuple at every level (unwrapping `Nullable`/`LowCardinality`/`Array`), which refuses Map `.keys`/`.values`: they use `SubstreamType::TupleElement` but have no per-element statistics. <details> <summary>Measurements (100k rows, one row group / stride per 10k)</summary> | Arm | master | this PR | |---|---|---| | ORC `WHERE tup.1 = 55555` | 200000 rows read | **20000** | | ORC `WHERE id = 55555` (control) | 20000 | 20000 | | Parquet `WHERE tup.1 = 55555` | 7 row groups / 0 pruned | **1 / 6** | | Parquet `WHERE id = 55555` (control) | 1 / 6 | 1 / 6 | Results identical in every arm. Refusal arms (Map `.keys`/`.values`, `.null`, `.size0`, unnamed tuple, `Array(Tuple)`, type-mismatch structure hint) return correct results with pruning off. Multi-level `tup.2.1` stays unpruned: correct, and a separate optimization. Regression sweep over `*functions_to_subcolumns*`, `*tuple_element*`, `*_parquet_*`, `*_orc_*` and the named pushdown tests, run on this build and on an unmodified master build for attribution: no regression attributable to this change. New tests are 50/50 green under randomized settings. </details> Also noticed, not touched here: reading a standalone dotted ORC tuple element with its inferred type returns column defaults, because `Nested::flatten` does not descend a `Nullable(Tuple)`. #109741 (open) rewrites that helper for the `Arrow` spelling.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Fix window RANGE frame peer groups ignoring COLLATE
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113079 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results and a logical error in window functions when the window `ORDER BY` uses `COLLATE`. The input is sorted with the collator, but peer groups for a `RANGE` frame were computed with a raw byte comparison, so values equal under the collation were treated as different peers. This cut the frame short, moved the frame start, and in debug and sanitizer builds raised `Equal values are not contiguous within the range assumed to be sorted`. ### Description Reachable from ordinary SQL: ```sql SET enable_analyzer = 1; SELECT count() OVER (ORDER BY v COLLATE 'en-u-kn-true' RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) FROM (SELECT arrayJoin(['1', '01', '1', '01']) AS v); ``` Under numeric collation `'1'` and `'01'` are equal, so all four rows are one peer group and every row must report `4`. On master I get `2, 2, 4, 4`, and roughly half the runs of a debug build abort instead. Root cause: the input is sorted by `full_sort_description`, whose `ORDER BY` entries carry the collator, but `WindowTransform` re-derived peer groups with the raw `IColumn::compareAt`. The collated sort may interleave rows that are collation-equal but byte-different, which also violates the contiguity precondition of the equal-range scan, hence the logical error. The fix compares `ORDER BY` keys the same way the input was sorted, at every site that decides peer membership: `arePeers`, two in `advanceFrameEndCurrentRow`, and the `GROUPS` scan in `findPeerGroupEnd`. It uses the same `collator && isCollationSupported()` guard as `LimitTransform`, `FillingTransform` and `SortCursor`. Both equal-range scans share one helper, so `RANGE` and `GROUPS` cannot disagree about what a peer group is. `PARTITION BY` is untouched, since it cannot carry a collator. No new `IColumn` method; uncollated queries keep the existing fast path. `GROUPS` frames landed in master while this was open and were affected the same way. Verified in both directions against pristine master, plus mutants that each disable one part of the fix. The test also covers a peer group spanning blocks. Found by the [AST fuzzer](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113079&sha=1fa1618de2aec34c81676d2bdb999826a8d6fd19&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%2C%20old_compatibility%29) (STID 2508-46a9), but pre-existing: it reproduces on pristine master with queries containing no ranking function. Two adjacent issues I am not fixing here: the old analyzer silently drops `COLLATE` from a window `ORDER BY`, so this only affects `enable_analyzer = 1`; and `PARTITION BY` rejects `COLLATE` outright.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Fix a crash when a spilling join re-enters a HashJoin whose data was released
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a server crash during a JOIN that spills to disk. When an allocation failed while `GraceHashJoin` rehashed its buckets, the in-memory join was left either holding released data or absent altogether, and another build thread could dereference it. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/50220 (closed), the same re-entry as an exception. ### Description Found by `Stress test (amd_msan)`: [CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=81944&sha=fbbf9f1945f2ff9e205acc3a289f64bbaacb8fb6&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_msan%29). `Address: 0x20. Access: read.` on a TPC-DS q27 join with `max_bytes_before_external_join`. That PR touches no join code; the bug is master's. **Root cause.** `HashJoin::addBlockToJoin(const Block &, bool)` calls `materializeColumnsFromRightBlock`, which reads `data->sample_block` one call before its own `if (!data) throw` check, so it dereferences first: `0x20` is that read with `data` null. `releaseJoinedBlocks` resets `data` and only then allocates while extracting blocks, so a throw there exits `addBlockToJoinImpl` before it clears `hash_join`, and `tryConvertSlots` re-enters the released join. **Change.** The check moves ahead of the dereference, which also covers the other release site, `SpillingHashJoin::switchToGraceHashJoin`. In `addBlockToJoinImpl` the join is detached before `releaseJoinedBlocks`, so no throw leaves one reachable. A second, pre-existing state is guarded too: a throw in the re-scatter after `hash_join = nullptr` unwinds the lock with the member null and skips the rebuild, so `getTotalRowCount` and `getTotalByteCount` could already dereference null where `chassert` is compiled out, while the spill scheduler reads them concurrently. That needs a standalone `grace_hash` join, not the trace's route; this change only adds a further way in, a throw in `releaseJoinedBlocks`. Both return `0`. **Validation.** The unit test is replaced by a stateless SQL test, per review. A failpoint arms the throw at the statement that causes the bug, `releaseJoinedBlocks` resetting the data before it finishes allocating, making the crash deterministic through the `grace_hash` rehash path. Verified on a server, arms distinguished by build id: before the fix it dies reading `0x20` in `materializeColumnsFromRightBlock` with the recorded frames; after it, the query reports the injected fault and the server stays up. Reverting the detach-before-release also leaves the test red. It does not pin the hoisted check, since the detach nulls the pointer first, nor reach the count readers, whose scheduler defaults off; covering those from SQL needs a second failpoint and cross-connection pause ordering, which I will add on request. The `grace_hash` and `spilling` stateless tests pass unchanged.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Fix data race and use-after-free on DataLakeConfiguration::current_metadata
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113265 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a data race and a use-after-free on the metadata of a DeltaLake or Iceberg table. Two concurrent queries that read `total_rows` or `total_bytes` from `system.tables` for the same table could have one query replace the table's metadata while the other was still reading it, which could crash the server. Closes #113265. ### Description Two concurrent `SELECT ... FROM system.tables` scans over the same DeltaLake or Iceberg table race on `DataLakeConfiguration::current_metadata`. The field was a plain `std::unique_ptr` with no synchronization, while the configuration is shared: `StorageObjectStorage::totalRows` and `totalBytes` both call the mutating `configuration->update()` and then read the metadata back. TSAN reported the pointer race, but the consequence is worse. The read path was `assertInitialized()` followed by a separate `current_metadata->totalRows(...)` statement, while `update()` destroys the old metadata, so a reader can pass the null check and then call through the freed pointer. A local TSAN repro shows both the race and a heap-use-after-free freed by `~DeltaLakeMetadataDeltaKernel` on that line, and it kills the server. `current_metadata` becomes a `std::shared_ptr` guarded by a mutex, and every reader takes a copy of the pointer under the lock and calls through that copy. Holding a strong reference for the whole call is what closes the use-after-free: guarding only the null check would narrow the window without removing it. Writers build the new metadata outside the lock and publish under it, and the displaced object is destroyed after the lock is released, because `~IcebergMetadata` waits for its background prefetch task. Seven of the eight touched source files are there only because `getExternalMetadata` had to stop returning a raw pointer, so its six consumers keep the metadata alive while they use it. `StorageSystemIcebergFiles` needs that: it parks the pointer across `generate()` calls. The metadata subclasses are unchanged, and all 12 template instantiations are covered because the fix is in the template body. `TSA_GUARDED_BY` under `-Weverything -Werror` makes any remaining unguarded access a build error. Validation: a TSAN repro of 4 concurrent unrestricted `system.tables` scans reports the race 29 times before the fix and 0 after, at identical query counts (48 scans each), and the server survives only with the fix.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Refuse to read Apache Paimon primary-key tables instead of returning superseded rows
signals.text: Refuse to read Apache Paimon primary-key tables instead of returning superseded rows <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113360 (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113360 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reading an Apache Paimon primary-key table now throws `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` instead of silently returning wrong results. Merge-on-read is not implemented, so the reader returned the raw union of the snapshot's data files, including row versions superseded by later upserts. Set `paimon_allow_unmerged_primary_key_reads = 1` (or `compatibility = '26.7'`) to keep reading the files unmerged and accept the incorrect results. Closes [#113360](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113360). ### Description Reading a Paimon primary-key (LSM) table returned stale rows silently: after `INSERT (1,'old'),(2,'two')` then `INSERT (1,'new')`, Spark returns `1 new / 2 two` while `paimonLocal(...)` gave `1 new / 1 old / 2 two`. **Root cause.** All three read modes of `PaimonMetadata::iterate` funnel into `collectDataFilesFromManifests`, whose only data-removing filters are a `seen_files` set keyed on the file *path* and dropping whole `Kind::DELETE` files: no row ordering, no primary-key or sequence-number comparison. An upsert's new file and the old version's are both `ADD` entries, so every row of both is emitted. **The change.** `iterate` now throws when the schema declares primary keys, unless the new session setting `paimon_allow_unmerged_primary_key_reads` (default `false`) is on. It sits above all three mode branches, so one check covers them. Merge-on-read needs per-row key/value/row-kind decoding and merge-engine semantics absent from the tree. The hatch is there because `paimon*()` table functions are ungated, unlike the `Paimon*` engines, so an unconditional refusal would break queries working today; the docs now state the limitation. The guard keys on the primary key, not on table options: a single-commit or compacted table does read correctly today and now throws, but `full-compaction.delta-commits = 1` alone compacts nothing and `deletion-vectors.enabled` alone returned 0 of 2 rows, so neither option identifies the safe case. The check is per query, not the constructor, where a throw breaks `Merge` over a catalog database. **Validation.** New stateless test `04749_paimon_primary_key_unmerged` with a committed two-snapshot fixture (README has the recipe): the default `SELECT` and `count()` throw, the opt-in and `compatibility = '26.7'` both return the raw union, `DESCRIBE` works, an append-only table still reads, 50/50 randomized runs pass. Six mutants: five each redden a different arm, the sixth pins the error code. The hatch restores the previous output byte-for-byte on all 13 shapes I measured.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Add mutation completion time `finish_time` to `system.mutations`
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/89216 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105255 Adds a `finish_time` column to `system.mutations` reporting when a mutation was completed; `0` means the mutation is not finished yet or its completion time is unknown. This is a rework of #105255 that avoids any new persistent state: no mutation-file format changes and no new Keeper znodes, so there is no upgrade path, no cleanup changes, and no retry/idempotency concerns. For non-replicated `MergeTree` tables the value is tracked in memory (like `latest_fail_time`) and stamped only when the completion is observed by the event that caused it: the commit of the last mutated part, or the creation of a mutation that has no parts to process. Mutations whose completion moment was not observed (entries loaded at startup, parts removed by `DROP PARTITION`) report `0` instead of a fabricated timestamp. For `ReplicatedMergeTree` tables the value is per-replica and equals the modification time of the replica's `mutation_pointer` znode — the write that marks mutations done on the replica. After the replica state is reloaded (e.g. server restart), the completion time of the mutation the pointer points at is restored from the znode `mtime`; older completed mutations report `0`. A cluster-wide completion time can be obtained with `max(finish_time)` grouped by `mutation_id` across replicas. Note for the CH Inc sync: `SharedMergeTree` constructs `MergeTreeMutationStatus` positionally and will need a follow-up to populate `finish_time`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a `finish_time` column to `system.mutations` that records when a mutation was completed. Unfinished mutations and mutations whose completion time is unknown report zero. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
signals.author: nikitamikhaylov

signals.title: Rename `allow_experimental_adaptive_codec_selection` to `enable_adaptive_codec_selection`
signals.text: Renames the MergeTree setting `allow_experimental_adaptive_codec_selection` to `enable_adaptive_codec_selection`. The `allow_experimental_` prefix is the pre-tier way of gating a feature. The `EXPERIMENTAL` tier in the declaration already carries that information and is exposed as `tier` in `system.merge_tree_settings`, so the prefix duplicates it in the one place that is expensive to change later: the name. When the feature graduates, a prefixed name has to be renamed and the old spelling carried as an alias forever. That is why the tree already holds `allow_experimental_analyzer` -> `enable_analyzer`, `allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type` -> `enable_nullable_tuple_type` and `allow_experimental_database_iceberg` -> `allow_database_iceberg`. With the tier doing the gating, graduation becomes a one-word change. `enable_` matches the neighbouring MergeTree booleans (`enable_block_number_column`, `enable_block_offset_column`, `enable_mixed_granularity_parts`). **Why this can be a plain rename.** The setting was added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111834 and has not shipped in any release: its `SettingsChangesHistory` entry sits in the unreleased `26.8` block, which this PR updates in place. So there is no alias, no `MAKE_OBSOLETE` and no compatibility entry, and nothing for `compatibility` to revert. The tier stays `EXPERIMENTAL` and the default stays `false`; only the name changes. The autogenerated settings reference pages (`docs/reference/settings/merge-tree-settings/allow-experimental.mdx`, the manifest, the settings explorer and the legacy-route map) still spell the old name. They are generated from a binary's introspection tables by the nightly docs job (`ci/jobs/docs_autogen_nightly.py`), so they are deliberately not hand-edited here and the setting will move to its new group page on the next run. Hand-written prose in `docs/reference/statements/create/table.mdx` is updated. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111834 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required)
signals.author: fm4v

signals.title: Fix missing materialized-CTE gate when a `Merge` table has several children
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113184 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113489 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111194 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113043 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108924 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed the `LOGICAL_ERROR` `Reading from materialized CTE '...' before its materialization completed - DelayedPortsProcessor gate is missing in the query plan` raised when a `Merge` table with more than one child reads a materialized CTE that the outer query references. ### Description `ReadFromMerge::createChildrenPlans` optimizes every child plan on its own, and `resolveMaterializingCTEs` claims a materialized CTE globally through `MaterializedCTE::is_materialization_planned`. The first child plan to be optimized therefore moved the CTE's plan into *its own* tree, and every other `DelayedMaterializingCTEsStep` for that CTE - in the sibling children and in the outer plan - degenerated into a gate-less `MaterializingCTEsStep`. The CTE's writer then sat in one child's pipeline while readers sat in another, with no `DelayedPortsProcessor` between them, so a sibling's in-place `IN`-set build read the storage while it was still empty and `ReadFromMemoryStorageStep` raised the exception (in debug and sanitizer builds it aborts the server). Reproducer on master, deterministic (20/20), also with `max_threads = 1`, and a plain `EXPLAIN` is enough because the set is built during plan optimization: ```sql SET enable_analyzer = 1, enable_materialized_cte = 1; CREATE TABLE t (x UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY x; INSERT INTO t SELECT number FROM numbers(10); CREATE TABLE tdist AS t ENGINE = Distributed(test_shard_localhost, currentDatabase(), t); CREATE VIEW tconst AS SELECT toUInt64(1) AS x; WITH t AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT number AS c FROM numbers(2)) SELECT count() FROM merge(currentDatabase(), '^(tconst|tdist)$') WHERE (x IN (t)) AND (x NOT IN (t)); ``` Children are visited in table-name order, so `tconst` is planned first and claims the CTE, and the `Distributed` child that follows builds the set in place while the CTE is unbuilt. Renaming so the `Distributed` child sorts first makes the same query pass, which is what pins the mechanism. **Fix.** A child plan no longer claims a CTE that the outer query references as well. `removeDelayedMaterializingCTEsStepFor` strips those steps from the child plan before it is optimized, leaving the outer plan - whose `MaterializingCTEsStep` sits above the whole merge - as the single owner that gates every child. This is the same reasoning `DelayedCreatingSetsStep::makePlansForSets` already applies to pre-built `IN`-subquery plans. The set of CTEs to strip comes from walking the outer `query_info.query_tree`, so a CTE defined *inside* one child (a `View` with its own `WITH ... AS MATERIALIZED`) is left owned by that child - it is the only reader, and stripping it unconditionally would leave it with no materialization at all. **Validation.** New `04811_materialized_cte_merge_child_gate` covers the failing child order, the explicit-subquery form, a satisfiable predicate that pins the data rather than only the absence of the exception, the `EXPLAIN` route, the reverse child order that always worked, and the view-owned-CTE case that must keep materializing inside the child. Every failing arm reproduces 5/5 on a master binary and passes 5/5 after the change. The `materialized_cte` suite is green. This is one shape of a recurring family - the same assertion is also reported in #113184 and addressed for other shapes by #113489, #111194 and #113043 - so the underlying `is_materialization_planned` claim being global while the gate is per-plan is worth revisiting separately. It surfaces constantly in the AST fuzzer; found via https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=9d0b1a25ba7aa4579c95a65baca002d1dd7a1e47&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%29

signals.title: Add experimental Wallaby floating-point compression codec
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66467 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110613 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the experimental `Wallaby` lossless compression codec for `Float32` and `Float64` columns: it adaptively picks the cheapest of constant, decimal (Frame-of-Reference or zigzag-delta bit-packing, with PFOR-style patching and ULP-adjustment lanes), or XOR encoding per 1024-value block. Gated behind the `allow_experimental_codecs` setting. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) **Motivation.** This follows the evaluation of the `Chimp` codec proposal (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66467) and of the newer floating-point compression literature: `ALP` (SIGMOD 2024), `Elf` (VLDB 2023), `Camel` (SIGMOD 2025), `Kangaroo` (SIGMOD 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3802076, in production in Alibaba Lindorm since 2024), and the independent evaluation "Beyond Compression" (PVLDB 18(11), 2025). No single family dominates: integerization (`ALP`) wins on decimal-mappable data and decompression speed; the XOR family wins on non-decimal and mixed-precision data; run-length collapse wins on repetitive IoT data. `Wallaby` picks per 1024-value block, and its delta-packing of integerized values exploits time-series smoothness that neither `ALP` (plain Frame-of-Reference) nor the XOR codecs use. **Patent note.** The mantissa-erasure preprocessing shared by `Elf`, `Elf+`, `SElf*` and `Kangaroo` (erasing low mantissa bits derived from the decimal-place count and exponent) is covered by patent US 12,289,120 B2 (Chongqing University, granted 2025-04-29), including the decompression side. `Wallaby` deliberately does not implement it. All building blocks used here are prior art or openly licensed: `Gorilla` XOR (2015), windowed references with an explicit index (Chimp128, VLDB 2022), integerization with FOR bit-packing (`ALP`, MIT-licensed reference, already in ClickHouse as the shared `FFOR` helper), and delta/zigzag/run-length encoding. The encoder-side reference search is three O(1) hash probes, not Kangaroo's LZ-history algorithm; the on-disk format is original. **Decimal-scale chooser.** The decimal scale (`alpha`, now signed) is chosen per vector by measurement, not by a fixed rule: candidates are generated from four sources (the scales of 32 sampled values, with the sample grown up to 256 exactly when a stronger pruning bound would pay for itself; the trailing-decimal-zero structure of the quantized reference, which enumerates scales at which subsets of the vector become exact; the minimal scales of exception values, which discovers a high-precision minority the sample missed; and the exact scales behind tolerant votes, for when a voted scale fails on the rest of the vector), each candidate is evaluated against the full vector, and the smallest measured payload wins. Exceptions are bounded only by a size-based budget — a candidate is abandoned exactly when its exceptions alone already make it larger than the best encoding known for this vector, or when the running width of its packed lanes provably cannot come in under it. Pruning uses only provable bounds (counted sampled failures and failure carry-over from wider scales — never width extrapolation, which can prune true winners), so the chooser never skips a scale that could win. The scale that won the previous vector is evaluated first, and homogeneous vectors stay at a single full pass. **Lane capping, ULP-adjustment lanes, signed scales** (added after reading the pcodec, `ALP`, and FastLanes internals). The packed lane width can be capped below the widest value, exiling outliers into the existing exception list — PFOR-style patching, chosen in closed form from a width histogram for Frame-of-Reference and by an exact chain walk for the delta lanes. Values that integerize only up to a small distance are absorbed by a second bit-packed lane set of zigzag ULP adjustments instead of 10-byte raw exceptions (the idea behind pcodec's `FloatMult`): decimals disturbed by lossy arithmetic — a `Float32` round trip, a unit conversion — no longer force the vector to XOR. The scale is signed as in `ALP`'s `(e, f)` factorization: a negative scale divides by a power of ten, so integers ending in decimal zeros (cents, millisecond timestamps holding whole seconds) pack their cofactors, including magnitudes beyond the `Int64` domain. The XOR window search additionally probes the previous value's lookback distance, which interleaved series keep hitting. Per vector, the candidates compete on the cheaper of the exception list and the adjustment lanes, and only the winner takes one capping pass. These mechanisms are what moved sensors `temperature` −7 %, sensors `pressure` −3 %, weather `tempMax` −2.7 %, and the synthetic `smooth gauge` −11 % against the previous revision of the tables below. **Synthetic benchmarks** (this machine, `clickhouse local`, 10M `Float64` values per dataset, `max_threads = 1`, compressed size after `OPTIMIZE FINAL`; insert is the best of 3 runs, `SELECT` is `sum(x)`, mean of 5 runs; `PCO` is the pcodec Rust crate linked as a codec by #110613, compiled into the same binary, at its default level 8; smallest size and fastest insert / select per row in bold — times are in seconds, lower is better; dataset-specific, not a general claim. The `Chimp` numbers in the previous revision of this description were measured against an older encoder revision and are omitted; the qualitative picture for `Chimp` — robust on non-decimal data, slow to decompress — is unchanged): | Dataset | ZSTD(3) | Gorilla | FPC | ALP | PCO | **Wallaby** | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | sine+2dp noise — size | 33.5 MB | 81.9 MB | 68.7 MB | 22.7 MB | **11.4 MB** | 15.2 MB | | — insert / select, s | 0.45 / 0.098 | 0.93 / 0.092 | 0.80 / 0.079 | 0.32 / **0.019** | 1.01 / 0.079 | **0.31** / 0.024 | | random walk 3dp — size | 32.6 MB | 66.0 MB | 64.1 MB | 20.0 MB | 14.6 MB | **13.9 MB** | | — insert / select, s | 0.41 / 0.085 | **0.15** / 0.081 | **0.15** / 0.075 | 0.30 / **0.018** | 0.95 / 0.061 | 0.31 / 0.024 | | prices 2dp (no smoothness) — size | 41.2 MB | 72.5 MB | 74.7 MB | **25.2 MB** | 25.8 MB | 25.2 MB | | — insert / select, s | 0.46 / 0.104 | 0.17 / 0.085 | **0.15** / 0.082 | 0.32 / **0.019** | 0.85 / 0.056 | 0.43 / 0.025 | | repeats (runs of 100k) — size | **0.06 MB** | 1.3 MB | 5.0 MB | 0.39 MB | 0.07 MB | 0.13 MB | | — insert / select, s | 0.08 / 0.013 | **0.07** / 0.017 | 0.13 / 0.054 | 0.24 / 0.012 | 0.14 / 0.018 | 0.08 / **0.010** | | smooth gauge (full precision) — size | 74.5 MB | 66.6 MB | 54.4 MB | 70.2 MB | **15.5 MB** | 52.0 MB | | — insert / select, s | 0.19 / 0.089 | 0.16 / 0.085 | **0.14** / 0.074 | 0.30 / **0.030** | 1.31 / 0.064 | 1.01 / 0.043 | | real doubles (sin×exp) — size | 78.6 MB | 82.5 MB | 73.9 MB | 80.1 MB | **64.1 MB** | 78.2 MB | | — insert / select, s | 0.21 / 0.090 | 0.17 / 0.091 | **0.15** / 0.078 | 0.38 / **0.021** | 1.11 / 0.065 | 0.79 / 0.123 | | random bits (incompressible) — size | 80.0 MB | 82.5 MB | 85.0 MB | 80.1 MB | **80.0 MB** | 80.0 MB | | — insert / select, s | **0.12** / 0.023 | 0.23 / 0.091 | 0.15 / 0.081 | 0.27 / **0.022** | 0.79 / **0.022** | 0.50 / **0.022** | **Real datasets** (from the [sample datasets](https://clickhouse.com/docs/get-started/sample-datasets): [ClickBench hits](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench), 100M rows — it has no `Float` columns, so representative numeric columns are cast to `Float32`/`Float64`, which is exactly the "floats that are really integers" shape common in practice; [mgbench](https://clickhouse.com/docs/getting-started/example-datasets/brown-benchmark) `logs1` machine metrics, 22M rows, `Nullable(Float32)` as in the reference schema; [environmental sensors](https://clickhouse.com/docs/getting-started/example-datasets/environmental-sensors) 2019-06 BME280, 31.2M rows, `Float32`; [NOAA weather](https://clickhouse.com/docs/getting-started/example-datasets/noaa), 100M rows, tenths stored as `Float32` with 1 decimal). All columns are pre-sorted by the reference schema's `ORDER BY`; compressed size of the column after `OPTIMIZE FINAL`, one binary for all codecs. Best floating-point codec in bold; `ZSTD(3)` shown as the generic-compression baseline: | Column | ZSTD(3) | Gorilla | ALP | PCO | **Wallaby** | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | mgbench `load_one` | 44.5 MB | 86.1 MB | 88.9 MB | **66.8 MB** | 71.1 MB | | mgbench `cpu_user` | 32.0 MB | 75.5 MB | 79.0 MB | **53.8 MB** | 58.0 MB | | mgbench `mem_free` | 48.4 MB | 73.9 MB | 82.5 MB | **53.7 MB** | 65.5 MB | | sensors `temperature` | 74.4 MB | 132.3 MB | 59.6 MB | 64.9 MB | **55.2 MB** | | sensors `humidity` | 80.2 MB | 125.4 MB | 55.7 MB | 82.8 MB | **55.5 MB** | | sensors `pressure` | 99.1 MB | 131.9 MB | 98.1 MB | **79.7 MB** | 95.1 MB | | weather `tempMax` | 29.8 MB | 102.3 MB | 33.9 MB | **24.5 MB** | 29.3 MB | | weather `precipitation` | 56.4 MB | 144.5 MB | 131.9 MB | **33.3 MB** | 72.2 MB | | hits `EventTime` (F64) | 235.6 MB | 244.4 MB | 215.9 MB | **128.1 MB** | 215.9 MB | | hits `ResolutionWidth` | 37.9 MB | 52.5 MB | 141.7 MB | **43.1 MB** | 46.6 MB | | hits `UserID` (F64) | 149.7 MB | 152.4 MB | 684.2 MB | **120.3 MB** | 155.2 MB | Compression / decompression time on the same runs, in seconds — lower is better, best per row in bold (insert best-of-3 / `sum(x)` mean-of-5, `max_threads = 1`; the select column includes the scan-and-sum overhead): | Column | ZSTD(3) | Gorilla | ALP | PCO | **Wallaby** | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | mgbench `load_one` | 0.43 / 0.12 | **0.24** / 0.15 | 0.35 / **0.06** | 0.95 / 0.10 | 2.00 / 0.19 | | mgbench `cpu_user` | 0.39 / 0.10 | **0.22** / 0.14 | 0.33 / **0.05** | 0.79 / 0.10 | 1.66 / 0.16 | | mgbench `mem_free` | 0.37 / 0.13 | **0.24** / 0.15 | 0.26 / **0.05** | 1.05 / 0.10 | 1.46 / 0.16 | | sensors `temperature` | 0.80 / 0.18 | 0.32 / 0.21 | **0.30** / **0.06** | 1.72 / 0.16 | 1.71 / **0.06** | | sensors `humidity` | 0.76 / 0.18 | 0.34 / 0.21 | **0.30** / **0.05** | 1.51 / 0.12 | 1.91 / 0.06 | | sensors `pressure` | 0.42 / 0.15 | 0.33 / 0.21 | **0.31** / **0.06** | 1.65 / 0.11 | 2.49 / 0.07 | | weather `tempMax` | 0.76 / 0.17 | **0.54** / 0.27 | 0.57 / **0.10** | 1.31 / 0.20 | 1.00 / **0.10** | | weather `precipitation` | 1.16 / 0.33 | **0.70** / 0.45 | 1.14 / **0.13** | 3.02 / 0.53 | 2.98 / 0.40 | | hits `EventTime` (F64) | 3.31 / 1.09 | **1.02** / 0.57 | 2.59 / **0.16** | 6.59 / 0.47 | 3.19 / 0.18 | | hits `ResolutionWidth` | 0.94 / 0.28 | **0.60** / 0.34 | 0.91 / **0.12** | 2.32 / 0.34 | 1.70 / 0.31 | | hits `UserID` (F64) | 1.57 / 0.42 | **0.85** / 0.45 | 2.16 / **0.24** | 3.42 / 0.44 | 3.33 / 0.50 | **Encoder cost.** Compared with the previous revision of this table, compression is 1.2–2.8x slower while decompression is unchanged or slightly faster (`smooth gauge` decodes 44 % faster now that a decimal mode wins it instead of XOR). Benchmarking the intermediate revision that contains only the provable-bound chooser rework attributes the cost: on the mgbench and sensors `temperature` columns that rework alone accounts for 60–80 % of the slowdown (`load_one` 0.81 → 1.74 s of the final 2.00 s), while on sensors `pressure` and hits `EventTime` the wider candidate space that the new mechanisms open dominates (1.43 → 2.49 s and 2.15 → 3.19 s). The trade was made knowingly: the size wins above come from the same revisions, and the encoder keeps a running lane-width floor that abandons hopeless scans mid-vector and a double-buffered winner so no scale is quantized twice. **Comparison with PCodec.** `PCO` is the strongest competitor overall. On ratio it is the smallest floating-point codec on 9 of the 11 columns, and the standalone `pco` CLI compressing each column as one chunk does better still (e.g. mgbench `load_one` 36.7 MB, weather `precipitation` 32.2 MB): per-64-KiB-block operation costs pcodec 20-45 % of its ratio, since every block re-learns its tANS tables and delta state. On compression speed the two are now roughly at parity — `Wallaby` up to 2x faster on the hits columns and weather `tempMax`, `PCO` up to 2x faster on the mgbench and sensor columns. On decompression `PCO` is 1.5–2.7x slower than `Wallaby` on the columns where a `Wallaby` decimal mode wins (sensors, weather `tempMax`, hits `EventTime`) and *faster* on the XOR-mode columns (mgbench, hits `UserID`) — the serial XOR bitstream is the slowest of `Wallaby`'s decode paths, while pcodec's decode cost is uniform. Against `ALP`, `Wallaby` is smaller on all 11 columns — dramatically so where `ALP`'s Frame-of-Reference degenerates (hits `UserID` 155 MB vs 684 MB, hits `ResolutionWidth` 47 MB vs 142 MB, weather `precipitation` 72 MB vs 132 MB). A correction to earlier revisions of this description: in-engine `PCO` was previously reported as 10-70x slower. That measurement came from a local build affected by a build-system bug that compiles all vendored Rust code with `opt-level = 0` unless `-DSANITIZE=` is passed explicitly (a `contrib/corrosion-cmake` condition mistakes `SANITIZE=OFF` for an enabled sanitizer; CI is unaffected because it always passes the flag). The numbers above are from a corrected build; a separate fix for the build system is being prepared. **Where `Wallaby` is not the winner.** On columns dominated by entropy redundancy rather than numeric structure — the three mgbench columns, weather `precipitation`, hits `ResolutionWidth`/`UserID` — plain `ZSTD` and/or `PCO` produce smaller data. Chaining helps exactly there, because the XOR/EQUAL residues are more entropy-codable than raw floats: | Column | `ZSTD(3)` | `ALP, ZSTD` | `Wallaby, ZSTD` | |---|---|---|---| | mgbench `load_one` | **44.5 MB** | 56.0 MB | 49.0 MB | | mgbench `cpu_user` | **32.0 MB** | 46.1 MB | 35.6 MB | | mgbench `mem_free` | 48.4 MB | 54.4 MB | **42.4 MB** | | sensors `temperature` | 74.4 MB | 58.2 MB | **54.2 MB** | | sensors `humidity` | 80.2 MB | 55.1 MB | **55.0 MB** | | sensors `pressure` | 99.1 MB | 97.8 MB | **90.1 MB** | | weather `tempMax` | 29.8 MB | 29.2 MB | **27.6 MB** | | weather `precipitation` | 56.4 MB | **54.6 MB** | 65.7 MB | | hits `EventTime` (F64) | 235.6 MB | **212.8 MB** | 213.0 MB | | hits `ResolutionWidth` | **37.9 MB** | 57.8 MB | 43.2 MB | | hits `UserID` (F64) | **149.7 MB** | 192.5 MB | 154.5 MB | `CODEC(Wallaby, ZSTD)` is the best of the three on 5 of the 11 columns — on the sensor columns and weather `tempMax` now by a clear margin where the previous revision tied `ALP, ZSTD` — and within 0.1 % on `EventTime`. The interesting exception is `precipitation`, where `ALP, ZSTD` wins because `ALP`'s plain Frame-of-Reference lanes on zero-dominated data are almost pure zero bytes, which `ZSTD` collapses better than `Wallaby`'s already-compact XOR runs. Side observation from benchmarking (independent of this PR): for `Nullable` columns the null-map substream appears to be stored uncompressed (+1 byte per row for every codec, including `LZ4`/`ZSTD`) — visible as a constant +22 MB / +31.2 MB across all codecs on the mgbench / sensors columns. Worth a separate look. Correctness: bit-exact round trip is verified by the encoder for every value with a per-value raw-exception fallback (`NaN` payloads, infinities, denormals, signed zeros, arbitrary bit patterns are all preserved; verified on random bit patterns and on all real datasets by multiset checksums in tests; the sensors dataset contributes 9298 genuine `NaN` values). The decoder validates all lengths and bounds, so corrupt input causes an exception, not undefined behavior; a decompression fuzzer target is included. An adversarial review of the current revision additionally round-tripped ~15M hostile values (per-block scale flips, `NaN` payloads, subnormals, domain edges) bit-exactly on both float widths. Note on the `NativeFormat` spec: the spec enumerates the column codec method bytes accepted on the `decompress=1` input path, so this PR adds the `0xa0` (`Wallaby`) entry with an experimental-status note, matching the existing `SZ3`/`Quantized`/`ZXC` entries. #### CI Settings (Only check the boxes if you know what you are doing): - [ ] Allow: All Required Checks - [ ] Allow: Stateless tests - [ ] Allow: Stateful tests - [ ] Allow: Integration Tests - [ ] Allow: Performance tests - [ ] Allow: All Builds - [ ] Allow: batch 1, 2 for multi-batch jobs - [ ] Allow: batch 3, 4, 5, 6 for multi-batch jobs --- - [ ] Exclude: Style check - [ ] Exclude: Fast test - [ ] Exclude: All with ASAN - [ ] Exclude: All with TSAN, MSAN, UBSAN, Coverage - [ ] Exclude: All with aarch64, release, debug --- - [ ] Do not test - [ ] Woolen Wolfdog - [ ] Upload binaries for special builds - [ ] Disable merge-commit - [ ] Disable CI cache

signals.title: Reject zero-length PromQL ranges
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Reject zero-length PromQL ranges and explicit zero subquery steps, round positive selector ranges up to the table timestamp precision, and reject unrepresentable explicit subquery steps.** ### Summary Prometheus rejects zero-length range selectors and explicit zero subquery steps. ClickHouse previously accepted them because the parser only checked the duration syntax. The parser now rejects zero and negative range or explicit step values. Positive selector ranges that are finer than the table timestamp precision are rounded up to the next representable tick, while positive explicit subquery steps that are not representable at that precision are rejected. Omitted steps such as `up[5m:]` and positive unit durations such as `up[1ms]` remain valid. Duration-unit exactness is calculated from the original millisecond remainder, so large whole-second durations are not misclassified when a higher-precision representation would overflow. ### Tests Added parser coverage for zero and negative ranges, zero and unrepresentable steps, positive unit and decimal ranges, scientific notation, large durations, ceiling overflow, and omitted steps.
signals.author: fallintoplace

signals.title: Parse PromQL octal numeric literals
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Parse PromQL legacy octal numeric literals with Prometheus-compatible semantics.** ### Summary Prometheus parses integer literals with base 0 before falling back to floating-point parsing. As a result, `0755` and `-0755` are parsed as `493` and `-493`, while values such as `08`, `0759`, `0755.0`, and `0755e1` still use decimal parsing. ClickHouse's PromQL parser previously used decimal parsing for all non-hexadecimal, non-duration numbers, so `0755` was parsed as `755`. This change adds a narrow octal pre-pass for integer-shaped literals. Invalid octal digits, floating-point forms, and integer overflow continue through the existing decimal parser. The behavior follows the Prometheus parser: - [Prometheus number parsing](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/parse.go#L650-L660) - [Prometheus octal parser tests](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/parse_test.go#L109-L136) ### Tests Added parser coverage for: - **Cases:** 0755` and `-0755` - **Cases:** 0_755` - Decimal fallback cases `08`, `0759`, `0755.0`, and `0755e1`
signals.author: fallintoplace

signals.title: Honor an explicit structure argument for data lake table function reads
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113361 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed the `structure` argument of the `paimon*` and `iceberg*` table functions being reported by `DESCRIBE` but ignored by `SELECT`, so one expression yielded two schemas and a declared column absent from the lake metadata failed with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` after `DESCRIBE` had listed it. An explicit `structure` is now used for reads, as it already was for `s3` and `file`, so it can select a subset of the columns or override their types; a declared type the data files cannot supply now raises an error instead of silently using the metadata schema. Inserts, the persistent `Paimon*`/`Iceberg*` engines and `deltaLake*` are unchanged. Closes #113361. ### Description `DESC paimonLocal(p, 'Parquet', 'f_int Int64')` reported `Int64` while `SELECT toTypeName(f_int)` on the same expression reported `Nullable(Int32)`. `icebergLocal` diverged too. The table function was already correct: `getActualTableStructure` parses the argument (what `DESC` reads) and `executeImpl` passes the same columns to the storage. The storage then replaced the whole `StorageInMemoryMetadata`, columns included, whenever the per-format schema reload was enabled, unconditional for Paimon and Iceberg. That happens at five sites, one on every query, so fixing the constructor is not enough. A `preserve_structure_for_reads` flag is now computed in both table function `executeImpl` overrides and retained by both storage classes, set only when a structure was supplied, the query is not an `INSERT`, and the format's schema reload is not a user opt-in. All five reload sites go through one helper that still pins `datalake_table_state` unconditionally and, when the flag is set, keeps the declared columns. The snapshot's sorting key is resolved against the metadata schema, and read-in-order consumes it together with the columns, so once the columns are final the key is kept only while every column its expression reads is still present with the same type. A cluster initiator injects its own resolved columns, which are the snapshot's, so a worker keeps the key; a declared type that retypes or omits a key column clears it everywhere. Deliberately unchanged, each measured: the persistent engines, where a DDL column list creates the remote schema; `INSERT INTO TABLE FUNCTION iceberg*(...)`; `DatabaseDataLake` catalog tables; and `deltaLake*`, whose reload is an opt-in. A conflicting structure now fails in the reader; a subset or compatible override works, as for plain `file`. The new stateless test asserts `DESC` and `SELECT` on one expression: green with the change and red without, with ten live lines and twenty-one controls.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Fix negative subquery timestamp alignment in PromQL
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Align negative PromQL subquery timestamps to the preceding step.** ### Description alignTimestampWithStep currently uses the signed C++ remainder directly. For a negative timestamp that is not divisible by the step, this rounds toward zero instead of down to the previous step. When a subquery offset makes its effective timestamp negative, the evaluation grid can therefore move forward by one step. This change normalizes negative remainders before subtracting them, so timestamps are aligned to the greatest step boundary not greater than the input. ### Tests - PromQL subquery regression using `vector(time())[40s:20s] offset 31s` at outer timestamp 10, which exercises effective timestamps below the Unix epoch. - **Checks:** -m py_compile tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py - **Checks:** --check

signals.title: Skip the custom-key parallel replicas read when the requested stage cannot absorb finalized data
signals.text: <!--- A technical comment, you are free to remove or leave it as it is when PR is created The following categories are used in the next scripts, update them accordingly utils/changelog/changelog.py tests/ci/cancel_and_rerun_workflow_lambda/app.py --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE` and an exception in `GroupingAggregatedTransform` when reading a `Merge` table with one child being a `Distributed` table under custom-key parallel replicas (`parallel_replicas_mode = 'custom_key_sampling'` or `'custom_key_range'`). Closes [#113741](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113741). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes The custom-key parallel replicas branch of the planner replaces the plan of a table expression with a remote read at the fixed stage `WithMergeableStateAfterAggregationAndLimit`, ignoring the stage the plan was requested up to. A `Merge` table over a `Distributed` child plans all of its children up to `WithMergeableState` through an interpreter, so a `MergeTree` child's plan produced finalized (post-aggregation, post-`LIMIT`) data where the parent `ReadFromMerge` expected partial aggregation states: `CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE` for `count`, and the exception `Chunk should have AggregatedChunkInfo/ChunkInfoWithAllocatedBytes in GroupingAggregatedTransform` when the finalized type structurally coincides with the state type. Only the analyzer path is affected. The fix allows the custom-key read only when the requested stage is `Complete` or `WithMergeableStateAfterAggregationAndLimit` itself; a child planned to a partial stage now runs as a plain local read, as it does when parallel replicas are off. Found by the targeted AST fuzzer on https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110972, where it is unrelated: the failure reproduces on master without `parallel_replicas_allow_merge_tables` (verified on a binary with that PR's changes swapped out to the merge base). Fuzzer report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110972&sha=ac0a584ce316ace31f4dbc16b38e1262a2344751&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%2C%20old_compatibility%29 (STID `3970-479a`). Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113741 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110972 <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Backported to: `26.7.4.29`, `26.5.7.52` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Fix PromQL changes for consecutive NaNs
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **PromQL: do not count consecutive NaN samples as changes.** ### Description PromQL changes() compares consecutive samples in a range vector. The ClickHouse implementation used curr != prev, which treats NaN -> NaN as a change because NaN is not equal to itself. Prometheus explicitly treats consecutive NaN samples as unchanged. The time-series summary predicate now follows Prometheus for changes(), while the resets() path remains unchanged. The regression test uses changes(vector(NaN)[80:10]) and expects zero changes. Prometheus documents changes() [here](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#changes), and its implementation [explicitly excludes the NaN -> NaN case](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/functions.go#L2464-L2468). ### Tests - **Checks:** --check - **Checks:** -m py_compile tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py
signals.author: fallintoplace

signals.title: Fix PromQL sgn() for NaN and negative zero
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **PromQL: preserve NaN and negative zero in sgn().** ### Description Prometheus sgn() returns -1 when the sample is less than zero, 1 when it is greater than zero, and the original sample otherwise. The current ClickHouse lowering maps sgn() directly to sign(). For NaN, ClickHouse sign() returns 1, and for negative zero it returns an ordinary zero. The PromQL lowering now mirrors Prometheus with multiIf(x < 0, -1, x > 0, 1, x). The generic ClickHouse sign() function is unchanged. Prometheus documents sgn() [here](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#sgn), and its implementation [returns the original value in the default branch](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/functions.go#L1889-L1900). The regression tests cover sgn(vector(NaN)) and sgn(vector(-0)). ### Tests - **Checks:** --check - **Checks:** -m py_compile tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py

signals.title: Reject STREAM with parallel replicas at plan-build time
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110144 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `LOGICAL_ERROR` when a `SELECT` used the `STREAM` modifier on a named table together with parallel replicas in the read-tasks mode. With a materialized CTE used as an `IN` set in `PREWHERE`, the server raised `Reading from materialized CTE ... DelayedPortsProcessor gate is missing in the query plan` (a server abort in debug and sanitizer builds). A table carrying `STREAM` is now rejected when parallel replicas are requested: at `enable_parallel_replicas = 2` the query fails with `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED`, at `1` it runs without them, exactly as already happens for `FINAL`. ### Description `MergeTreeDataSelectExecutor::read` already refuses `STREAM` with parallel replicas, but its `enable_parallel_reading` argument is `canUseParallelReplicasOnFollower` (`StorageMergeTree.cpp:385`, `StorageReplicatedMergeTree.cpp:6305`), so the refusal only fires on a follower: the initiator builds the plan it should have refused and runs it. `STREAM` also suppresses the eager set build: `ReadFromMergeTree::applyFilters` early-returns for a streaming read (`ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:2593`), and that inplace build is what materializes a CTE, so a materialized CTE used as an `IN` set stays unmaterialized and its ungated `StorageMemory` read raises the error at `ReadFromMemoryStorageStep.cpp:87`. The fix extends the existing `FINAL` check in `Planner::buildPlanForQueryNode` (`Planner.cpp:2306` on master) to `STREAM`. It runs before `buildJoinTreeQueryPlan`, so no storage read is reached, and it clears `allow_experimental_parallel_reading_from_replicas` rather than skipping one branch, covering `parallel_replicas_plan_based` too. For `STREAM` it applies on an initiator only. The enclosing `canUseTaskBasedParallelReplicas` is role-blind, and a follower that cleared the setting here would lose its own read-side refusal, so an old initiator plus a new follower silently did a full local `STREAM` read instead of failing; measured on a two-server cluster at `enable_parallel_replicas = 1`, it now fails with `ILLEGAL_STREAM` as it does on two old servers. `FINAL` keeps its unconditional handling, having no read-side refusal to preserve. Scope, measured: this covers the read-tasks mode on a named table, the reported carrier. The custom-key and sampling-key modes never reach the guard's enclosing `canUseTaskBasedParallelReplicas` branch, and `STREAM` with `parallel_replicas_mode = 'custom_key_sampling'` hangs identically before and after this change; that hang stays open. A `TableFunctionNode` carrying `STREAM` is not covered either. An earlier revision covered both and was reduced on review. #110972 rewrites this same loop; a merge has to keep both sides. Found by the AST fuzzer on #110144

signals.title: Reject window PARTITION BY and ORDER BY over an aggregate function state
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113247 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A window `PARTITION BY` or `ORDER BY` over an `AggregateFunction` column is now rejected with `ILLEGAL_COLUMN`, as top-level `ORDER BY` over such a column already was. Previously such a query was accepted by at least one analyzer, and window `PARTITION BY` partitioned differently depending on `max_threads`. The refusal also covers a state nested in `Array`, `Tuple`, `Map`, `Variant` or `SimpleAggregateFunction`. A `SimpleAggregateFunction` over an ordinary type, `QBit`, and `GROUP BY` and `DISTINCT` over a state, are unaffected. ### Description The two partitioning paths react differently to a state: the sort path calls `ColumnAggregateFunction::compareAt`, a stub returning `0` unconditionally, so all states collapse into one partition, while the scatter path hashes their raw bytes and scatters them. On the reporter's fixture `dense_rank()` gives `1,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8` at `max_threads = 1` and `1,1,2,3,1,4,2,5,6` at `max_threads = 8`. Validation missed it because window `PARTITION BY` routes through `validateGroupByKeyType`, which rejects only `Dynamic` and `Variant`, not through `validateSortingKeyType`, which carries the comparability check. The old analyzer's window `ORDER BY` branch validated no sort-key types at all, so `rank() OVER (ORDER BY st)` over nine distinct states returned nine `1`s there while the analyzer refused it. Both clauses are now guarded in both analyzers; guarding one leaves the other wrong. The predicate is the existing `hasAggregateFunctionType` rather than a comparability predicate, which would also reject `QBit`; control rows pin that for both clauses. It follows a `SimpleAggregateFunction` to its storage type, so `SimpleAggregateFunction(sum, UInt64)` stays accepted while `SimpleAggregateFunction(any, AggregateFunction(uniq, UInt64))` is refused. `GROUP BY` and `DISTINCT` over a state are stable and untouched, so the shared helper is unchanged. No `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` entry is owed, as in PR 105450. Validated on debug builds with each server's `buildId` asserted before any verdict: the test fails on the parent and passes here, 50 randomized and 50 plain runs pass, each mutant is caught only by the rows meant to catch it, and a 162-test window slice has the same deterministic failures on both binaries. <details><summary>Compatibility note on projections</summary> A projection whose SELECT contains `OVER (PARTITION BY <state>)` could be created before this change. A server restart still loads the table and all its rows, dropping the projection from `system.projections` so its parts stop being used. An explicit `ATTACH TABLE` of such a table instead fails with `ILLEGAL_COLUMN` and leaves it detached until the next restart. The merged `Dynamic` and `Variant` equivalent, PR 105450, behaves the same way on master today. No stateless test can pin this, because the fixed binary cannot create the projection the case starts from. The `ORDER BY` half adds nothing here: a projection sorting a window by a state is refused identically before and after. </details> One boundary left for you to rule on, also asked in the issue thread: a state reached through `Dynamic` shows the same instability but is not covered, `Dynamic` exposing no children; it needs `allow_suspicious_types_in_group_by = 1`, whose error text already warns about unexpected results. A state inside `Variant` *is* refused. Both pinned by the test.

signals.title: Support GCS vended credentials in Unity Catalog
signals.text: Unity Catalog on GCS vends an OAuth token in `gcp_oauth_token`, but `UnityCatalog` only parsed AWS temporary credentials for S3-compatible locations. As a result, table metadata could be listed while reads failed because no storage credentials were created. Parse the GCP OAuth token as `GCSCredentials` for both initial credential resolution and refresh. Add focused coverage for GCS parsing and refresh while preserving the existing S3 behavior, and update the user-facing support descriptions. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110149 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support Unity Catalog vended credentials for tables stored in GCS.
