signals.title: Revert "Revert "NATS: add inline credentials setting""
signals.text: Reverts https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114178, restoring the `nats_credentials` setting of the `NATS` table engine (originally added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110733), and fixes the reason of the original revert: the possibility of referencing arbitrary server paths through `nats_credential_file`. `nats_credential_file` is a path on the server filesystem: the server opens it with its own privileges, and during authentication the credentials are sent to `nats_url`, which comes from the same query. So a path taken from SQL lets anyone who can define a `NATS` source probe the local filesystem (the error text distinguishes a missing file, a permission error, and a file without a seed), and exfiltrate files the server can read to a NATS server they control (the part of the file before the seed line is sent verbatim in the `CONNECT` frame's `jwt` field). See the analysis in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110733#discussion_r3750203599. This hole predates #110733 (`nats_credential_file` exists since 24.2), but with the inline `nats_credentials` setting restored, the path form is no longer needed in SQL at all. The restriction, modelled on `StorageMySQL::getSSLParams` (`e700bbec4c84c585`): `nats_credential_file` is accepted only from a named collection defined in the server configuration file, or as `nats.credential_file` in the server configuration itself. Every SQL spelling — the `SETTINGS` clause, an engine-argument override `NATS(collection, nats_credential_file = ...)`, or a named collection created by `CREATE NAMED COLLECTION` — throws `BAD_ARGUMENTS` with a message directing to `nats_credentials`. It is rejected on provenance, whether the query assigned the key at all, rather than on the resulting value, so an override with the empty string cannot silently drop the credentials the operator configured. Loading from previously-validated metadata (server startup, force-restore, and short-syntax `ATTACH`) is exempt via `isLoadingFromExistingMetadata`, so existing tables keep working after an upgrade; a user-issued full `ATTACH TABLE` query is still checked. `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY SETTING` is not a bypass: the `NATS` engine does not support settings alter. Replacing a configured path with inline `nats_credentials` from the query remains allowed — the path itself is not used then — as long as the named collection permits it. Because the contents are the only spelling a query has, `nats_credentials` inherits the override permission of the path key it replaces, the same way `ssl_ca_pem` does for `ssl_ca` in `findOverrideForbiddingKey`: credentials the operator pinned with `<nats_credential_file overridable="false">` cannot be replaced through the contents form either, in either spelling, while the contents form stays usable when `allow_named_collection_override_by_default` is disabled (it is not a new key, it replaces one the collection defines). The `SETTINGS` clause is applied on top of the collection values without passing through the named-collection override check, so `resolveCredentialSource` enforces the same permission for both spellings. An empty `nats_credentials` is refused as well: it can only drop the credentials a collection carries, in either form, never replace them with other ones. Tests: a new stateless test `04891_nats_credential_file_path_restriction` covers all rejected SQL spellings and the accepted configuration-file sources, using `NATS` named collections added to the stateless-test server configuration (`tests/config/config.d/named_collection.xml`, with `nats_url = '127.0.0.1:1'`, so passing the validation surfaces as `CANNOT_CONNECT_NATS`) — one with a plain `nats_credential_file`, one where it is locked with `overridable="false"`, and one without credentials at all; `04665_nats_credentials_named_collection` is updated — the `nats_credential_file` query-override direction is now rejected. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110733 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114178 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/85213 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `NATS` table engine accepts credentials inline in the new `nats_credentials` setting (the same payload as a `.creds` file), and no longer accepts `nats_credential_file` from SQL: the path is a reference to a file on the server filesystem, which the server opens with its own privileges, so it can only be specified in a named collection defined in the server configuration file, or as `nats.credential_file` in the server configuration itself. A query may replace such a configured path with inline `nats_credentials`, unless the operator pinned it with `<nats_credential_file overridable="false">`. Tables created before this restriction keep working after an upgrade.

signals.title: Fix inconsistent AST formatting for a subquery argument of the view table function
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114004 (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114004 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed formatting of a subquery argument of the `view` and `viewIfPermitted` table functions when the enclosing query has a trailing `SETTINGS` clause. Such a query was formatted as `view((SELECT ...))`, which cannot be parsed back, so the query failed the internal format-parse-format check and raised `Inconsistent AST formatting`. ### Description `ASTQueryWithOutput::formatImpl` sets `parent_has_trailing_settings` so an inner `ASTSelectWithUnionQuery` parenthesizes its individual SELECTs, keeping the re-parser from consuming the trailing `SETTINGS` into the last SELECT. The flag is inherited down the format frame, so it also reached the argument of `view` / `viewIfPermitted`. There the parentheses are both redundant and rejected: the closing paren of the table function already terminates the select, and `ViewLayer::parse` bails out on a parenthesized lone select (`ExpressionListParsers.cpp:2981-2991`). The formatted text therefore did not parse back. The trailing `SETTINGS` clause is the trigger. Without it nothing sets the flag and the output is already correct. This clears the flag at the two places that cross the `view` argument boundary, which is what three other boundary owners already do: `ASTSubquery.cpp:98`, `ASTCreateQuery.cpp:1113` and `ASTAlterQuery.cpp:1032`. `ViewLayer` is the only producer of a bare-select function argument and serves exactly these two functions, so the two sites are the complete set. The issue frames parser-versus-formatter as the fork. This takes the formatter side, on the grounds that the parentheses carry no meaning in this position and that the same reset is the established pattern; the parser side would widen the accepted grammar to fix an output bug. The call is his to close. One output change beyond the broken shape: a multi-select argument such as `view(SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT 2)` also loses its branch parentheses. That form parsed before and parses now. Validation: `DESCRIBE TABLE view(SELECT 1) SETTINGS input_format_orc_use_fast_decoder = 0` aborts a debug server with `Logical error: 'Inconsistent AST formatting'` before the change and returns `1 UInt8` after it. The new test fails on the unpatched binary and passes 50/50 under randomized settings on the patched one. The `formatQuery` / round-trip / `1941` stateless family was run on both binaries and the failure sets are byte-identical. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1436` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Record TopK-filtered granules in the query condition cache
signals.text: <!--- A technical comment, you are free to remove or leave it as it is when PR is created The following categories are used in the next scripts, update them accordingly utils/changelog/changelog.py tests/ci/cancel_and_rerun_workflow_lambda/app.py --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Granules fully filtered by the dynamic threshold of an `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` (TopK) read are now recorded in the query condition cache, so repeat runs of such queries skip them at the mark-selection stage instead of re-reading and re-filtering most of the table. On the ClickBench Q24/Q26 shapes (`SELECT SearchPhrase FROM hits WHERE SearchPhrase <> '' ORDER BY EventTime LIMIT 10`), a warm run drops from ~95M rows / ~12000 granules read to ~1.3M rows / ~160 granules, and from ~15–30 ms to ~8 ms on a 96-core machine. The `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` (TopK) optimization pushes a dynamic `__topKFilter` threshold into the `MergeTree` read as a PREWHERE, dropping rows that cannot beat the running top-N. But the granules it emptied were never recorded in the query condition cache: the PREWHERE write path in `MergeTreeSelectProcessor::read` rejects non-deterministic conditions, and `__topKFilter` is one. Only the downstream WHERE `FilterTransform` wrote entries, at whole-chunk granularity, which learns almost nothing (a single surviving row voids the attribution of the whole chunk) — measured on hits, warm runs still selected 11766 of 12348 granules and re-read ~95M of 100M rows. The original out-of-tree build of this optimization (PR #81944, commit `2e2f594308f4` plus the follow-up making the TopN dynamic filters deterministic and reusable for the cache) recorded them and skipped ~98% of granules on warm runs — that is the 2–3x Q24/Q26 gap measured in issue #114639. Recording these granules is sound: for a fixed plan and data, the running threshold only tightens, so a granule none of whose rows survive the filter contains no row that could reach the final top-N, regardless of the threshold trajectory. The entries are keyed with the TopK plan salt (`TopKFilterInfo::condition_hash`: sort column, type, `LIMIT`, direction, `NULLS` direction, collation locale, number of sort columns, and the part-set snapshot), mirroring what the WHERE write path already does since #104478/#110507 — only the same TopK plan over the same part set ever reuses them. Changes: - `isDeterministicAllowingTopKFilter` (two identical static copies in `updateQueryConditionCache.cpp` and `ReadFromMergeTree.cpp`) moved into `VirtualColumnUtils`. - The TopK salt is plumbed to the reader via `MergeTreeReaderSettings::query_condition_cache_top_k_salt`. - The PREWHERE write path accepts a `__topKFilter`-bearing condition when the salt is present, folding the salt into the cache key. Any other non-deterministic condition is still never cached. - The PREWHERE consult path (`filterPartsByQueryConditionCache`) applies the salt exactly when the PREWHERE contains `__topKFilter`, so the keys match the write side; deterministic user PREWHERE conditions keep using plain, unsalted entries shared with non-TopK queries. - `04217_query_condition_cache_topk` and `04242_query_condition_cache_topk_collate` pin exact cache entry counts, which double (each TopK plan now writes a WHERE entry and a PREWHERE entry per part). - New test `04891_query_condition_cache_topk_prewhere_granules` isolates the PREWHERE write path with a WHERE-less TopK query (on current master such a query writes no cache entries at all), asserts that the ASC and DESC plans do not share granule decisions, and that a warm run selects fewer marks. - New performance test `topk_query_condition_cache.xml` with the ClickBench Q24/Q26 shapes over `hits_100m_single`. Measured on the 100M-row single-part ClickBench `hits` (96-core aarch64, hot, interleaved runs): warm Q24/Q26 at 0.007–0.009 s, on par with the original bench-opt build (0.009–0.011 s), against 0.015–0.03 s for current master; warm runs read 159 of 12348 granules against master's 11766. A first run with an empty cache shows no measurable overhead (0.016–0.019 s with the mechanism on and off). Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114639 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110507

signals.title: Stop SeaweedFS deleting live object folders in stateless CI
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113828 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Since 2026-08-12, `s3 storage` stateless jobs intermittently fail an ordinary INSERT with `Code: 499 ... Immediately after upload: Object ... suddenly disappeared (S3_ERROR)`. The object really was destroyed: SeaweedFS's asynchronous empty-folder cleaner counts a folder's entries and then deletes the folder without excluding a PUT arriving in between, so a write landing in that window is lost. From a failing master run's own artifacts: ``` 16:18:17.675651 EmptyFolderCleaner: deleting empty folder /buckets/test/test/jys 16:18:17.676290 PUT of the object SUCCEEDS, 282 bytes 16:18:17.678805 verifying HEAD -> 404 16:18:17.681060 WriteBufferFromS3: Nothing to abort (so ClickHouse did not remove it) ``` This started with #113828, which replaced MinIO with SeaweedFS. ClickHouse keys objects as `<prefix>/<3 chars>/<random>`, so the bucket holds thousands of shallow folders that empty and refill continuously, and that churn arms the race: in one job 34,819 of 45,578 cleaner log lines were deletions, peaking at 3,238 per minute. CIDB has 0 hits in the preceding 180 days, then hits on 2026-08-12 only. I set the filer's empty-folder cleanup delay past any job's lifetime, so no folder becomes eligible for deletion while the suite runs. The cleaner keeps running and keeps queueing; only its eligibility window moves, and the folders persist in an instance destroyed at job end. No `src/` change: `s3_check_objects_after_upload` caught a genuinely destroyed write. Retrying or relaxing it would have hidden a real lost object. Validated against the shipped script, arms differing only by these lines: without the change the cleaner deletes 13 folders and 0 of 12 survive; with it, 0 deletions and 12 of 12 survive while the queue still holds its 12 items past 3m03s, where the baseline drained at 2m03s. The race is upstream's, which already carves `.uploads` out of this same cleaner for the identical reason (`empty_folder_cleaner.go:247`); this only keeps CI out of its way.

signals.title: Allow overriding the HTTP method for SELECT through the url table function and URL engine
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/62352 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `http_method='POST'` — as a key-value argument of the `url` table function and the `URL` table engine, or through the `http_method`/`method` named collection keys — now applies to `SELECT` queries: reads use `POST` instead of the default `GET`, for servers that accept only `POST`. Schema inference follows the configured method. `PUT` keeps its write-only meaning: a `SELECT` through a configuration with `http_method='PUT'` still uses `GET`. ### Implementation notes - `IStorageURLBase::getReadMethod()` now returns `POST` when the configured `http_method` is `POST`. `PUT` still applies to writes only (pre-signed upload URLs, #44326), and `INSERT` behavior is unchanged: `POST` by default, `PUT` when configured. - The write path no longer mutates the shared `http_method` member when defaulting to `POST` — the storage instance is shared between queries, so persisting the write default would have flipped subsequent reads of the same table from `GET` to `POST` (and raced concurrent reads). - Schema inference (`getTableStructureAndFormatFromData` and the URL read-buffer iterator) uses the same effective read method instead of hardcoded `GET`, for both `url()`/`URL` and `urlCluster`. - The `http_method = '...'` (or `method = '...'`) key-value argument is parsed by `StorageURL::evalArgsAndCollectHeaders` alongside `headers(...)`, kept in the `CREATE` AST (so it survives `SHOW CREATE TABLE` and DETACH/ATTACH), validated to be `POST`/`PUT`, and rejected when the URL scheme dispatches to another backend (`file://`, `s3://`, ...), mirroring `headers(...)`. - In the analyzer, the argument's left-hand identifier is excluded from column resolution (`skipAnalysisForArguments`), like `headers(...)`. - Documentation for the `url` table function and the `URL` engine is updated. The new stateless test `04869_url_select_http_method` asserts the method actually used on the wire via `system.query_log.http_method`: default `GET`, `POST` override for both the data and the schema-inference requests, `PUT`-configured `SELECT` staying on `GET`, the `URL` engine path, rejection of unsupported methods, and persistence of the argument in the table DDL. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signals.title: Promote ConstantValue to Core with Field-free value accessors
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113051 --> Continue removing `DB::Field` from constant handling by promoting the owning single-constant type to a shared primitive with `Field`-free value accessors. ### What - **Move `ConstantValue` from `Analyzer/` to `Core/`.** It bundles `{size-1 ColumnConst, DataTypePtr}`. It carries a `DataTypePtr`, and `DataTypes` depends on `Columns`, so `Core` is the correct layer (this also removes a lower layer having to reach up into `Analyzer` for the type). It stays deliberately distinct from `ColumnWithTypeAndName` (size-1 const invariant, no name, scalar accessors). - **Add value accessors** that read row 0 of the size-1 column without materializing a `Field`: `isNull`, `getUInt`, `getInt`, `getFloat64`, `getBool`, `getDataAt`. `ConstantNode` gains matching delegators, and `ConstantNode::getValue` now delegates to a single transitional `ConstantValue::getField`. - **`evaluateConstantExpressionAsColumn` now returns `ConstantValue`** instead of `std::pair<ColumnPtr, DataTypePtr>`. Callers updated: `numbers`/`primes`/`generateSeries`/`values` table functions, `ActionsVisitor`, `InterpreterSelectQuery` (LIMIT/OFFSET), prometheus/timeSeries selectors, and the gtest. The two `getStringConstArgument` helpers now read the value directly via `isNull`/`getDataAt`. ### Behavior No user-visible change: the value is the same size-1 const column with the same exact type, just bundled and readable without a `Field`. `ConstantValue`'s `Field` constructor and `getField` remain as the only `Field` entry/exit while the analyzer still folds constants into `Field`s; a later phase removes them. ### Verification `gtest_convert_column_to_type`, `gtest_evaluate_constant_expression`, and a `numbers`/`generate_series`/`values`/`LIMIT` (integer + fractional)/`IN` stateless spot-check. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113051 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Not for changelog: internal refactor toward removing `DB::Field`; no user-visible behavior change.

signals.title: Stop Parquet background reads before releasing the format's read buffer
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114612 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed heap memory corruption when reading Parquet through an input format that owns its read buffer, for example a dictionary with `SOURCE(FILE(... format 'Parquet'))`. Background prefetch and decode tasks could still read and write through the buffer after the pipeline released it, which could abort the server. ### Description Closes #114612, reported by @ PedroTadim, who asked me to go ahead in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114612#issuecomment-5278451991. A `ReadBuffer` handed to an input format via `addBuffer()` lives in the format's `owned_buffers`. `ISource::work()` calls `onFinish()` on both the clean and the exception path, reaching `IInputFormat::resetReadBuffer()`, which clears `owned_buffers` and destroys the buffer. `ParquetV3BlockInputFormat` did not override that hook, and `Parquet::Prefetcher` holds a non-owning `SeekableReadBuffer *` to the same buffer, so background tasks kept using a destroyed object. It is not only a bad read: the report on the issue is a 1 MiB **write** into freed heap through `ReadBuffer::next()`, silent on a release build. `~Prefetcher()` does the right handshake, but only at format destruction, later than `onFinish()`; that window is the bug. The fix overrides `resetReadBuffer()` to drain background tasks before the base class releases the buffers, mirroring `ParallelParsingInputFormat::onFinish()`. Three details are forced by the surrounding code: the hook is `resetReadBuffer()`, not `onFinish()`, since it frees the buffers and has a second caller in `StreamingFormatExecutor`; the reader is drained but kept alive, because `getMatchedBuckets()` reads row group metadata after exhaustion; and `ReadManager` is drained before `Prefetcher`, because decode tasks re-enter `readSync` inline via `getRangeData()`. Sibling teardown paths: `resetParser()` already destroys the reader before delegating, `onCancel()` cancels it, and the reuse route through `StreamingFormatExecutor` calls `resetParser()` on every exit, so a drained reader is never reused. No fuzzer needed: `ReadBufferFromFile` leaves `use_pread` false, so a local file takes `SeekAndRead`, and any `CREATE DICTIONARY ... SOURCE(FILE(... format 'Parquet'))` whose load throws reaches it. Validated on ASAN: the added test fails 7/7 unfixed, passes 11/11 fixed; a standalone reproducer 31/33 unfixed, 0/35 fixed; a negative control with only the override reverted reddens at the unfixed rate. Parquet and polygon-dictionary suites gave an identical failing set on both binaries (187 each); 50 randomized-settings repeats passed clean. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Backported to: `26.7.4.42` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Do not hold the DDL guard during TRUNCATE
signals.text: `TRUNCATE TABLE` held the table's DDL guard while removing data, and truncate can wait for running merges or for other replicas to process `DROP_RANGE`. Any DDL on that name — including background threads that need it — was blocked for that whole time. Release the guard before `IStorage::truncate` for databases with UUIDs, matching `ALTER TABLE ... DROP PARTITION`, which never took it. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `TRUNCATE TABLE` no longer blocks concurrent `DROP`, `RENAME` and other DDL queries on the same table while the data is being removed.

signals.title: Read a subcolumn of an `ALIAS` parent through a `Merge` table instead of a default
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112975 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix reading a subcolumn (`.size0`, `.null`, a tuple element, `String.size`) through a `Merge` table when the underlying table declares the parent column as `ALIAS`. Such a read returned the type default, and when the parent was selected in the same query it could return the value of an unrelated column. ### Description Selecting `arr.size0` from a `Merge` table returns `0` when the child declares `arr` as an `ALIAS` column, while the same query against the child returns the correct `5`: ```sql CREATE TABLE ag (n UInt64, arr Array(UInt8) ALIAS [1,2,3,4,5]) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO ag (n) VALUES (77); CREATE TABLE mg (arr Array(UInt8), n UInt64) ENGINE = Merge(currentDatabase(), '^ag$'); SELECT arr.size0 FROM mg; -- 0, should be 5 ``` Root cause: `ColumnsDescription::add` registers no subcolumns for an `ALIAS` column, because the value has to be extracted after the expression is evaluated. So `arr.size0` does not resolve against the child, but does against the `Merge` table, where `arr` is ordinary. `ReadFromMerge::getModifiedQueryInfo` reads that as "the child does not have this column": it substitutes a constant default, and its `with_aliases` loop skips the column, so the child is never asked for the data. With the parent also selected, alias expansion put the alias's dependency column in the child read list, and the misaligned read surfaced that value under the subcolumn's name. The analyzer already implements the extract-after-evaluation contract, turning such a name into `getSubcolumn` over the alias expression. This teaches both guards to recognise the case and route it to the existing alias branch with the full identifier, adding no new carrier. Also wrong for `Tuple.a`, `String.size` and `Nullable.null` (a NULL read back as non-NULL), under `optimize_functions_to_subcolumns` 0 and 1, and it mis-scoped a row policy. `Map` subcolumns raise `NO_SUCH_COLUMN_IN_TABLE` before and after. The old analyzer raises `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` and is unchanged, hence the `no-old-analyzer` tag. `MATERIALIZED` and `DEFAULT` parents were already correct, and the default substitution for a child genuinely lacking a column is preserved; both have test arms. A mistyped child (`String ALIAS` under an `Array(UInt8)` Merge column) stays as it is, because `String` has no `size0`. That conversion case is #112975.

signals.title: Precompute hashes and prefetch for fixed-size-keys aggregation methods
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114638 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104475 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): For the `keys32`/`keys64`/`keys128`/`keys256` family of aggregation methods (several fixed-size keys packed into one integer), precompute the per-row canonical hashes in one pass over the batch-packed keys and reuse them to software-prefetch the target bucket and to skip rehashing the key in `emplace`. Previously the look-ahead prefetch computed every key and its hash twice per row. --- This extends the precomputed-hash + prefetch mechanism that #104475 introduced for the `prealloc_serialized` family to `HashMethodKeysFixed` (multi-key `GROUP BY` over numeric columns, e.g. ClickBench Q30/Q31/Q32). When the whole block of keys is batch-packed upfront (`prepared_keys`), the per-row canonical hashes are computed in one pass on the first `emplace`/`find` call and reused both for the look-ahead prefetch and for the insert itself, replacing the generic look-ahead in `Aggregator::executeImplBatch` that builds every key holder and hashes it a second time per row. Details: - The runtime gates mirror `prealloc_serialized`: batch-packed keys available, `enable_software_prefetch_in_aggregation`, and the `min_bytes_for_prefetch` hash-table size threshold (checked lazily on the first call, when `Data` is known). Nullable and low-cardinality variants never use `prepared_keys` and are excluded at compile time. - A new concept `HasPrefetchByHashMemberFunc` compiles the path out for tables without hash-addressed buckets (`FixedHashTable` behind `keys16`). Set, JOIN and `arrayUniq`-style callers of `HashMethodKeysFixed` pass no settings context, so nothing changes for them. - `HashMethodSerializedContext` carried only the settings and is now the shared `HashMethodSettingsContext`, also used by `HashMethodKeysFixed::createContext`. - `HashTable::isEmptyCell` (the `findKey` short-circuit for precomputed hashes, used in the `no_more_keys` mode) is made zero-key-aware: the zero key is stored outside the buffer, so an empty cell at the key's place proves nothing when the zero key is present. The existing user (`prealloc_serialized`) never produces empty keys, so this was latent; an all-zeros fixed key is common (the ClickBench `hits` table has a `SearchEngineID = 0, ClientIP = 0` group). Correctness was verified against an unpatched build of the same commit on the full ClickBench `hits` dataset (identical single part, 99,997,497 rows): full-result checksums for `keys32`/`keys64`/`keys128`/`keys256`, nullable keys and `prealloc_serialized`; the all-zero key group; the `no_more_keys` path (`max_rows_to_group_by` with `group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'`); and external aggregation (spill + merge). All results are identical. An honest note on measured impact, from the investigation written up in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114638#issuecomment-5285053418: in a local interleaved A/B on a (noisy, shared) 96-core aarch64 box, this change measures neutral on ClickBench Q30/Q31/Q35 — the generic look-ahead prefetch already covered these methods, so the remaining saving is one packed-key load plus one CRC per row. The issue's local reproduction numbers for these queries turned out to be dominated by an unrelated effect (the memory-based `max_threads` cap from #100383, which the pre-#100383 baseline build does not have — details in the issue). The perf tests that exercise these exact shapes (`tests/performance/clickbench.xml` Q30/Q31/Q32, `group_by_fixed_keys.xml`, `hash_table_sizes_stats.xml`) should be the arbiter on dedicated hardware.

signals.title: Support aggregate functions in the trivial GROUP BY LIMIT optimization
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114637 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114695 The trivial `GROUP BY ... LIMIT n` optimization (`optimize_trivial_group_by_limit_query`, default `true`) now also fires for projections **with aggregate functions**, e.g. ClickBench Q17 (`SELECT UserID, SearchPhrase, COUNT(*) FROM hits GROUP BY UserID, SearchPhrase LIMIT 10`), while keeping the aggregate values of the returned keys **exact**. **Why it was restricted.** The settings-based rewrite (`max_rows_to_group_by = n + offset` with `group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'`) enforces the cutoff per aggregation stream: a key kept by one stream and rejected by another loses the other stream's rows and comes out of the merge with an undercounted value. Returning an unspecified subset of the groups is fine for `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY`; returning wrong values is not. **How it works now (shared kept keys, zero hot-path cost).** The streams aggregate completely normally until the first one exceeds `n + offset` distinct keys (the pre-existing per-block `checkLimits`). That stream publishes a frozen seed of exactly `n + offset` kept keys with empty aggregate states (`ManyAggregatedData::SharedKeptKeys`); every stream then rebuilds its hash table to exactly that key set — keeping the states it accumulated for the kept keys, dropping the rest — and continues on the pre-existing `no_more_keys` path against a table of `n + offset` keys. Streams that finished consuming before the freeze are rebuilt by the last stream before the merge. Every row before the freeze is aggregated normally and every later row of a kept key finds its key in the rebuilt table, so the merged values are exact; the dropped keys are absent from every rebuilt table and never reach the result. The rebuild reuses the existing two-stage machinery (`convertToChunks(final = false)` + `mergeOnBlock`), so the hot aggregation loops in `Aggregator.cpp` are untouched. **Where it fires.** The cutoff is detected in the planner and enabled only when the node performs the complete aggregation itself (first and second stage): partial states sent to a remote initiator would be merged with other nodes' states, whose kept keys differ, and the values would be undercounted again — across nodes instead of across threads. On the shards of distributed queries and on the replicas of parallel-replicas reading it stays off. The settings-based rewrite of `OptimizeTrivialGroupByLimitPass` remains for aggregate-free projections (it is sound cross-shard). For the 8/16-bit key methods (fixed hash maps bounded by the key space) the cutoff stays inert and the aggregation is complete and exact. External aggregation is disabled when the cutoff is armed (spilled buckets would bypass the restriction); memory stays bounded by roughly `n + offset` keys plus one block of keys per stream. **Guards for wrong results of the existing optimization.** The shape check (shared between the pass and the planner, `getTrivialGroupByLimit`) now also rejects `DISTINCT`, `QUALIFY`, window functions and `arrayJoin` in the projection. These consume or filter the groups after the aggregation, and all four cases were verified to return wrong results on master with the default settings (e.g. `SELECT DISTINCT intDiv(k, 25000) FROM t GROUP BY k LIMIT 3` returned 1 row instead of 3; `SELECT count() OVER () FROM t GROUP BY k LIMIT 5` returned ~100 instead of 100000). Test `04837` pins all four in both the top-level (pass) and subquery (planner) forms. The guards are also submitted separately as the minimal backportable bug fix https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114695 (issue https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114693); whichever merges second needs a trivial conflict resolution. **Measured** on a 96-core aarch64 box, `SELECT number % 100000000 AS k, count() FROM numbers_mt(200000000) GROUP BY k LIMIT 10`: 0.06–0.13 s with the optimization vs 0.37–0.94 s without (interleaved hot runs on a shared machine). The values of the returned keys match the full aggregation exactly (verified by the `04836` join-against-truth tests for `UInt64`/`String`/`LowCardinality`/`Nullable`/two-key shapes, `count`/`sum`/`min`/`max`/`uniqExact`, with `OFFSET`, under single-stream and 16-stream execution, from aggregate projections, and over `remote()`). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The trivial `GROUP BY ... LIMIT n` optimization (setting `optimize_trivial_group_by_limit_query`) now also applies to queries with aggregate functions in the projection, such as ClickBench Q17: once any aggregation thread exceeds `n + offset` distinct keys, all threads are restricted to a single shared set of kept keys, so the hash tables stay small while the aggregate values of the returned keys remain exact (about 2x on ClickBench Q17). Additionally, the optimization no longer fires for queries with `DISTINCT`, `QUALIFY`, window functions, or `arrayJoin` in the projection, where it could return wrong results. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Parallelize single-level to two-level conversion in Aggregator::prepareVariantsToMerge
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114640 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107490 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/pull/1360 When some per-thread aggregation states convert themselves to two-level mid-scan, `Aggregator::prepareVariantsToMerge` converts all the remaining single-level variants **sequentially on one thread**. Initializing a two-level variant allocates and zeroes 256 bucket tables, and there is one variant per query thread, so on machines with many cores this serial loop dominates short aggregation queries. This regime became reachable after #107490: the accurate aggregation memory accounting makes `group_by_two_level_threshold_bytes` (default 50 MB) engage for queries with **few groups but heavy states** (e.g. `uniqExact` over ~300 groups, where the states sum to hundreds of MB while the hash tables stay tiny). Previously the query-tracker delta under-reported such memory (each thread batches up to `max_untracked_memory` before propagating), so the threshold effectively never fired for this shape. Once it fires mid-scan, only the variants that happen to execute a block after the crossing convert themselves (measured: ~25 of 192 on ClickBench Q11), and the merge preparation then serially converts the remaining ~170. Effect on ClickBench (`c7a.metal-48xl`, 192 cores), hot runs, bisected and measured via manual ClickBench dispatches (evidence and result files in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/pull/1360): | build | Q10 | Q11 | |---|---|---| | master `c79b0d9227e` (4 min before #107490) | 0.133 | 0.092 | | master `32129f76fca` (4 min after #107490) | 0.297 | 0.165 | | master 07-11 (`ab8535b3ab0`) | 0.391 | 0.213 | | master 07-11 + `group_by_two_level_threshold_bytes=0` | 0.093 | 0.102 | | pre-#107490 + `group_by_two_level_threshold=1` (uniform early conversion) | 0.132 | 0.095 | The last two rows show the cost is specifically the serial merge-prep conversion after a mid-scan flip: disabling the bytes trigger recovers fully, and uniform early conversion (which happens in parallel, each thread converting its own variant during the scan) is also fast. The daily ClickBench dashboard shows the same regression on both `c7a.metal-48xl` and `c8g.metal-48xl` (192 physical cores) since 2026-07-19, and not on machines with 96 or fewer physical cores. The fix converts the remaining single-level variants in parallel on the aggregator thread pool, following the existing `ThreadPoolCallbackRunnerLocal` pattern used elsewhere in the file. Converting distinct variants concurrently is safe: `AggregatedDataVariants::convertToTwoLevel` touches only the variant's own members. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Parallelize the single-level to two-level conversion of per-thread aggregation states before merging. This fixes a 2-3x regression of short `GROUP BY` queries with heavy aggregate states (e.g. `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)`, ClickBench Q10/Q11) on machines with very many cores, introduced in 26.7 development builds when the aggregation memory accounting was made accurate. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Fix wrong results of the trivial GROUP BY LIMIT optimization with DISTINCT, QUALIFY, window functions or arrayJoin
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114693 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114690 The trivial `GROUP BY ... LIMIT` optimization (`optimize_trivial_group_by_limit_query`, default `true` since 26.5) caps the aggregation at `LIMIT + OFFSET` distinct keys, which is only sound when the LIMIT directly cuts the produced groups. The shape check missed four constructs that consume or filter the groups **between** the aggregation and the LIMIT, and each of them returned wrong results with default settings (verified on master; reproducers in the issue and in the added test): - `DISTINCT` collapses the projected groups: `SELECT DISTINCT intDiv(k, 25000) FROM t GROUP BY k LIMIT 3` returned **1 row instead of 3**. - A window function in the projection is evaluated over all groups (`hasWindow` only catches the named `WINDOW` clause, not an inline `OVER ()`): `SELECT count() OVER () FROM t GROUP BY k LIMIT 5` returned **~100 instead of 100000**. - `arrayJoin` in the projection can drop rows (empty arrays), so the kept groups may produce fewer rows than the LIMIT while more groups exist: **1 row instead of 10**. - `QUALIFY` filters the groups after the aggregation: **0 rows instead of 10** (a `QUALIFY` on plain group keys alone is pushed down below the aggregation and was not affected; a window function in the projection keeps it in place). The pass now skips these shapes. https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114690 contains the same guards as part of a shared shape-check helper; whichever merges second needs a trivial conflict resolution, and this separate pull request keeps the wrong-results fix minimal and backportable on its own. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed wrong results of the trivial `GROUP BY ... LIMIT` optimization (setting `optimize_trivial_group_by_limit_query`) for queries with `DISTINCT`, `QUALIFY`, window functions, or `arrayJoin` in the projection: these consume or filter the groups after the aggregation, so capping the aggregation at `LIMIT + OFFSET` keys could return too few rows or wrong values. The optimization no longer applies to such queries. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Support PromQL histogram_fraction for classic histograms
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **PromQL: support `histogram_fraction()` for classic histograms.** ### Description **What was missing** Prometheus supports `histogram_fraction(lower, upper, b)` for estimating the fraction of observations between two bounds. ClickHouse previously rejected this function in TimeSeries PromQL queries. **What this PR adds** - **Add:** support for classic Prometheus bucket series. - Reuses the existing classic histogram handling used by `histogram_quantile`. - Matches Prometheus behavior for interpolation and bucket edge cases. - Keeps different histogram metric names separate during aggregation. - Removes the input metric name from the result. Example: ```promql histogram_fraction(0.1, 0.5, http_request_duration_seconds_bucket) ``` ### Why this matters **This is used for real latency and SLO queries**, not only parser compatibility. - **Pyrra:** generates `histogram_fraction()` in native-histogram latency SLO rules. See the [query generator](https://github.com/pyrra-dev/pyrra/blob/main/slo/promql.go#L761-L784) and [example SLO config](https://github.com/pyrra-dev/pyrra/blob/main/examples/pyrra-connect-latency.yaml#L14-L20). - **Grafana SLO:** uses it in a [request-latency SLI query](https://grafana.com/docs/plugins/grafana-slo-app/latest/sli-examples/latency/). - **Grafana Mimir:** documents it for calculating the [fraction of requests in a latency range](https://grafana.com/docs/mimir/latest/visualize/native-histograms/). - **Prometheus:** uses it for [fraction and Apdex calculations](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/histograms/). Without this function, PromQL copied from these workflows fails in ClickHouse. ### Scope - **Supported:** classic `*_bucket` histogram series. - **Supported:** constant scalar lower and upper bounds. - **Not supported yet:** native histogram samples. - **Not supported yet:** non-constant bound expressions. Native histogram samples are not supported by the current TimeSeries Engine. This PR intentionally covers the classic bucket form first. ### References - [Prometheus histogram functions](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#histogram_fraction) - [Prometheus classic histogram implementation](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/quantile.go) ### Changes - **Function support:** add `histogram_fraction` to the TimeSeries function registry and support documentation. - **Execution:** add a Prometheus-compatible classic histogram fraction aggregate. - **Shared logic:** reuse the histogram SQL-building pipeline with `histogram_quantile`. - **Precision:** preserve Float64 bound literals for Float32 tables and exact cumulative-count differences for large UInt64 counts. ### Tests - **Interpolation:** normal buckets, `rate()` input, negative bucket bounds, and bounds inside buckets. - **Bucket edges:** exact boundaries, degenerate buckets, `+Inf`, `NaN`, malformed `le`, and out-of-range bounds. - **Grouping:** range queries with multiple histogram groups and `sum by (le)` aggregation. - **Input validation:** invalid argument types and non-constant bounds. - **Float32:** regression coverage for precision near an `le` boundary. - **UInt64:** regression coverage for one-count differences above `2^53`. - **Compliance:** add classic histogram fraction queries to the PromQL compliance cases. - **Checks:** `git diff --check` and Python syntax validation for the integration test files.

signals.title: CI: run the full test suite only when review threads are resolved
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114724 While a PR has unresolved review threads, running the full test suite is a waste: the code is expected to change again once the review comments are addressed. This PR implements the gate requested in the issue: - A new `review_threads.py` pre-hook in the `Config Workflow` counts the PR's unresolved review threads (via GraphQL `reviewThreads`) and stores the state in the workflow kv data. While threads are unresolved, `should_skip_job` runs only builds and the preliminary checks (`Style check`, `Fast test`), plus the `Code Review` job — the AI review keeps re-checking pushed code and resolves its own addressed threads, which is what re-triggers the full suite automatically. - The `can_be_merged.py` post-hook re-checks the live thread state at finish time and turns the `Mergeable Check` red while threads are unresolved, or while only the limited pipeline ran (even if the threads were resolved mid-run — the full suite still has not run). The per-run verdict is recorded in a new `Review Threads` commit status, which doubles as immediate feedback on the PR. This also makes the decision on the AI review's comments once they are ready, as suggested in the issue: comments posted during the run are seen by the finish-time check. - A new `Rerun On Review Threads` workflow detects state changes and re-runs the last completed `PR` workflow run for the current head commit whenever the recorded verdict disagrees with the live state (thread resolved/unresolved, new review comments, the override label added/removed). Previously succeeded jobs are restored from the CI cache, so the re-run only executes the previously skipped jobs. Review-thread events on PRs from forks carry a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`, so they are relayed through a trivial `Review Threads Signal` workflow and handled on its `workflow_run` completion in the trusted default-branch context; `PR` workflow completions are watched too, to catch threads resolved while a run was still in flight. A safety cap (5 attempts per run) prevents any reconciliation bug from re-running one workflow forever. - The gate can be bypassed with the new `ignore-unresolved-threads` label (fetched fresh from the API, so adding the label and re-running works; the label also triggers the re-run automatically). `ci-force-all` bypasses it as well, like all other job filtering. - `retry_infra_failures.yml` learned to not treat a `Finish Workflow` failure caused by this merge gate as an infrastructure failure. - Failure direction: if the thread state cannot be fetched at config time, nothing is skipped (fail toward more testing); at finish time the check fails close (the `Mergeable Check` goes red). The `ignore-unresolved-threads` label has been created in the repository. Documentation: a new `Review threads check` section in `docs/resources/develop-contribute/contribute/continuous-integration.mdx`. Tests: `ci/tests/test_review_threads_gate.py` pins the decision functions and their integration into `should_skip_job` (what is skipped, what keeps running, the merge-gate truth table, the commit-status description budget). ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required)

signals.title: CI: run only the selected tests in the sanitizer functional tests in PRs
signals.text: The sanitizer flavors of `Stateless tests` ran the whole suite in every pull request: 17 jobs for the ASan/UBSan, TSan and MSan builds. Under the assumption in the issue - that the stress tests with sanitizers are a stronger check than a plain functional run - those jobs now run only the tests selected for the change. The new `selected tests` option of `ci/jobs/functional_tests.py` runs an ordinary functional test run over the subset that `Targeting` already computes for the targeted check: the tests the pull request changes, the tests that already failed in this pull request, and the tests covering the changed lines according to the coverage database. Unlike the `targeted` check, it does not rerun that selection many times - it is a plain run with a shorter list of tests. The selection is a few hundred tests, so the batches of the full-suite jobs collapse into a single job per flavor: 17 jobs become 8. What still covers the whole suite in a pull request: the debug and plain binary functional test jobs, and the stress tests, which run the functional tests under every sanitizer with heavy concurrency and randomized settings. The master workflow is unchanged and keeps running the full suite in every flavor. Also in this change: * When the selection cannot be fetched (the coverage database or the GitHub diff is unavailable), the job fails rather than silently run an unbatched, weaker version of the former sanitizer configuration. Retrying restores the intended selected-test run. * Tests the job flavor would never run (`no-parallel` tests in a `parallel` job and vice versa) are dropped from the selection, and the job is skipped when nothing is left for it. * `clickhouse-test` exits with code 1 when every test it was given is filtered out - e.g. all the selected tests are tagged `no-tsan` in a TSan job. For a run over an explicit list of tests (flaky, targeted, `selected tests`) that is now reported as SKIPPED instead of a failure; for a full-suite run it stays a failure, since there it means a broken filter. Unit tests for the new logic are in `ci/tests/test_selected_tests_run.py`. `.github/workflows/pull_request.yml` was regenerated via `python3 -m ci.praktika yaml`. ### Verification in this pull request's own CI This pull request changes no source file and no test under `tests/queries`, so nothing is relevant to select and the new jobs correctly report SKIPPED. To exercise the path that actually runs a subset, commit 85362432c858e0cd9aadbf57f2895888b9d35863 temporarily touched `00001_select_1.sql` (reverted in the following commit). On that commit, with all builds served from the cache: * `Stateless tests (amd_tsan, parallel, selected tests)` and `Stateless tests (amd_asan_ubsan, distributed plan, parallel, selected tests)` ran, and the report shows the three selection passes followed by the single selected test - `00001_select_1 OK 1.01s`. * `Stateless tests (amd_asan_ubsan, db disk, distributed plan, sequential, selected tests)` skipped, because the only changed test is parallel-safe and the flavor filter left it nothing to run. Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114730&sha=85362432c858e0cd9aadbf57f2895888b9d35863&name_0=PR Possible follow-up, not done here: once the test list is short, the job start dominates the run - in the TSan run above, `Start ClickHouse Server` (which prepares the stateful datasets `test.hits`, `test.visits`, TPC-DS and TPC-H) took 324 seconds out of a 418-second job. Skipping the stateful preparation when no stateful test is selected needs a reliable way to tell, so it is left out of this change. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114725 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ...

signals.title: Adaptive lazy execution of short-circuit function arguments (continues #73776)
signals.text: This continues #73776 by @lgbo-ustc, whose branch was ~17 months behind `master` and could no longer be merged mechanically (27 conflicting files in the hottest central code). The author's commits are preserved; on top of them this reconciles the change with the current `master` and reworks the plumbing. Short-circuit evaluation decides *statically* which arguments of `and`, `or`, `if` and `multiIf` are executed lazily. Lazy execution is not free: the rows which are not needed are filtered out and the result is expanded back to the original size. When the filtered out part is small, or the argument itself is cheap, this overhead is larger than the work it saves. This adds an opt-in adaptive mode: the execution of every function is profiled (elapsed time and processed rows), and every 20000 rows the decision is revisited per action - lazy execution is turned off when the estimated cost of the full execution is lower than the measured cost of the lazy execution, and turned back on when the per-row cost of the action grows significantly. Actions whose function can throw an exception on invalid input values (for example `intDiv(1, 0)`) are never switched to eager execution, so the short-circuit protection is preserved. The mode is disabled by default and enabled with the new experimental setting `enable_adaptive_short_circuit_lazy_execution`. Changes on top of the original branch: * The flag no longer travels through `ExpressionStep`/`FilterStep` constructors, the query plan optimizations, the planner and the step serialization. It lives in `ExpressionActionsSettings` next to `enable_lazy_columns_replication`, which removes ~20 files from the change and all the ripple through `QueryPlan/Optimizations`. * `ExpressionActions::execute` and `executeOnColumns` stay `const`; the free `executeAction` became a member with three virtual hooks (`shouldExecuteLazily`, `executeFunction`, `finalizeBlockExecution`) which `AdaptiveExpressionActions` overrides. * The profile plumbing follows the current `IExecutableFunction` chain, including `executeWithoutReplicatedColumns`, which did not exist when the branch was written. * `is_no_except` is computed only when the setting is enabled, so nothing changes for the default path. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental setting `enable_adaptive_short_circuit_lazy_execution`, which enables dynamic evaluation of whether a short-circuit function's argument should be lazily executed. The execution of the functions is profiled at runtime, and the lazy execution of an argument is disabled when it costs more than executing the argument on all the rows. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/73776
signals.author: alexey-milovidov

signals.title: Build Debian packages for the release builds only
signals.text: The `Stress test` was the only job installing the Debian packages of the debug, sanitizer and CFI builds, and it can take the plain `clickhouse` binary instead — that binary is built and uploaded for every build type anyway. Every other consumer of the packages (`Install packages`, `Compatibility check`, `Upgrade check`, the server Docker images and the release jobs) runs on a release build. So the release builds keep their packages, and nine of the eleven packaging steps go away, together with the `DESTDIR` install that copies the whole binary, and the upload and download of the resulting packages. The stress test now sets up the paths the packages own from the binary: `install_binary` in `stress_tests.lib` symlinks `/usr/bin/clickhouse*` at it, installs the default `config.xml` and `users.xml`, and unpacks the self-extracting archive up front — decompressing a sanitizer build under `clickhouse start` would eat into its wait for the pid file and race any concurrent `clickhouse local`. `install_packages` stays for the upgrade check, which installs an actual release. Symbolization is unaffected: `clickhouse_split_debug_symbols` leaves `programs/clickhouse` untouched and strips only the copy it installs, so the binary artifact carries its debug info even for a release build. For the sanitizer builds `clickhouse-common-static-dbg` was empty to begin with, since they do not set `SPLIT_DEBUG_SYMBOLS`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required)

signals.title: Fix a server crash when merging -OrNull/-OrDefault states under group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114690 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a server crash that happens when aggregate states of the `-OrNull` or `-OrDefault` combinators are merged with `group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'` and a non-zero `max_rows_to_group_by`, for example when a query reads through an aggregate projection. ### Description Under `group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'` the aggregator freezes its hash table once `max_rows_to_group_by` is exceeded, and every subsequent row whose key is absent gets the overflow-row pointer. That pointer is `nullptr` whenever `overflow_row` is off, which is the case for any query that is not `GROUP BY ... WITH TOTALS`, so `places[i] == nullptr` is a normal value on the merge path meaning "this key did not fit, skip the row". `Aggregator::mergeStreamsImplCase` states this in an in-source comment and hands the array to `mergeBatch` without filtering. Every batch consumer honours that contract except `AggregateFunctionOrFill::mergeBatch`, which unconditionally dereferenced `places[i]` to OR its trailing "was anything aggregated" flag byte, so a null place became a write through a null pointer. `IAggregateFunctionHelper::mergeBatch` and `AggregateFunctionOrFill::addBatch` already carry the same `if (places[i])` guard; this adds the third and last instance of it. Reproduced on master `bf580ecb357f39df87f814ad214698f2c8aeab17` with a debug build: a `MergeTree` table with an aggregate projection queried with `max_rows_to_group_by = 10, group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'` dies with `Address: 0x8. Access: write` at `AggregateFunctionOrFill.h:258`, for both `-OrNull` and `-OrDefault` and for both the single-number and the fixed-keys aggregation methods. The added test covers those arms plus both `-Tuple`/`-OrNull` nesting orders, and fails (the server dies) without the change. Behaviour changes only for rows the aggregator has already decided to drop, so no query that never trips `max_rows_to_group_by` under mode `any` is affected. Found by the targeted AST fuzzer (`AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted)` and `..., old_compatibility`, STID 2575-398a): https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114690&sha=9b5110134d760b3aace6e8c767073cb51c338233&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%29. The defect is on master and independent of that PR, which only made the path easier to hit.

signals.title: Do not read FINAL merging columns that the output header no longer carries
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/91849 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `LOGICAL_ERROR` ("Unexpected number of kept output positions after removing unused columns from `ReadFromMergeTree`") raised by a `SELECT ... FINAL` whose `PREWHERE` uses a column that `FINAL` needs for merging (`ver`, `is_deleted`, `sign`) and which does not select that column. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/91849 ### Description A `SELECT ... FINAL` whose `PREWHERE` consumes a merging column it does not select fails with `LOGICAL_ERROR: Unexpected number of kept output positions after removing unused columns from ReadFromMergeTree`. `removeUnusedColumns` added back to the read set every `getColumnsRequiredForMergingFinal` column, including ones `PREWHERE` had consumed and the output header no longer carried. `kept_output_positions` is sized from the old header, so the header recomputed from the widened read set was longer and tripped the count assertion. That widening is redundant: `initializePipeline` already appends the sorting-key columns plus `is_deleted`/`sign`/`version` for `FINAL`, and passes `original_column_names` separately so the extras are projected back off. So retain a merging column at analysis time only when the output header has it. The header keeps its size, `kept_output_positions` stays correct, and the assertion is kept. This is option 1 of the two I put to @antaljanosbenjamin above, reached by not widening the read set at all, so no position mapping is rebuilt and no grown root header has to be reconciled. Say so if you would rather the general fix (option 2) land. It also drops the first version's `canRemoveUnusedColumns` exclusion, so pruning now applies where that version declined it. The merge still gets its key columns: `is_deleted` stays in the read set, and every merging mode returns the same deduplicated rows as with `query_plan_remove_unused_columns = 0` on multi-part tables. Test `04906` covers both entry points, four merging modes, the optimizer-moved `PREWHERE`, the two late header rebuilds and duplicate output names, and asserts pruning still applies. Found by the AST fuzzer and the stress test on unrelated pull requests; also reproduces on a plain `FROM t FINAL`. - `AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107305&sha=1a49e7372d0f969cd06d7ba237d8eb3b3461e814&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%29 - `Stress test (arm_asan_ubsan, s3)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108069&sha=77f495e71c33bb2c27441fa12f9deb0fdb7e24f2&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%2C%20s3%29

signals.title: Remove `WINDOW VIEW`
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/61069 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113493 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114097 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/75191 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114738 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/88706 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The experimental `WINDOW VIEW` feature is removed, together with the `WATCH` statement and the `windowID` function. It has been non-functional since version 24.12 (inserts into the source table were silently not delivered to window views) and was never supported by the analyzer, which is enabled by default since 24.3. The settings `allow_experimental_window_view`, `window_view_clean_interval`, `window_view_heartbeat_interval`, and `wait_for_window_view_fire_signal_timeout` are kept as obsolete no-ops. The time-window functions `tumble`, `tumbleStart`, `tumbleEnd`, `hop`, `hopStart`, and `hopEnd` are kept. If you still have window views defined, drop them before upgrading: a server that finds a window view in its metadata fails to start (`Cannot parse definition from metadata file ... (SYNTAX_ERROR)`), the same way the removal of the `Lazy` database engine behaves. Similar functionality will be reimplemented on top of streaming queries (issue [#114738](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114738)). The removal, in detail: - `src/Storages/WindowView/` (`StorageWindowView`, `WindowViewSource`, `StorageBlocks`), `WatermarkTransform`, the `ParserCreateWindowViewQuery` parser, and the whole `WATCH` statement stack (`ParserWatchQuery`, `ASTWatchQuery`, `InterpreterWatchQuery`, the `IStorage::watch` virtual) — window views were the last implementor of `watch`, and the `WATCH` statement was already documented as deprecated. - The `ASTCreateQuery` watermark/lateness fields and their AST JSON serialization and validation. The `clickhouse_json` boundary fails closed rather than silently reinterpreting legacy payloads: `ASTCreateQuery::readJSON` rejects a set `is_window_view`, watermark strategy or `allowed_lateness` flag and the `watermark_function` / `lateness_function` children (otherwise such a payload deserialized as an ordinary `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` and was executed as an immediate-population table create), while `ASTViewTargets::readJSON` rejects the `Inner` target kind, which nothing produces any more and which formatted back to parser-impossible `INNER ENGINE ...` SQL. Both are covered by `04892_ast_json_removed_window_view_state`; the `PushingToWindowViewSink` and `ViewType::WINDOW` branches in `InsertDependenciesBuilder`; window-view special cases in `InterpreterCreateQuery`, `InterpreterInsertQuery`, `StorageFactory`, `DatabaseOrdinary`, `DatabaseReplicated`, `DDLDependencyVisitor`, `QueryFuzzer`, BuzzHouse, and the ArrowFlight table-type mapping. - The `windowID` function and the `UInt32` single-argument forms of `tumbleStart`/`tumbleEnd`/`hopStart`/`hopEnd` (they only accepted `windowID` output). The rest of the time-window function family stays, since these are ordinary functions usable in a regular `GROUP BY` and are exactly the vocabulary for the streaming-queries replacement. - The keywords `WATCH`, `EVENTS`, `ALLOWED_LATENESS`, and `STRICTLY_ASCENDING` (the `WATERMARK` keyword stays: the streaming-queries `WATERMARK FOR` clause uses it), the error code `QUERY_IS_NOT_SUPPORTED_IN_WINDOW_VIEW`, and the corresponding fuzzer dictionary and ANTLR grammar entries. - Kept for compatibility: `QueryViewsLogElement::ViewType::WINDOW` (so existing `system.query_views_log` tables keep their schema) and `ViewTarget::Inner` (so old DDL log entries still parse), following the same pattern as the `LIVE VIEW` removal. - The `allow_experimental_window_view` constraint in `tests/docker_scripts/stress_tests.lib` is kept (only the constraint, not the profile value, which would mark an obsolete setting as changed and add a `system.warnings` entry): the upgrade check runs the previous release's suite under the previous release's binary, whose window-view tests are not dropped afterwards because `--upgrade-check` implies `--fake-drop`, and the leftover metadata would then stop the new server from starting. - Tests: the four remaining window-view tests are removed. The pure time-window-function coverage of `01049_window_view_window_functions` moved to a new `04891_time_window_functions` test, which also pins the new `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` behavior of `tumbleStart(UInt32)`. - Docs: the `Window View` section of `CREATE VIEW`, the `WATCH` page (with its navigation entries and locale twins) are removed and the old-slug redirects retargeted; the window-view entries are removed from the generated settings/functions reference pages (second commit, hence the `pr-autogenerated-docs` label): the `window-view.mdx` settings page, the four settings' entries in the pages/manifest/navigation/settings explorer, and the `windowID` section of `time-window-functions.mdx`. The unrelated drift accumulated on master since the last nightly regeneration is deliberately not included; the nightly docs-autogen job will pick it up. Why now: the feature has been non-functional since Dec 2024 — commit `ceae84c87a2` removed the explicit view-dependency registration and `DDLDependencyVisitor` never extracted the source table of a `CREATE WINDOW VIEW`, so inserts into the source table were silently not pushed to window views, and direct inserts failed with `std::out_of_range` (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113493). Nobody noticed for ~1.5 years. It was never ported to the analyzer (with `enable_analyzer = 1`, the default, existing window views load permanently inert), its tests were removed in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/73822 because they were inherently flaky, and it kept costing triage time (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114097 is a recent server SIGSEGV through `getSourceTableSelectQuery`). The full assessment, including the plan for reimplementing this functionality on top of streaming queries (`SELECT ... FROM t STREAM`, `WATERMARK FOR`, emit-on-watermark windowed aggregation), is in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114738. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Support DEFINER / SQL SECURITY for dictionaries
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/85293 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support `DEFINER` and `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` for dictionaries, like for views. A dictionary with a local `CLICKHOUSE` source can name the user whose privileges its load runs with, instead of storing a user and password in `SOURCE(...)`. Rotating that user's password no longer breaks the dictionary. ### Description A dictionary with a `CLICKHOUSE` source authenticates every load with the credentials in `SOURCE(...)`, so rotating that password breaks all later reloads. A deployment issuing short-lived credentials must embed a long-lived one, or load as `default` with excess authority. Name the identity instead: `DEFINER = dict_owner`, with no `USER`/`PASSWORD` in `SOURCE(...)`. The load then runs with that user's privileges, consults no credential, and is bounded by the definer's settings constraints. It reuses the view definer machinery, inheriting the `SET DEFINER` grant check and the guard against dropping a live definer. `04869_dictionary_definer.sh` covers rotation against a stored-credential control, privilege and settings bounding, `SET DEFINER`, the metadata round trip, every rejection, and locality both ways, each arm mutation-verified. Scoped to a **local** `CLICKHOUSE` source, as @ pufit confirmed on the issue: any other authenticates against a foreign system with credentials a locally resolved identity cannot replace, so the clause is rejected at `CREATE` time. Locality is decided on the effective configuration, resolving named collections and `PORT tcpPort()` first; an unprovable source is rejected too. `DEFINER` is the only accepted type and must name somebody: `INVOKER` because a dictionary loads from a background pool with no invoker, `NONE` because nothing consults the type at load time. A dictionary without the clause is unchanged; `CREATE TABLE ... ENGINE = Dictionary(...) SQL SECURITY ...` keeps failing closed. Three limits come from the shared UUID-keyed definer registry, and each is master's behaviour for views today: an ephemeral `<user>:definer` clone can go uncollected when a `CREATE` is rejected late or the object leaves a UUID-bearing database; drop protection does not apply in `Memory` or `Ordinary` databases; and a `DROP USER` racing a `CREATE` can pass its dependency check before the object registers (over 60 attempts, 21 hits for views on master against 2 for dictionaries here).

signals.title: Do not let a post-run coverage diagnostic discard a finished test run's exit code
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `NightlyCoverage` shards exit 1 after every test has already passed. CIDB gets a pseudo-test row `clickhouse-test` / FAIL whose whole context is `clickhouse-test exited with code 1`, while the report shows the shard `OK` with `Failed: 0`. On master: 83 such rows in 30 days, 26 nights, all 8 shards, 6 of them on one nightly. Cause: `main()`'s post-run coverage block printed one diagnostic line built from two `FINAL` aggregates over `system.coverage_log`, the only two statements in that block outside a `try/except`. `clickhouse_execute` defaults to `timeout=30` and re-raises after 5 retries, and the aggregates sit at that cap: the job's own exporter runs the same aggregate over the same 23.4-25.4M rows in 20-29s. The `TimeoutError` propagates out of `main()`, so `sys.exit(exit_code.value)` never runs and Python exits 1 with every result already collected. That costs a red job for a non-failure, and an exit status that no longer separates a test failure from a teardown timeout. The statement is deleted rather than guarded because in this job it is a vestigial duplicate: `CoverageExporter.do()` re-runs the identical aggregate about 30s later, prints a strict superset of the numbers, and raises when the row count is zero. Nothing reads `cov_rows`/`cov_tests`. A local run drops the export stage, so it loses the line rather than seeing it duplicated. Validated locally: the extracted block exits 1 before the change and 0 after, with negative controls confirming the probe is specific to this timeout. Every remaining `clickhouse_execute` in the post-run block is now guarded (checked by AST). The pre-run block is untouched: it is meant to fail the run when coverage is broken. Two siblings are left alone: `coverage_indirect_calls` is redundant the same way but already guarded, and `reportCoverage` is unguarded but no CI job passes `--report-coverage`. CI report, shard 3/8 of the 2026-08-13 nightly: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=3da3cf323b91553960bdf55780a3b94e9deb5793&name_0=NightlyCoverage&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_llvm_coverage_per_test%2C%20per_test_coverage%2C%203%2F8%29

signals.title: Reject an absurd `kafka_num_consumers` instead of failing an allocation
signals.text: `kafka_disable_num_consumers_limit` lifts the `kafka_num_consumers` limit derived from the number of CPU cores, but nothing else bounded the value. With the setting enabled, a `CREATE TABLE ... ENGINE = Kafka ... kafka_num_consumers = 9223372036854775807` reached `StorageKafka::StorageKafka`, where `consumers.resize(num_consumers)` threw `std::length_error`. That surfaces as `Logical error: 'std::exception. Code: 1001, type: std::length_error, e.what() = vector` (STID 2508-3132) and aborts in the debug build. Found by the AST fuzzer, which randomizes `kafka_disable_num_consumers_limit` and fuzzes the `kafka_num_consumers` literal of `04662_kafka_num_consumers_attach`: - https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=101783&sha=1656dc6761df74e97d13d3fe888a20bd58ce0f57&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%2C%20old_compatibility%29 - Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/101783 A single consumer can read any number of partitions, so an absolute cap of 10000 consumers is now enforced regardless of `kafka_disable_num_consumers_limit`, and an over-large value is rejected with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`. The 1000 consumers used by `04662_kafka_num_consumers_attach` keep working. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Reject an absurdly large `kafka_num_consumers` with a clear error instead of failing an allocation inside the `Kafka` table engine. Previously, with `kafka_disable_num_consumers_limit` enabled, such a value produced a `std::length_error` exception.
