signals.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/series
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ****Prometheus HTTP API:** implement **`/api/v1/series`** for **`TimeSeries`** tables.** ### Why this matters **Prometheus clients** use **`/api/v1/series`** to discover the label sets stored for active series. This endpoint is used by **Prometheus-compatible tools** such as **Grafana** when they need to populate metric and label selectors. ClickHouse **`TimeSeries` tables** can store labels in the main **`tags` Map**, in dedicated columns configured with **`tags_to_columns`**, or in a mixture of both layouts. The endpoint needs to expose the **same logical series** regardless of how those labels are stored. ### Description This PR adds **Prometheus `/api/v1/series` support** for **`TimeSeries` tables**. The endpoint is available through both a **dedicated `/api/v1/series` handler** and the **combined `/api/v1` handler**. It supports **GET requests** and **`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` POST requests**. Supported parameters: - **`match[]`** selects series by metric name and label matchers. Repeated parameters are combined as a **union** and overlapping results are returned only once through **deduplication**. - **`start` and `end`** select series overlapping the requested **time range**. - **`limit`** limits the number of returned series and reports when the response was **truncated**. ### Changes - **Selector parsing:** parse Prometheus series selectors with equality, inequality, regular-expression, and negative regular-expression matchers. - **Storage compatibility:** support metric names, labels in the **`tags` Map**, dedicated tag columns, and mixed rows that use both storage layouts. - **Label normalization:** normalize missing labels to the **Prometheus empty-value semantics** and include the full logical label set in each response. - **PromQL compatibility:** support quoted label names and anchor regular expressions to the **complete label value**. - **Input validation:** validate selectors and timestamps before executing the query. - **Time ranges:** apply the time-range filter when trusted min/max data is available. When it is not available, keep the request valid and return the **compatible candidate superset** allowed by the Prometheus API. - **Result limits:** support zero and positive limits, exact-limit responses, truncation reporting, and invalid-value errors. - **Access control:** read the underlying series metadata through the **`TimeSeries` table-function path** after checking access to the configured **`TimeSeries` table**. Unknown routes are resolved before authorization, so they keep the normal **404 response**. - **Existing endpoints:** apply the configured **`TimeSeries` table access boundary** consistently to the existing Prometheus query endpoints. - **Query lifecycle:** run the generated query through the **normal query pipeline** and keep **query logging** and **query completion handling** intact. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - **Matcher operators:** metric-name and label selectors with all matcher operators. - **Repeated selectors:** repeated **`match[]`** parameters, selector unions, and overlapping-result deduplication. - **Storage layouts:** Map labels, dedicated tag columns, missing labels, mixed carriers, conflicting carriers, and **`__name__`**. - **Regex and names:** quoted label names and whole-value regular-expression anchoring. - **Selector validation:** invalid and unbounded selectors, including the valid **`{host!~".*"}`** case. - **Time ranges:** two-sided, one-sided, inclusive, and invalid time ranges. - **Min/max behavior:** requests with and without trusted min/max metadata. - **Limits:** zero, exact, positive, maximum, and invalid **`limit`** values. - **HTTP methods:** GET and form POST requests. - **Authorization:** wrapper-only **`SELECT` grants**, access checks for all query endpoint families, and unknown-route handling. - **Observability:** query completion records and the existing query API limit behavior. Also ran **Python syntax checks** and **`git diff --check`**. ### Documentation **Documentation is written.** The **TimeSeries engine documentation** now covers the Prometheus handler configuration and the **`/api/v1/series` endpoint parameters**. ### Stack This is the **base PR** for the follow-up Prometheus API endpoints: - **#114868** adds **`/api/v1/labels`**. - **#114869** adds **`/api/v1/label/<name>/values`**.

signals.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/labels
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ****Prometheus HTTP API:** implement **`/api/v1/labels`** for **`TimeSeries`** tables.** ### Why this matters **Prometheus-compatible clients** use **`/api/v1/labels`** to discover the label names available in matching series. This is useful for **Grafana dashboards**, variable pickers, and integrations that need to build label selectors without fetching every series first. The endpoint follows the same **logical label model** as the series endpoint. It reads labels stored in the **`tags` Map** and in dedicated columns configured with **`tags_to_columns`**. ### Description This PR adds **Prometheus `/api/v1/labels` support** for **`TimeSeries` tables**. The endpoint returns a **sorted, distinct list of label names**. It includes **`__name__`** when at least one matching series exists and supports both **unfiltered discovery** and filtering by matching series. Supported parameters: - **`match[]`** filters the series used to build the label-name list. Repeated selectors are combined as a **union**. - **`start` and `end`** restrict the matching series by their **time range**. - **`limit`** limits the returned label names and reports when the response was **truncated**. ### Changes - **Label discovery:** collect distinct names from the canonical metric name, the **`tags` Map**, and configured dedicated tag columns. - **Selector support:** reuse the Prometheus series-selector and matcher behavior from **`/api/v1/series`**. - **Storage compatibility:** support both normal TimeSeries storage and **`tags_to_columns`** layouts while preserving the logical label set. - **Repeated selectors:** combine repeated **`match[]`** parameters without returning duplicate label names. - **Time ranges:** apply trusted min/max bounds when available and keep ranged requests valid with the **approximate superset** behavior allowed by Prometheus when bounds are unavailable. - **Result limits:** support empty, zero, positive, maximum, and invalid **`limit`** values, including the Prometheus truncation warning. - **HTTP handling:** support the dedicated endpoint and the **combined `/api/v1` handler**, with endpoint parameters kept separate from ClickHouse settings. - **Access control:** enforce the configured **`TimeSeries` table authorization boundary** before reading the underlying target tables. - **Query lifecycle:** execute through the **normal query pipeline**, preserve query completion handling, and record the request in **`query_log`**. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - **Label collection:** distinct names, sorted output, **`__name__`**, Map labels, and dedicated columns. - **Selectors:** metric filters, label filters, repeated **`match[]`** unions, and requests with no matching series. - **Time ranges:** matching and non-matching intervals, including empty optional parameters. - **Limits:** truncation warnings and the **`limit`** parameter behavior. - **Authorization:** wrapper-only **`SELECT` grants** on the configured `TimeSeries` table. - **Observability:** successful requests recorded as **`QueryFinish`** entries. - **Shared behavior:** the related Prometheus query and series API regression coverage. Also ran **Python syntax checks**, **XML parsing**, and **`git diff --check`**. ### Documentation **Documentation is written.** The **TimeSeries engine documentation** now describes the `/api/v1/labels` handler and its supported parameters. ### Stack This PR is **stacked on #114867** and includes the **`/api/v1/series`** changes. After **#114867** merges, this branch can be rebased onto `master`.

signals.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/label/<name>/values
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ****Prometheus HTTP API:** implement **`/api/v1/label/<name>/values`** for **`TimeSeries`** tables.** ### Why this matters **Prometheus-compatible clients** use **`/api/v1/label/<name>/values`** to discover the values available for a label. This is used by **Grafana dashboards**, variable pickers, and integrations that need to populate label-value selectors. Prometheus also supports **escaped UTF-8 label names**. The endpoint must decode those names correctly while preserving malformed or intentionally literal values in a predictable way. ### Description This PR adds **Prometheus `/api/v1/label/<name>/values` support** for **`TimeSeries` tables**. The endpoint returns a **sorted, distinct list of values** for one label. It supports metric names through **`__name__`**, labels from the **`tags` Map**, dedicated columns configured with **`tags_to_columns`**, series selectors, time ranges, and result limits. Supported parameters: - **`<name>`** identifies the label whose values should be returned, including Prometheus **`U__...` escaped names**. - **`match[]`** filters the series contributing values. - **`start` and `end`** restrict the matching series by their **time range**. - **`limit`** limits the returned values and reports when the response was **truncated**. ### Changes - **Value discovery:** return distinct values for ordinary labels and the special **`__name__`** metric-name label. - **Storage compatibility:** read values from the **`tags` Map** and dedicated **`tags_to_columns`** columns using the same logical label semantics as the other metadata endpoints. - **Name decoding:** decode valid Prometheus escaped label names, preserve malformed or overlong escape sequences as literal names, and reject an empty decoded label name. - **Selector support:** filter values by metric and series selectors, including unknown-label and no-match cases. - **Time ranges:** apply trusted min/max bounds when available and keep ranged requests valid with the **approximate superset** behavior allowed by Prometheus when bounds are unavailable. - **Result limits:** support empty, zero, positive, maximum, and invalid **`limit`** values, including the Prometheus truncation warning. - **HTTP handling:** add the label-values route to the **combined `/api/v1` handler** and keep endpoint parameters separate from ClickHouse settings. - **Access control:** enforce the configured **`TimeSeries` table authorization boundary** before reading the underlying target tables. - **Query lifecycle:** execute through the **normal query pipeline**, preserve query completion handling, and record the request in **`query_log`**. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - **Metric names:** values returned through **`__name__`**. - **Label values:** distinct Map values and values from configured dedicated columns. - **Escaped names:** valid UTF-8 decoding, malformed escape sequences, overlong escapes, and empty decoded names. - **Filtering:** selectors, unknown labels, and requests with no matching series. - **Time ranges:** matching and non-matching intervals, including empty optional parameters. - **Limits:** truncation warnings and the maximum valid **UInt64** limit. - **Authorization:** wrapper-only **`SELECT` grants** on the configured `TimeSeries` table. - **HTTP integration:** the main HTTP port, routing, and query completion records. Also ran **Python syntax checks**, **XML parsing**, and **`git diff --check`**. ### Documentation **Documentation is written.** The **TimeSeries engine documentation** now describes the label-values handler, escaped label names, and its supported parameters. ### Stack This PR is **stacked on #114867** and includes the **`/api/v1/series`** changes. After **#114867** merges, this branch can be rebased onto `master`.

signals.title: Sync BACKUP FROM SNAPSHOT settings and failpoints
signals.text: `BACKUP FROM SNAPSHOT` is already parsed in this repository (`ParserBackupQuery`, `ASTBackupQuery`), but the settings and failpoints of its **resumable** mode existed only in the Cloud repository. As a result the two settings surfaces and failpoint registries had drifted apart, and the shared files conflicted on every sync. This declares them here, and says plainly in each place that the feature behind them is available in ClickHouse Cloud only: - `resumable_backup_from_snapshot` — experimental session setting. - `resumable_backup_batch_size` and `resumable_backup_batch_size_bytes` — backup-query settings bounding how much work a failed attempt replays. - the `backup_from_snapshot_*` failpoints the feature's tests inject. Nothing in this repository reads the batch limits or injects the failpoints. The declarations exist so that both builds accept and reject the same queries, and so these shared files stop conflicting on every sync. `fromBackupQuery` still rejects a zero batch limit, keeping that validation identical in both builds. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-private/pull/67265 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ...

signals.title: Don't use JSON skip indexes for combined literal+sub-object subcolumns
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107039 --> `tryMatchJSONSubcolumnToIndex` rejected the sub-object prefix `^`, but not the combined prefix `@`, so ``json.@`a`` was matched against a `JSONAllPaths` index as a path literally named `` @`a` ``. No granule contains such a path, so all granules were pruned: ```sql SELECT count() FROM t WHERE isNotNull(json.`@\`a\``); -- 0, wrong SELECT count() FROM t WHERE isNotNull(json.`@\`a\``) SETTINGS use_skip_indexes=0; -- 2 ``` Reject the `@` prefix as well. Both prefixes are now recognised as the prefix character followed by a back-quote (the rule `tryGetPrefixedSubcolumn` uses), so ordinary paths like `` json.`@timestamp` `` keep using the index. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results when a filter on a combined literal+sub-object `JSON` subcolumn (``json.@`a``) was analyzed against a `JSONAllPaths` skip index: the subcolumn was treated as a path literally named `` @`a` ``, so all granules were skipped and the query returned fewer rows than it should. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signals.title: Follow-ups for CREATE HANDLER: parse limits of the stored query, docs, refactoring
signals.text: Follow-ups from https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106231 (`CREATE HANDLER`). Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106231 **Requested in review of #106231:** - The two predicates over `IAST::QueryKind` that describe the `readonly` mode - whether a query of that kind is rejected under it, and whether `readonly = 2` still lets it produce side effects - moved out of `SQLDefinedHandlerFromAST` into `Interpreters/QueryKindUnderReadonly.h`; `queryKindRequiresMutatingMethod` is renamed to `isQueryKindRejectedUnderReadonly` after the property it reports. The handler code keeps the statement-level refinements and the HTTP-method fences. - `currentHandler` and `currentRequestURL` were registered with `IntroducedIn` 26.6 (the development version when they were written); they are released in 26.8. **The one unresolved review finding:** a request could still lower the parse limits of a handler's query. `HTTPHandler::processQuery` relaxed `max_parser_depth` / `max_parser_backtracks` *before* applying the settings the request supplies, and a request names settings freely - so `GET /h?max_parser_depth=1` put the caller's value back and broke a handler the server itself had accepted. The relaxation now happens after the request settings. `max_query_size` had the same hole and did not even need a hostile request: a stored query longer than its default value is creatable and reloadable (both parse without a size limit) but failed on every invocation; it is now raised to fit the query text - not disabled, because `executeQuery` also uses `max_query_size` to decide how much of the request stream to read ahead in search of the query text, where `0` would make it read a single byte. New tests `04897_handler_request_parser_limits` and `04898_handler_large_query_invocation`, both verified to fail without the fix. **Documentation:** the `CREATE HANDLER` page was written into `docs/en/sql-reference/statements/create/handler.md` - a path in the legacy Docusaurus tree that `9440ca729a3` had already removed - so the only documentation of `CREATE HANDLER` / `ALTER HANDLER` / `DROP HANDLER` was published nowhere. It moves to `docs/reference/statements/create/handler.mdx`, with the frontmatter and internal links converted to that tree's conventions and the page registered in `docs/reference/navigation.json`. `docs/en/operations/system-tables/handlers.md` was a leftover copy of the generated `docs/reference/system-tables/handlers.mdx` whose hand-written `SHOW HANDLERS` / secret-masking paragraph had been lost; that paragraph is restored and the legacy copy deleted. The statement is now cross-referenced from the HTTP interface page, the `DROP` page and the `ALTER` overview, and the anchored (`RE2::FullMatch`) semantics of `URL REGEXP` are documented. Verified locally: all 30 SQL-defined-handler stateless tests pass against a server built from this branch (the 31st match of the `handler` filter, `03354_tcp_handler_async_insert_bug`, is unrelated and needs a writable `/var/lib/clickhouse/user_files`), and `04844_handler_deep_query_invocation` still passes without the fix, confirming it covered only the session-level limit. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Documentation (changelog entry is not required)

signals.title: Keep parent `ThreadGroup` alive for child counters
signals.text: Child `ThreadGroup` objects connect their memory and profile counters to parent counters through raw pointers, but did not retain ownership of the parent group. Asynchronous child work could therefore outlive its parent and access destroyed counters. Retain the parent until all child counters have been destroyed. The same CI report exposed that `04726_kill_undrop_table_busy_wait` runs with a `Replicated` database even though `UNDROP TABLE` is unsupported there. Mark the test accordingly so this configuration skips it. The full release `clickhouse` target builds successfully. CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=432b1ae96183f5b085835f4b0aece8d95ce9ce73&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_llvm_coverage%2C%20old%20analyzer%2C%20s3%20storage%2C%20DBReplicated%2C%20WasmEdge%2C%20parallel%2C%202%2F3%29&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_llvm_coverage%2C%20old%20analyzer%2C%20s3%20storage%2C%20DBReplicated%2C%20WasmEdge%2C%20parallel%2C%202%2F3%29 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a segmentation fault in asynchronous work when a child `ThreadGroup` outlives its parent and accesses destroyed memory or profile counters.

signals.title: AI functions: Make quotas per query not per block
signals.text: `AIQuotaTracker` was a stack local inside `executeImpl`, so every block and every pipeline stream started with a fresh allowance. The `ai_function_max_api_calls_per_query`, `ai_function_max_input_tokens_per_query` and `ai_function_max_output_tokens_per_query` limits therefore scaled with the data (one allowance per block per function) instead of bounding the query — any limit above the largest block's row count could never fire. The tracker is now a single instance owned by the query `Context` and shared by every AI function call in the query, with atomic counters for the concurrent pipeline threads. The limits now bound the whole query, as their names and documentation state. NOTE: The design decision was made to enforce the quota per-query (one query may have multiple AI function calls) not per-function-call. Enforcing per function call is also possible, but I decided that it doesn't make as much sense especially considering the setting names and the [documentation as currently written](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/settings/session-settings/ai-function#ai_function_max_input_tokens_per_query). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The AI-function quota settings (`ai_function_max_api_calls_per_query`, `ai_function_max_input_tokens_per_query`, `ai_function_max_output_tokens_per_query`) were enforced per block rather than per query, letting a query exceed the configured limit in proportion to the number of blocks and threads processed. They now bound the whole query.

signals.title: Cheaper per-sample add path in timeSeries*ToGrid aggregate functions
signals.text: The `timeSeries*ToGrid` aggregate functions pay a fixed cost for every incoming sample in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesBase`: computing the grid bucket index and looking the bucket up in a hash map. This PR makes both cheaper: - **Int64 fast path for the bucket-index computation.** `bucketIndexForTimestamp` used Int128 division and modulo per sample to stay overflow-safe for adversarial grid parameters. Now, when all grid parameters are bounded by 2^61 (checked once in the constructor; covers every practical case), the per-sample computation runs in plain Int64 arithmetic, dividing by the fixed `step` through a precomputed `libdivide` reciprocal — the `__udivmodti4` calls disappear from query profiles. The Int128 path is kept as-is for out-of-range parameters and single-point grids (`start == end`). - **Cached last-bucket pointer in the batch add loops.** Samples arrive sorted by timestamp within a series, so consecutive samples usually land in the same bucket; the loops now reuse the last bucket pointer and skip the hash-map lookup for same-bucket runs. Inserting into the map can invalidate the cached pointer, but an insert happens only on a bucket change, which re-acquires the pointer. Measured on tsbench, a PromQL benchmark over the ClickHouse `TimeSeries` engine (30 days of scrape data at 15 s step; scale 1 = 1.06 billion samples / 6112 series, Ryzen 9950X, query result cache disabled, best of 3): on a 30-day PromQL `rate` query scanning 69M samples, the per-sample Int128 division (`__udivmodti4`) was ~2% of CPU and the bucket-index computation ~3% — both disappear from the profile with the Int64 fast path; the whole rate-aggregation add path went from ~12% to ~8% of the query. A new performance test `tests/performance/timeseries_to_grid_scalar_add.xml` targets exactly this path: dense scalar samples (40M rows, 200 series, one sample per 15 s) aggregated with `step` = `window` = 300 s, so every in-range sample contributes to exactly one bucket and ~20 consecutive samples land in the same bucket. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up the `timeSeries*ToGrid` aggregate functions: per-sample bucket math now avoids Int128 division, and consecutive samples in the same bucket skip the hash-map lookup.

signals.title: Add a userspace page cache tier to the experimental ReaderExecutor
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103706 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/102282 Next incremental slice of the experimental `ReaderExecutor` (split of #103706), following the merged disk-cache provider #110029. Adds the userspace page (memory) cache tier: `PageCacheProvider` implements `ICacheProvider` over `PageCache` with zero-copy hits (the arena is pinned by a shared_ptr) and whole-block first-writer-wins fills via `PageCache::getOrSet`. `ReadPipeline` wires it as the first (fastest) tier of the executor cache chain when the page cache applies, and skips it on unknown-size sources. `ReadPipeline.cpp` is the only non-verbatim file; the provider and its gtest are ports from #103706. Gated by `use_reader_executor` (default off); the legacy read path is unchanged. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a userspace page cache tier to the experimental `ReaderExecutor` read path (`use_reader_executor`, off by default). signals.title: Do not abort the server when a loader worker cannot be spawned
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110174 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a server abort that happens when the global thread pool is momentarily saturated while tables are still loading. `AsyncLoader` now keeps running if it cannot spawn an extra loader worker and some worker will still drain the queued jobs, instead of calling `std::terminate`. ### Description `AsyncLoader::spawn` wrapped `scheduleOrThrowOnError` in `NOEXCEPT_SCOPE`, whose handler is unconditionally `std::terminate()`. A transient `CANNOT_SCHEDULE_TASK` from a saturated global thread pool therefore killed the server (`Received signal 6`) during table loading. Seen 4 times over 4 unrelated PRs and 4 build flavours in 30 days, e.g. [`Stress test (amd_tsan)`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114564&sha=899ae2ae7159a25243f5ecdfd16ef059e2941366&name_0=BackportPR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_tsan%29), whose `fatal.log` has `no free thread (threads=10000, jobs=10000)`. A spawn only has to succeed when nothing else will drain the pool's ready queue, so it now tells three states apart: - a worker that has entered `worker()` and is not inside `wait()` drains the queue now; - a worker inside `wait()` for a job of *another* pool resumes draining once that pool runs the awaited job; - neither of those means nobody ever will. In the first two cases `spawn` uses the non-throwing `trySchedule`, rolls back its `Pool::workers` increment on failure, warns and returns false. Only the last case keeps the fatal path, byte for byte: the queued jobs would be stranded, and throwing is not an option because `schedule` marks that region non-exception-safe. Covering it needs rollback-and-retry across the loading DAG, out of scope here. All 4 observed rows are recoverable. `BackgroundSchedulePool` narrows the same way (`929227464f9736b`). Two counters are added because `Pool::workers` also counts a worker still queued in the global pool, which drains nothing, and one blocked in `wait()`, which cannot take a job from its own pool's queue. A saturated pool is remembered so the failing thread creation happens once per episode rather than once per queued job, counted by the new `AsyncLoaderSpawnFailures` event; entering `wait()` clears that memo. Tests are gtests asserting which branch was taken, not just that the process survived. A SQL test cannot reach the line, since on master the whole call sits under `blockFaultInjections()`. Related: #110174, which removed the mask that hid this exception.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: TimeSeries: compare consecutive ids via raw columns in getGroupByID
signals.text: The function `timeSeriesIdToGroup` maps time-series ids to per-query group indexes and runs on every scanned row of every transpiled PromQL selector. Its implementation, `ContextTimeSeriesTagsCollector::getGroupByID`, has a fast path for sorted id streams: since samples arrive sorted by id (long runs of equal values), each row is first compared with the previous one, and on equality the previous row's group is reused. That per-row equality check went through a virtual `compareAt` chain (`ColumnTuple` and its two nested columns). This PR makes the fast path compare the raw column data directly for the standard id type `Tuple(UInt64, UUID)`: two integer comparisons per row instead of three virtual calls. Other id types keep the generic `compareAt` path. The standard id type now has a single definition, `standardTimeSeriesIDDataType` in `normalizeTimeSeriesDefinition` (also used where the default id type is resolved); the column check matches against it structurally and asserts the extraction, so a future change of the standard id type cannot silently bypass or desynchronize the fast path. Measured on tsbench, a PromQL benchmark over the ClickHouse `TimeSeries` engine (30 days of scrape data at 15s step; scale 1 = 1.06 billion samples / 6112 series on a Ryzen 9950X, query result cache disabled, best of 3): on a 30-day `rate` query scanning 69M rows, the virtual `compareAt` chain took 10-12% of CPU, reduced to ~4.5% with raw comparisons. The new performance test `tests/performance/timeseries_id_to_group.xml` targets exactly this path: a 40M-row sorted stream of `Tuple(UInt64, UUID)` ids in runs of 20000 equal values flows through `timeSeriesIdToGroup`, with the tags collector populated by `timeSeriesStoreTags` in an `IN` subquery, mirroring the shape of transpiled PromQL selectors. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up PromQL queries over `TimeSeries` tables: comparing consecutive time-series ids in `timeSeriesIdToGroup` now uses raw column data instead of virtual per-row comparisons.

signals.title: Fix AI functions embedding counters behavior on error
signals.text: `aiEmbed` and `aiSimilarity` under-report provider usage in `system.query_log` when a request fails: with the default `ai_function_throw_on_error = 1` the exception row shows `AIAPICalls = 0` and `AIInputTokens = 0`, although the provider was called and billed. Flipping only that setting records the call: | `ai_function_throw_on_error` | `AIAPICalls` | `AIRowsSkipped` | |---|---:|---:| | `1` (default) | 0 | 0 | | `0` | 1 | 1 | Same query and endpoint, with `ai_function_max_retries = 0` so exactly one attempt is made. **Cause.** `embedTexts` accumulates the counters in a local `EmbeddingResult` and returns it by value. When a failed request rethrows, `return` is never reached: the local is destroyed while unwinding and the caller's `embedding_result` is never constructed, so the caller's `ProfileEvents::increment` calls are both skipped and left with nothing to read. That defeats the intent stated at the accumulation site, which counts `api_calls` *before* issuing the request so that failed calls are still counted. **Fix.** `embedTexts` now reports `AIAPICalls` and `AIInputTokens` itself, from a `SCOPE_EXIT` guard, so the normal and throwing exits both publish them. They are plain locals rather than fields of `EmbeddingResult`, so no caller can count them twice. Callers keep their own row counters, which mean different things: texts for `aiEmbed`, pairs of texts for `aiSimilarity`. **Not covered.** Row counters are still dropped when the query throws. It delivered no rows, and preserving them would need `embedTexts` to take an out-parameter in both callers. **Tests.** Three integration tests, each verified to fail with the source reverted to `master`: one per caller for `AIAPICalls`, plus one driving the quota-exceeded throw so a batch succeeds first and `AIInputTokens` is non-zero. The failed-request tests cannot cover `AIInputTokens`, since there the first request fails and no tokens are consumed. The same defect on the text-generation path is fixed in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111830, which is what introduced a throwing path there. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111830 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `aiEmbed` and `aiSimilarity` reporting zero `AIAPICalls` and `AIInputTokens` in `system.query_log` when a provider request failed, despite the request having been made and billed.

signals.title: Scope WITH aliases to the SELECT that declares them when adding the default database
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104972 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104972 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed table names not being qualified with the default database when a `WITH` alias elsewhere in the same query happened to share the name. `ALTER TABLE other_db.t UPDATE v = (WITH RECURSIVE src AS (SELECT 7 AS id) SELECT max(id) FROM src) + (SELECT max(id) FROM src)` failed with `UNKNOWN_DATABASE`, the same expression through `UPDATE ... SET` silently read the session's `src` instead of `other_db.src`, and a view whose `UNION` branch referenced such a table could not be read from another database. Closes #104972. ### Description `AddDefaultDatabaseVisitor` records `WITH RECURSIVE` aliases and consults that record to avoid qualifying a name that is a CTE rather than a table. The record was one set shared by the whole visitor instance, with no `erase` or `clear` call site, so an alias declared inside one `SELECT` kept suppressing qualification for every identifier seen afterwards, including a genuine physical table. The leak is forward-only: a colliding name before the CTE is fine. The set becomes a stack of scopes, one pushed per `ASTSelectQuery` and popped by a destructor, so a `SELECT`'s subtree inherits the enclosing aliases and nothing outside it does. Lookups walk it innermost-first. Three cases follow: - The `WITH` list is now walked in the non-recursive case too. A recursive alias is registered before its element is visited, since it may reference itself; a plain alias after, so inside its own definition the name still denotes a table. This mirrors `ApplyWithSubqueryVisitor`, and it matters because `ApplyWithGlobalVisitor` copies a first branch's `WITH` list into later `UNION` branches without the `RECURSIVE` flag. - Enclosing scopes are searched for a plain name only when `enable_global_with_statement` is set, matching the resolver: `InterpreterSelectQuery` skips `ApplyWithAliasVisitor` without it, and the analyzer clears `allow_to_check_cte` for parent scopes. A recursive name is searched unconditionally, since its self-reference resolves inside its own definition, before that gate applies. - `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY QUERY` and `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` expand a plain CTE reference into a copy of its body first. Inside that copy the name denotes a table, so that binding is masked. Fixing the visitor covers all 13 construction sites at once. Validated on 34 arms: 11 fail on master and pass here, 23 pass on both as controls. Seven mutants pin the scope stack, the clone mask, the registration and lookup order, and the setting check.

signals.title: Read fresh in-memory metadata at the OPTIMIZE merge-selection read
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104822 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed data loss when a `RENAME COLUMN` runs concurrently with `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` on a `MergeTree` table: the merged part could be written with the pre-rename column list, permanently filling the renamed column with its `DEFAULT`. ### Description `26.3`-only fix for issue 80648, authorized in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113929#issuecomment-5229587902. `StorageMergeTree::optimize` calls `merge` synchronously on the query thread, so the merge-selection metadata read runs with a live query context. `MergeTreeData` overrides `getInMemoryMetadataPtr` with a per-query cache that `InterpreterOptimizeQuery` has already populated with the pre-`ALTER` snapshot, so the read returns metadata predating the rename while selection pairs it with parts that already carry the mutation. `MergeTask` takes `storage_columns` from that snapshot and never re-reads, so the merged part keeps the old column list and the renamed column stays `DEFAULT`. Passing `bypass_metadata_cache=true` makes the read honour the invariant the comment above it already states. `scheduleDataProcessingJob` keeps its bare read: its only caller is the background pool, which has no query context, so it already bypasses. `26.4` and later declare the accessor as `(ContextPtr, bool)` with no default, forcing every caller to state a context, so the read is already fresh there. `25.8` has the same bare read but ships `enable_shared_storage_snapshot_in_query` defaulting to `false`. `26.3` is the only supported branch with both the defaulted parameter and that setting `true`, which is why the backport of 104822 compiled unchanged as `getInMemoryMetadataPtr()` and took the cache-consulting path. Validation on two interleaved, load-matched servers built from this tree, setting at its default: base reddens 16 of 7000 iterations against 0 for the fix (Fisher exact p = 3.0e-05); swapping the binaries onto each other's port and data directory keeps the effect with the binary (30/7000 against 0/7000); 80 runner runs of the unmodified `04238_alter_rename_column_merge_race` per arm give 3 base failures with the exact CI signature and 80/80 on the fix. None of the 211 merge and mutation tests with a verdict in both arms regressed.

Every existing SIGINT test sends exactly one signal, which leaves `exit_after_signals` at 0 and returns false, so the … **Unique vs PR tests:** The PR's new gtest calls `safeExit` directly with each `LeakCheck` value; the CI python test covers the log-scanner filter. signals.title: Set the current Keeper component in TextIndexCountSource::generate
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113295 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Related: #113295 `SELECT count() FROM t WHERE hasAllTokens(str, [...])` is rewritten by the trivial-count-from-text-index optimization into a `ReadFromTextIndexCount` step (added in #111494). Its source runs on a pipeline execution thread: `TextIndexCountSource::generate` -> `computeCountForPart` -> `makeTextIndexInputStream` -> `IMergeTreeDataPart::getStreamNameOrHash(..., IDataPartStorage &)`, whose body probes the part storage with `existsFile`. On a disk that keeps part metadata in Keeper that probe is a real Keeper request, and `Coordination::ZooKeeper::pushRequest` throws `LOGICAL_ERROR` when no component is set for the scope. `generate()` is the outermost scope this step owns on that thread, and it set none: the step builds its own `Pipe`, so unlike the ordinary read path it never inherits the guard from `MergeTreeSource::tryGenerate`. This adds the one-line RAII guard at the top of `generate()`. The guard is a nesting-safe thread-local stack and every Keeper-reaching call above is a descendant of that scope, so no deeper placement is needed. Same shape as #113295 for `MergeTreeCodecBlockCountsSource::generate` and the sibling `MergeTreeTextIndexSource::generate`. Of the four callers of `makeTextIndexInputStream`, the other three already have an ancestor guard (`MergeTreeSource::tryGenerate` for both `MergeTreeReaderTextIndex` sites, the mutate/merge task guards for `MergeTextIndexesTask`); this step was the only gap. Category is `CI Fix or Improvement`, as in #113295 and #113386: the metadata-in-Keeper storage type is registered only under `#if CLICKHOUSE_CLOUD`, and `LOGICAL_ERROR` aborts only in debug and sanitizer builds, so this cannot happen in an official stable build. For the same reason no test is added: no public build reaches Keeper through `existsFile`. Validated with the existing `02346_text_index*` suite (plus 50/50 randomized runs of `02346_text_index_optimize_trivial_count`), an `EXPLAIN` assertion that the modified scope is the one the query executes, and a run with `enforce_keeper_component_tracking = 1`. Left alone: the plan-time `getDeserializedFormat` path can also reach `existsFile` for packed skip-index parts and is likewise unguarded, but it predates this step by three weeks and is not this failure's carrier.

signals.title: Fix coordination mode mismatch with a parameterized view subquery
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106039 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113622 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106039 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113622 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `Coordination mode mismatch for stream <table>: got Default, expected WithOrder` when a parameterized view is used as an `IN`-subquery of an ordered query with parallel replicas enabled. A parameterized view used this way no longer plans its inner read with parallel replicas coordination on a replica. ### Description `SELECT ... FROM t WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM pv(id = 'a')) AND id IN (SELECT id FROM pv(id = 'b')) ORDER BY id` with parallel replicas enabled aborted the server in debug and sanitizer builds, and threw in release. Root cause. A parameterized view resolves as a `TableFunctionNode`, so its arguments land in `skip_children` in `Planner/CollectSets.cpp` and the view call survives verbatim into the text sent to the replicas. The initiator plans the outer read in order from the sort key and announces `WithOrder`; each replica re-plans the view body, an unordered scan, and announces `Default`. Both key on the bare table name, so the second announcement reaches the first's coordinator and throws. `PlannerJoinTree.cpp` already guards a view planning its own read on a follower, but it compares `table_node` against the chosen `parallel_replicas_table`, and both are null, so it concludes "this is the chosen table" and leaves coordination enabled for the view. A table expression that is not a `TableNode` is now treated as not chosen, which is always correct: `parallel_replicas_table` is a `const TableNode *`, and both walks in `findTableForParallelReplicas` bail out on a table function. The union-children comparison is skipped for the same reason. A view referenced by name is a `TableNode`, so `parallel_replicas_allow_view_over_mergetree = 1` is unaffected. Validation. The test pins the five settings the divergence depends on, three of which the runner randomizes; each of the four that can vary was confirmed load-bearing by a negative control on the unfixed binary. It fails 8 of 8 randomized runs on master with the reported error and passes 100 of 100 here. Expected rows are parallel-replicas-off ground truth, so each query also asserts `ParallelReplicasHandleAnnouncementMicroseconds > 0` to show coordination was reached. The in-tree view, parameterized-view, trivial-view-pushdown and table-function tests are unchanged.

signals.title: Remove the stale TODO about unloading tables in reverse topological order
signals.text: `DatabaseCatalog::checkTableCanBeRemovedOrRenamedUnlocked` skips dependent tables from the same database when the removal comes from `DROP DATABASE`, and carried a TODO asking for the tables to be unloaded in reverse topological order instead. That ordering exists since https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97057: `InterpreterDropQuery::executeToDatabaseImpl` sorts the tables of a `DROP DATABASE` in reverse loading dependency order, so a dependent is always dropped before the table it depends on. The skip itself is still required, since the dependency graph is consulted per table while the database is being emptied, so only the obsolete TODO is replaced by a pointer to the code that maintains the invariant. Comment-only change. signals.title: Fix undefined behavior in DateTime64 reservoir quantiles
signals.text: The reservoir-sampling implementation of `quantile` and `quantiles` interpolates values in `Float64`. `DateTime64` ticks close to the upper `Int64` boundary can round to 2^63 exactly, making the conversion back to the native representation undefined. signals.title: Show why a job failed when it never uploaded its own report
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113382 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Not user-facing: CI report only. ### Description Two jobs on #113382 lost their runner mid-`Run`, and both report pages render nothing, so the failure looks like a 0-second job with no output: - https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113382&sha=f7f79281458bd4558f12725868c0035cbc7b8f5d&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%29 - https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113382&sha=f7f79281458bd4558f12725868c0035cbc7b8f5d&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%2C%20old_compatibility%29 praktika did detect the failure and did record the reason, but two defects hide it, and either one alone is enough to blank the page. `_finish_workflow` reported such a job only through `env.add_workflow_error(..., source=result.name)`. `source=` sets the `from` label, not the destination, so the message landed on the workflow node while the job's own node kept an empty `info`, and the page renders notifications from the node it resolved, which is the job. The `Status.ERROR` sites in `runner.py` already call `add_error` on the job's own result; this site did not. A job uploads its own `result_<job>.json` from inside the job, so a job that dies never uploads one and S3 answers 403. The page turned that 403 into "Report does not exist or expired" and returned, discarding the workflow report it had already fetched, which does contain the job's node. That early return is gone, and the cached per-job report is now overwritten on every fetch that came back, including a 403, so a page polling `sha=latest` cannot keep showing an older commit's node. The 403 check for the workflow report itself is unchanged. The runner loss is not fixable here and this does not try to. A test drives `_finish_workflow` against a stubbed environment and asserts the reason is in the uploaded workflow report; it fails if the added line is removed. For the page, a script extracts the relevant functions from `json.html` and replays the measured S3 responses: the reason appears only with both fixes, an older cached node never masks a new commit's, and the healthy and expired paths are byte-identical to before. No related open issue found.

signals.title: Add higher-order array functions to pack bits.
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/48830 Adds higher-order array functions that apply a lambda to each element of an array and pack the resulting bits into a compact representation. Useful for compression and quantization in vector-search workloads, where a single bit (or a small group of bits) is derived per dimension and packed into a fixed-width value. Six functions are added: - `arrayPackBitsToUInt64(f, arr)` — pack one bit per element into a `UInt64` (only the first 64 bits are used). - `arrayPackBitsToString(f, arr)` — pack one bit per element into a `String` of `ceil(size / 8)` bytes. - `arrayPackBitsToFixedString(f, n, arr)` — pack one bit per element into a `FixedString(n)`. - `arrayPackBitGroupsToUInt64(f, g, arr)` — the same, but the lambda returns an integer whose low `g` bits form a group, and the groups are packed contiguously (`N·g` bits). - `arrayPackBitGroupsToString(f, g, arr)` - `arrayPackBitGroupsToFixedString(f, n, g, arr)` Bits are packed most-significant-bit first within each byte and groups are packed contiguously, one after another (a group does not occupy a whole byte). The `*ToUInt64` variants interpret the packed byte stream in little-endian byte order, as requested in the issue, so `arrayPackBitsToUInt64(f, arr) = reinterpretAsUInt64(arrayPackBitsToString(f, arr))` and likewise for the group variants. The implementation is a single `ArrayPackBitsImpl` template parameterized by the result column type and a `PackGroups` flag. `FunctionArrayMapped` is extended with a `return_fixed_string` trait so that an implementation returning a `FixedString` can forward the constant size argument to `getReturnType`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added higher-order array functions to pack bits: `arrayPackBitsToUInt64`, `arrayPackBitsToString`, `arrayPackBitsToFixedString`, `arrayPackBitGroupsToUInt64`, `arrayPackBitGroupsToString`, `arrayPackBitGroupsToFixedString`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) The functions carry embedded `FunctionDocumentation` (description, syntax, arguments, returned value, examples), from which the user-facing documentation is generated.

signals.text: ### Changelog category: - New Feature ### Changelog entry: Added the `group_by_each_block_no_merge` setting (off by default). When enabled, a query with `GROUP BY` is processed in a streaming fashion: aggregation is performed, finalized, and flushed for every block of data, without fully merging the partial results. This is intended for special cases such as populating a materialized view with `POPULATE`, where the partial results are merged later in the background. signals.title: Implemented SIEVE eviction in cache framework
signals.text: Implements the `SIEVE` cache eviction policy in the cache framework (`CacheBase`), available alongside the existing `LRU` and `SLRU` policies. `SIEVE` is a simple, scan-resistant eviction algorithm: a single "hand" walks a FIFO queue of entries and evicts the first entry whose `visited` flag is clear, clearing the flag as it passes set entries. See the paper for details: https://junchengyang.com/publication/nsdi24-SIEVE.pdf This continues the original work by @Vectorshine, brought up to date with `master`: - Reworked `SIEVECachePolicy` to match the current `ICachePolicy` interface (`CurrentMetrics` tracking, `maxCount`, `contains`, per-entry `OnRemoveEntryFunction`), mirroring `LRUCachePolicy`. - Fixed a bug in `remove` where the stored queue iterator was advanced in place and the wrong node was erased. - Added unit tests in `gtest_sieve_cache.cpp`, including a step-by-step test of the eviction logic. - Randomized the mark and uncompressed cache policy across `LRU`, `SLRU` and `SIEVE` in stateless functional tests (`ci/jobs/functional_tests.py`) and the stress test (`tests/docker_scripts/stress_runner.sh`). `SIEVE` is only implemented for the `CacheBase`-backed caches, so the filesystem cache (backed by `FileCachePolicy`) is not randomized to it, and it is excluded during bugfix validation, which runs downloaded master-side binaries. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58910 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new cache eviction policy `SIEVE`. It can be selected for the in-memory caches backed by `CacheBase`, such as the mark cache and the uncompressed cache, via the corresponding `*_cache_policy` server settings (for example, `mark_cache_policy` and `uncompressed_cache_policy`). It is not available for the filesystem cache. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Improve the performance of `MODIFY TTL`
signals.text: `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY TTL` currently rewrites every part of the table, which on a large table means reading and writing all of its data just to change when rows expire. Very often the new TTL is the old one shifted in time - the retention period is extended or shortened, e.g. `create_time + INTERVAL 300 DAY` becomes `create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY`. In that case every row's expiry time moves by the same constant number of seconds, so the parts do not have to be rewritten at all: it is enough to shift the expiry timestamps ClickHouse already stores per part. This pull request adds that fast path, and the result for the user is that such a `MODIFY TTL` completes almost instantly instead of taking minutes or hours: ```sql CREATE TABLE test_fast_ttl (`id` UInt32, `name` String, `create_time` DateTime) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id TTL create_time + toIntervalDay(300); INSERT INTO test_fast_ttl SELECT number, 'AAA', date_sub(day, 100, now()) from numbers(100000000); -- Before ALTER TABLE test_fast_ttl MODIFY TTL create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY; -- 0 rows in set. Elapsed: 25.564 sec. -- After ALTER TABLE test_fast_ttl MODIFY TTL create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY; -- 0 rows in set. Elapsed: 0.046 sec. ``` There is nothing to enable and no new syntax: the optimization is applied automatically inside the `MATERIALIZE TTL` mutation that `MODIFY TTL` already produces, and a plain `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL` benefits from it as well. The observable result is exactly the same as before - the same rows expire and the parts end up with the same TTL bounds - only the work is avoided. Per part, the mutation now does one of the following: - the part is fully expired under the new TTL - it is replaced with an empty part; - no row of the part is expired yet - the part is cloned (its data files hardlinked) and only its stored TTL bounds are shifted; - otherwise - the part is rewritten exactly as before. The fast path is only taken when it is provably equivalent to the rewrite. It requires that the unconditional rows TTL (`TTL <expr>`) is the only TTL of the table, and that the old and the new TTL are the same date/time column shifted by constant fixed-length intervals, so that `new_ttl(row) - old_ttl(row)` is one constant for every row. Calendar `MONTH`/`YEAR` intervals, `DAY`/`WEEK` intervals in a time zone with daylight saving time, and row-dependent expressions are all rejected. The proof is redone for each part against the TTL expression (and time zone) that the part's stored timestamps were actually computed under, so a part that lags the table metadata, or was written by an older server, falls back to the regular rewrite rather than being shifted unsoundly. The same applies to the boundary cases of the stored timestamps themselves: a part containing a row whose TTL timestamp is exactly `1970-01-01 00:00:00` UTC (which ClickHouse treats as "no TTL"), a shift that would move some timestamp onto that value, and a part whose stored TTL is already fully expired (which the regular rewrite drops wholesale, even when the new TTL is longer) all take the regular rewrite. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY TTL` no longer rewrites the table's data when the new TTL is the old one shifted by a constant amount of time (the same date/time column plus fixed-length intervals), which is the common case of extending or shortening the retention period. Fully expired parts are replaced with empty ones and the rest are cloned with only their stored TTL metadata shifted, which makes such an `ALTER` nearly instant. Cases where the shift is not provably constant - calendar month/year intervals, day/week intervals in a time zone with daylight saving time, or row-dependent TTL expressions - fall back to the regular rewrite. `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL` benefits from the same optimization. <!--- Directly edit documentation source files in the "docs" folder with the same pull-request as code changes or Add a user-readable short description of the changes that should be added to docs.clickhouse.com below. When enabled, cached-file sizes are accounted in filesystem allocation units (block size) instead of the written byte count, so the `FilesystemCacheSize` metric, the eviction-size metrics, and `current_size` in `system.filesystem_cache_settings` use block-aligned accounting. Without it, a cached file smaller than one block (for example, a 1-byte file) is accounted as its written size while occupying a whole block on disk, which can make the reported cache size much smaller than the actual on-disk usage. The accounting is a block-aligned approximation of the physical size, not the exact allocated size. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written Documented the `use_real_disk_size` filesystem cache setting in `docs/en/operations/storing-data.md`. signals.title: Add early short-circuit evaluation for OR/AND in the analyzer to prevent unnecessary scalar subquery execution
signals.text: <!--- Disable AI PR formatting assistant: true --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): You can now enable early short-circuit folding for builtin `and` and `or` during analysis with the `enable_function_early_short_circuit` setting. This can skip executing dead single-row `count()` scalar subqueries while preserving normal type inference and semantic validation. Resolves #83017 ### Details When `enable_function_early_short_circuit` is enabled (and `short_circuit_function_evaluation` is not disabled), the analyzer detects decisive constants in builtin `and` / `or` expressions. The optimization is deliberately conservative. It is attempted only for expressions without outer-scope Identifier/Column dependencies and only for scalar subqueries of the statically single-row forms `SELECT count()` or `SELECT count(*)` without GROUP BY/window/HAVING/QUALIFY/LIMIT BY. All other scalar forms use normal analysis and execution. A dedicated temporary `QueryAnalyzer` resolves a clone in type-only mode using an isolated, cache-disabled scope. It never mutates the live resolver state. Scalar values are represented by non-constant type placeholders, and expressions containing aggregate/`arrayJoin` semantic carriers outside scalar-subquery boundaries are not replaced. Resolves #83017

signals.title: Cascades cost-based optimizer for distributed query plans
signals.text: A Cascades-style cost-based optimizer that chooses distribution strategies for the multi-stage distributed query plans of #106020. It explores alternatives in a memo (a shared store of equivalent plan fragments) with top-down, goal-directed search and picks the cheapest plan satisfying the required distribution and sorting properties, inserting exchange operators (plan steps that move rows between nodes) as needed. Implemented: - **Join strategies**: shuffle hash join, broadcast hash join (with `ReplicatedRead` — every worker repeats the same read of a small table instead of a network broadcast, assuming shared storage where all workers see the same data), replicated join (a small deterministic join is recomputed identically on every node over such reads, so its result never crosses the network; nested joins compose; `ANY` joins are excluded because the kept row depends on the build order), local join. - **Aggregation strategies**: two-phase (partial + merge), shuffle by group keys, local; `distributed_aggregation_memory_efficient` and `distributed_plan_force_shuffle_aggregation` are honored. - **Top-N**: two-stage distributed top-N (per-node bounded sort, sorted-merge gather, coordinator limit); disabled under `exact_rows_before_limit`, which needs the full row count. - **Read strategies**: parallel N-way read, replicated read, local read. For `FINAL`, #108148 (already in master) taught the rule-based distributed plan to split a `FINAL` read into disjoint primary-key-range buckets where that is safe; Cascades now reuses that machinery, so `FINAL` no longer forces a serial read here either. The coordinator ships each bucket's marks in the `read_bucket` task parameters. - **`IN (subquery)`**: follows the `rewrite_in_to_join` setting like the rest of the planner (the forced join form is removed). In the default set form the set-building subqueries are planned separately and distributed like any other query. - **Properties and enforcers**: distribution (node count, replication, partitioning columns with equivalence classes and the types the keys are cast to before hashing) and sorting; when a plan alternative lacks a required property, an enforcer inserts the step that provides it (`Gather`/`Shuffle`/`Broadcast`/`ScatterExchange`, `Sort`). - **Transformations**: join commutativity (only for semantics-preserving joins: `INNER ALL`, `CROSS`, `SEMI`/`ANY`/`ANTI`; never `ASOF`, and never `ANY` under `join_any_take_last_row`), two-phase aggregation split, two-stage top-N split. - **Cost model**: `work`, `network`, and `sequential` components, each priced as wall-clock per node: a shuffle moves 1/N of the data per node, a broadcast payload is ingested once by every receiver in parallel, and a gather funnels every row through one endpoint, so its transfer stays undivided and pays a per-row cost. A hash-table build counts as parallel work (`parallel_hash` shards it across threads); a fixed per-exchange overhead keeps small inputs local. A table read is priced on its scan volume - the rows the primary key keeps - not on its output estimate, so a filter off the sorting key cannot make a replicated re-read look free. Standalone filters (e.g. `HAVING`) are estimated from column NDVs with join-key equivalence classes; join estimates are clamped to join kind and strictness semantics; exchange costs use per-row byte widths measured from the parts' column sizes (followed through renames, not derived from types). All weights and calibration constants are overridable at query time. What this improves over the rule-based distributed planner, on TPC-H plans. The rule-based planner broadcasts a small table when its read is below `distributed_plan_max_rows_to_broadcast`, but it often cannot size the result of a join, so a small join result (`nation x region`, 5 rows after the region filter) is scattered across nodes, joined there, and shuffled again (repartitioned across nodes) by the next join key. It also often inserts a shuffle at join and aggregation boundaries even when the rows are already divided by the right key. Cascades estimates sizes through joins, knows which partitioning already holds, compares broadcast against shuffle by cost for each join, and recomputes a small deterministic join on every node when that is cheaper than moving its result. On TPC-H SF100 over 8 nodes (same binary, same run window; times are server-side means of the hot runs) the join-heavy queries improve: | Query | Rule-based -> Cascades | What changed in the plan | |---|---|---| | Q21 | 7.66 s -> 5.34 s | The four `supplier x nation` joins compute their small results once and broadcast them, so `lineitem` is not shuffled to meet them. | | Q09 | 4.07 s -> 2.47 s | `part` and `nation` are read in full by every node, so `lineitem` and `supplier` are not shuffled to meet them. | | Q08 | 2.39 s -> 0.99 s | `nation x region` (5 rows) is recomputed by every node; `part` is read in full per node, so `lineitem` is not shuffled to join it. | | Q02 | 2.14 s -> 0.84 s | The `supplier x nation x region` chain is recomputed by every node, so only `partsupp` and `supplier` are shuffled. The top-100 sort becomes two-stage, sending at most 100 rows per node. | | Q05 | 2.05 s -> 1.12 s | The whole dimension side (`orders x customer x nation x region`) is recomputed by every node over full local reads; `lineitem` joins it in place with no shuffle at all. | | Q17 | 2.72 s -> 1.78 s | The small per-part average is broadcast to every node, so the outer 600M-row `lineitem` read is not shuffled. | | Q11 | 0.49 s -> 0.26 s | `supplier x nation` is computed once and broadcast; `partsupp` joins it in place. | | Q12 | 0.76 s -> 0.59 s | The filtered `lineitem` rows (~30K of 600M) are gathered once and broadcast; nothing is shuffled. | The remaining queries change less. Summed over all 22 queries, hot server time drops from 36.8 s to 28.8 s (about 22% lower). The remaining regressions are the `IN (subquery)` queries Q18 (2.43 s -> 2.85 s) and Q20 (2.24 s -> 2.99 s). With the forced join rewrite removed, both run their `IN`s as sets in both modes, and the sets built are identical; the difference is in the plans around them. Cascades picks replicated-read shapes that rescan moderate tables on every node, which loses here for a structural reason: the main reads are filtered by `x IN <set>`, and the set contents do not exist at costing time, so the model cannot credit a shuffle-based plan for how few rows survive the set filter, while the replicated read's full scan is paid regardless. Two follow-ups: a cost-informed choice of the `IN` form, and set-filter selectivity from the subquery's output estimate. `EXPLAIN pretty = 1, estimates = 1` shows the chosen plan with a row estimate and the accumulated cost for each step. Also in this PR, two improvements to the shared bucketed-read machinery (they benefit the rule-based path too): the `FINAL` layer split no longer depends on the coordinator's core count, and a many-partition `FINAL` split groups its layers into the target task count instead of falling back to a serial read. Design, a worked example on TPC-H data (a simplified 3-table query traced through the memo), and current limitations are documented in `src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/Cascades/ARCHITECTURE.md`. Plan-shape tests cover the actual TPC-H queries (`03836_tpch_join_order_plans`), and focused tests pin the cost-model contracts (e.g. `04869_cascades_read_cost_granule_volume`, `04838_cascades_filter_selectivity`). Disabled by default. Requires the analyzer; remote execution requires the stateless-worker configuration, while `distributed_plan_execute_locally = 1` runs the stages in-process without it: ```sql SET enable_cascades_optimizer = 1, make_distributed_plan = 1; ``` For tests, `param__internal_cascades_cluster_node_count` overrides the cluster size, `param__internal_cascades_cost_config` overrides the cost model configuration, `param__internal_join_table_stat_hints` injects table statistics, `param__internal_cascades_task_limit` lowers the task budget (it can never raise it). Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106020 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental Cascades cost-based optimizer for distributed query plans, enabled by `enable_cascades_optimizer = 1` together with `make_distributed_plan = 1`. It chooses between shuffle, broadcast, replicated, and local join strategies, two-phase, shuffle, and local aggregation, two-stage distributed top-N, and parallel and replicated reads by estimated cost, inserting exchange operators as needed. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation written in [/docs](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/tree/master/docs)

signals.title: Feature: Enable overlay databases for server.
signals.text: Enables server-side `Overlay` databases. An `Overlay` database is a read-only facade that exposes the union of the tables of several underlying databases, resolving each table name through the listed sources in order (the first source that has the table wins). DDL on the facade is rejected — it has no storage of its own — while `SELECT` and pass-through `INSERT` resolve to the underlying source table. Reading or writing through the facade requires the corresponding grant on both the facade database and the underlying source, and the facade's row policies are combined with the source's. Previously an `Overlay` database existed only as the implicit default database of `clickhouse-local`. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/52764 <!--- A technical comment, you are free to remove or leave it as it is when PR is created The following categories are used in the next scripts, update them accordingly utils/changelog/changelog.py tests/ci/cancel_and_rerun_workflow_lambda/app.py --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow creating `Overlay` databases. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Avoid usage of `Field` in KeyCondition when checking ranges
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/91836 --> During primary key index analysis, `MergeTree` compares every mark boundary of every analysed key column against the ranges of the filter. Those boundaries are materialized as `Field` values: for a `String` or `Decimal` key column each boundary allocates and copies the value, once per mark range per key column. This adds a second representation of the same information, selected by the new setting `use_column_refs_for_primary_key_index_analysis`: a boundary becomes a reference into the index column it comes from (a column pointer plus a row number), comparisons go through `IColumn::compareAt`, and no `Field` is constructed. The atom ranges of the condition are converted into the same representation once, when the `KeyCondition` is built. The representation applies on top of `use_lightweight_primary_key_index_analysis` (#91836), which selects *which* key columns are analysed; this setting changes *how* the values of those columns are represented. `forAnySparseHyperrectangleRefs` and the reference overloads of `KeyCondition::checkInRange`, `KeyCondition::checkInHyperrectangle` and `MergeTreeSetIndex::checkInRange` mirror their `Field` counterparts one-to-one. The part's partition-minmax bounds are materialized once per part into one-row columns that the reference bounds point into. Applying a monotonic function chain to a reference evaluates the function over the whole in-memory index at once; the result column is cached per (function, input column) and reused across all the mark ranges of a part. Two cases cannot be represented as a reference, and both keep using `Field` so that pruning is never weaker than without the setting: - an atom whose constant has no exact representation as a value of the key column's type (`d <= toDateTime64('...')` over a `DateTime` key), because a reference can only be compared against a column of its own type; - a key column analysed only through its partition-minmax bound, which has no column to apply a function chain to. The setting is disabled by default and randomized in the functional tests. **It is not yet a win**: on a 2.5M-mark part, index analysis alone is 3.3-3.6x slower than the `Field` representation for a two-column key and 16.6x slower for an 18-column one (see the measurements in the comments). The `Field` path materializes each boundary once per mark range and then compares cached values, while the reference path pays a virtual `IColumn::compareAt` per comparison, and the enumeration performs several comparisons per boundary. Making this pay off needs a cheaper comparison, e.g. a comparator resolved per key column once per part. `04846_column_refs_primary_key_index_analysis` runs a set of queries under both representations and compares the results *and* the `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` output, so a divergence in pruning fails the test. `tryPrepareSetColumnsForIndex` no longer keeps the prepared `IN` set column `Nullable` when the key column is not: a NULL element can never match a non-`Nullable` key, and the reference representation cannot compare a `Nullable` column against a non-`Nullable` one. This makes some `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` outputs report a smaller set (`03733_has_function_key_condition_explain`). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Nothing user-facing yet: the setting this adds is experimental, disabled by default, and does not currently improve anything (see the measurements above). The category becomes `Performance Improvement` if the representation is made faster than the `Field` one. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Allow multiple key condition atoms per predicate leaf
signals.text: If we have, ```sql CREATE TABLE test ( dt DateTime ) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY (toYYYYMM(dt), toDate(dt), toStartOfHour(dt), dt) SETTINGS index_granularity = 1; INSERT INTO test SELECT toDateTime('2026-01-01 00:00:00') + number * 3600 FROM numbers(24 * 40); ``` Then, for query such as: ```sql EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT count() FROM test WHERE dt = toDateTime('2026-01-10 00:00:00'); ``` Currently, we use only one primary key column: ```response Keys: dt Condition: (dt in [1768003200, 1768003200]) Parts: 1/1 Granules: 960/960 ``` PR will use all the keys applicable: ```response Keys: toYYYYMM(dt) toDate(dt) toStartOfHour(dt) dt Condition: and((toStartOfHour(dt) in [1768003200, 1768003200]), and((toDate(dt) in [20463, 20463]), and((toYYYYMM(dt) in [202601, 202601]), (dt in [1768003200, 1768003200])))) Parts: 1/1 Granules: 2/960 ``` ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow each predicate leaf to use all applicable primary key expressions for pruning. For example, if the primary key is `toYYYYMMDD(dt), toDate(dt), dt` and the filter condition is `WHERE dt >= toDateTime('2026-01-10 00:00:00')`, ClickHouse will be able to use all three primary key expressions to prune as much as possible, instead of currently using only one of them. Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/33056. Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/99960. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Fix hang in `--queries-file` / `-q` when stdin is a pipe with no data
signals.text: `ClientBase` eagerly called `isStdinNotEmptyAndValid` to check for trailing stdin data on every `INSERT`. That helper calls `!std_in.eof()`, which performs a blocking `read(0, ...)`. When stdin is a pipe that is open but has no data and no `EOF` (common in CI, Docker, stress tests, and `--queries-file` invocations), the read blocks indefinitely and the client hangs until it is killed by timeout. Concretely, this caused an exception (signal 11 after timeout) in the stress test `03538_analyzer_scalar_correlated_subquery_fix`: the process hung on `read(0, ...)` and was killed. The fix replaces the eager blocking probe with a non-blocking one: `poll(timeout=0)` first asks "does stdin appear to have data right now?", and only when it does we fall through to `isStdinNotEmptyAndValid` to confirm and consume it. This: - avoids the hang on open empty pipes — `poll` returns 0 immediately; - preserves deterministic rejection of `inlined data + stdin` mixed input — when stdin actually contains data (the case asserted by `04064_inline_insert_data`), `poll` returns `POLLIN` and we still throw `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`; - is best-effort by design: a slow producer pipe (e.g. `(sleep 1; echo) | clickhouse-client ...`) may not have written by the time `poll` runs, in which case the trailing stdin payload is ignored. This is preferable to the alternative of a hard hang, and is documented in the helper. Covered cases (`is_async_insert_with_inlined_data`, `is_inline_insert_data`, and the appending-stdin path in `sendData`) all go through the same probe so the hang is closed for `--queries-file`, `-q`, and `--inline-insert-data` modes.
