signal.title: Sync BACKUP FROM SNAPSHOT settings and failpoints
signal.text: `BACKUP FROM SNAPSHOT` is already parsed in this repository (`ParserBackupQuery`, `ASTBackupQuery`), but the settings and failpoints of its **resumable** mode existed only in the Cloud repository. As a result the two settings surfaces and failpoint registries had drifted apart, and the shared files conflicted on every sync. This declares them here, and says plainly in each place that the feature behind them is available in ClickHouse Cloud only: - `resumable_backup_from_snapshot` — experimental session setting. - `resumable_backup_batch_size` and `resumable_backup_batch_size_bytes` — backup-query settings bounding how much work a failed attempt replays. - the `backup_from_snapshot_*` failpoints the feature's tests inject. Nothing in this repository reads the batch limits or injects the failpoints. The declarations exist so that both builds accept and reject the same queries, and so these shared files stop conflicting on every sync. `fromBackupQuery` still rejects a zero batch limit, keeping that validation identical in both builds. signal.title: Web UI prototype for framing formats
signal.text: Prototype changes to the Web UI (`programs/server/play.html`) to test and showcase the framing formats feature. This is a draft for experimentation and review of the client-side experience, not intended to merge as-is. It builds on the framing-formats server work in #110127 (this branch is based on that PR, so the diff includes those commits until it merges into `master`). What the prototype does: - Streams every query with the `EventStream` framing format over HTTP (`framing_output_format=EventStream`, `send_logs_level=trace`), decoding data / progress / log / profile_events / exception packets as they arrive - so progress and logs work regardless of the output format (including `FORMAT Pretty`, binary formats via base64, and images). - Shows realtime CPU, memory, and disk usage like `clickhouse-client`, aggregated per host (total and max/host), switching to peak RAM when the query finishes. The meter state is owned by each tab: the CPU counters in `profile_events` packets are per-packet increments, so a query running in a background tab keeps accumulating them, and reopening the tab continues the meter from its live values (rather than restarting near zero). - Merges elapsed time, realtime metrics, and rows/bytes read stats into a single progress area with the progress-bar gradient rendered behind all of them; the text is tinted by a mask clipped from the same gradient so it stays readable over the fill. - Displays server logs in real time, colored like the client, with a Logs button available even on exception; the log view stays fast for 100k+ lines while keeping native browser search, bounding retention to the most recent 100k lines (older lines are dropped and counted in a marker line). The full response text kept for the tab/history snapshot is also capped as it is collected (at ~100 KB, the size above which the snapshot is dropped), so a single large framed data/log burst is not retained in full only to be discarded later. A failed run whose reply outgrew that cap is persisted as a compact snapshot that keeps the exception carrier in the form its framing kind replays (the terminal `event: exception` block, the `{"packet":"exception",...}` line, or the plain `{"exception":...}` line, captured at stream-read time since the capped text stops growing before the terminal exception arrives), so reopening or reloading a failed tab still shows the error reason. - Base64-decodes every `data`/`totals`/`extremes` payload (the `EventStream` wire encodes each block as a single base64 `data:` field and the `Content-Type` carries `payload=base64`), deciding the rendering by the output format: the default format is reassembled into the table, an image format (or bytes carrying an image signature) is rendered as an inline image once the stream completes, and any other format is decoded and shown incrementally as raw text. - Uses a framing-compatible default format for queries without an explicit `FORMAT` clause: the framed request asks for `JSONCompactStringsEachRowWithNamesAndTypes` (the framing rejects the in-band-progress `JSONStringsEachRowWithProgress`) and the client reassembles the compact rows into the table renderer's shapes; on the server side (#110127) the compact family emits totals and extremes under framing, so `WITH TOTALS` and extremes-based column coloring keep working on the default path. When such a format is shown as raw text instead (an explicit `FORMAT JSONCompactEachRow`), only the `data` packets are concatenated, so the rendered text is exactly the plain output of that format rather than one carrying the totals and extremes rows the format itself drops. - Propagates a framed `exception` packet as a query failure even when the HTTP status was already 200 (so `Run all` stops at the failed statement) - and, when a query chooses its own `JSONEachPacket*` framing that fails before the 200 OK header (coming back as a non-200 `application/x-ndjson` packet stream ending with a `{"packet":"exception",...}` line), shows those packets verbatim and records `framing_kind = 'ndjson_packets'` for replay rather than rendering the whole stream as one opaque error string; retries framing-incompatible explicit formats (e.g. `FORMAT JSONEachRowWithProgress`, `FORMAT Template`) once without framing for read-only queries (read-only-ness is resolved with a CTE-aware lexer walk - `WITH y AS (SELECT 1) INSERT INTO t SELECT * FROM y` is a write - shared with `Run all`'s grouping, so such a statement is also a barrier there and never runs in parallel with the reads that follow it; the port with regression coverage lives in `src/Parsers/tests/gtest_play_query_is_read_only.cpp`); a retried `JSON*EachRowWithProgress` format that itself reports a failure in-band - a trailing `{"exception":...}` object while the HTTP status stays 200 (`http_write_exception_in_output_format`) - is detected as a failure too, keyed off the output format rather than only a user-chosen `JSONEachPacket*` framing, so `Run all` stops after such a retried query fails; and does not add its own framing to a query that sets its own `framing_output_format` to a real framing choice (the response is then dispatched by content type, so the requested packets are shown verbatim); a query that sets `framing_output_format = 'None'` is refused client-side instead, since this page's rendering depends on framing (values the page cannot know upfront - `= DEFAULT`, a reset to the session/server default, and query-parameter placeholders like `= {fmt:String}` - are classified conservatively the same way and refused, rather than sent with a request shape the response might not match); likewise a standalone `SET framing_output_format = ...` is refused, because it would change the setting for the whole session (with a `session_id`) while the page keeps adding its own framing per request - a query-level `SETTINGS framing_output_format = ...` clause is the supported way to choose framing for one query. A query that carries its own `framing_output_format` is also refused for download (the setting would override the download's chosen `default_format`, so the file would be the framing packet stream), and if such a query fails, its history snapshot - the raw `JSONEachPacket*` packet stream - is replayed as raw text on tab-switch/reload rather than as one opaque error string. - Pins `framing_output_format=None` on every request that expects an unframed response (the plain/chart request, the compatibility retry, the download, and the panel/server-status/completion queries), rather than only omitting the setting - otherwise a framing carried by the connection URL or by the HTTP session behind it would frame those responses too. A query-level `SETTINGS framing_output_format = ...` clause is applied after the URL parameters, so a query that intentionally chooses a framing still overrides the pin. - Records the framing kind (`event_stream` / `ndjson_packets` / none) with each result snapshot and keys the history/tab replay off it, instead of guessing from the payload's first bytes - so a raw result whose text happens to start with `event:` (e.g. `SELECT 'event: data' FORMAT RawBLOB`) or `{"packet":` is not reparsed as a framing stream after a tab switch or reload. A snapshot recorded as `ndjson_packets` is replayed as raw text regardless of whether the run succeeded and of its underlying output format, matching the live path - so a successful user-framed `JSONEachPacket*` result whose format has its own restore path (a table or a `JSONCompactColumns` chart) is not reparsed as that format's JSON. The snapshot also records whether the framed stream was truncated, so replay keeps the live fail-closed behavior for images: a cut-off framed `FORMAT PNG` response that showed only its error live reopens from history / Back / Forward as that error too, never as a partially decoded picture (a failed but complete stream - a terminal `exception` packet after the payload - still renders its collected image, as live). - Detects both the query's `FORMAT` clause and its `framing_output_format` setting with the WASM lexer rather than a raw text match, so a mention inside a string literal or a comment - e.g. `SELECT 'FORMAT JSONCompactColumns'` - does not make the page silently opt out of its own framing. The detection is positional, not keyword-adjacent: a settings context is recognized by its `name = value` list grammar (a column merely named `settings` does not open one), and a `FORMAT` clause candidate must follow a token that ends an expression (so in `WITH 1 AS format SELECT format JSONCompactColumns SETTINGS max_threads = 1` both `format` words are identifiers, not a clause). The download reuses the same `FORMAT`-clause detection (now returning the clause span) to strip only a real trailing `FORMAT` clause from the download query, leaving text or ordinary SQL like `SELECT 'FORMAT TSV' AS s` untouched. Both detectors also accept a quoted spelling of the name - the server parses setting names and `FORMAT` names with identifier parsers, so a backquoted `framing_output_format` or format name is real - comparing by the unquoted name. Regression coverage for both lives in `src/Parsers/tests/gtest_play_detect_explicit_format.cpp` and `gtest_play_detect_framing_setting.cpp` (ports of the token walking onto the real `DB::Lexer`). - Dispatches on the response output format case-insensitively. Format names are case-insensitive in ClickHouse (`FormatFactory` looks them up by their lowercased name), while `X-ClickHouse-Format` echoes the identifier exactly as the `FORMAT` clause spelled it, so `FORMAT jsoncompactcolumns` used to lose the chart renderer, a lowercased default format lost the table renderer, and the late in-band exception probes did not recognize `FORMAT xml` / `FORMAT json` / `FORMAT jsoneachrowwithprogress` - a query failing after its `200 OK` header was then reported as a success and `Run all` continued past it. Every dispatch now compares a lowercased copy of the format name. - On the server side (#110127), framed pulling `SELECT` queries now also end with the documented final `progress` packet carrying `result_rows` / `result_bytes` / `memory_usage`, matching the native protocol and the no-result path. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Prototype Web UI changes to test framing formats (draft). Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110127

signal.title: Push tuple element predicates into Parquet and ORC subcolumn reads
signal.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112575 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Filter pushdown now works for `Tuple` subcolumns in Parquet and ORC files. A predicate such as `WHERE tup.1 = 555555` over `file()`, `s3()` or `url()` now prunes row groups and row index strides using the tuple element's own statistics instead of reading the whole file. ### Description Closes: #112575 Three independent defects, all needed for the reported query to prune. Parquet's reader itself was fine. **The analyzer never produced a subcolumn.** `StorageFile`/`StorageURL`/`StorageObjectStorage` return `false` from `supportsOptimizationToSubcolumns`, so `tupleElement(tup, 1)` was never rewritten to `tup.1`; the pass also accepted only `TableNode`, skipping table functions. That blanket `false` keeps #106147 fixed (`NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK` on `.null` in PREWHERE), so rather than flipping it this adds a narrow `supportsOptimizationToTupleElementSubcolumns` virtual defaulting to the existing one, with a `{Tuple, tupleElement}`-only allow-list. `04303_object_storage_prewhere_isnotnull_subcolumn` passes unmodified. Source identity also moves to the table-expression node: every `file()` resolves to the same `_table_function.file` ID, so two such sources shared a key. Accepting table functions generally also makes `format()`, `values()` and `view()` eligible for the other transformers; those storages already answer `supportsSubcolumns()`, so the default covers them. **ORC's search argument builder resolved top-level names only,** so any dotted name emitted `YES_NO_NULL` while the read path in the same file resolved them recursively. Resolving recursively also reaches the flattened-`Nested` descent, which rewrites the type it is given, so the builder keeps the key's own type: an array-typed predicate over a flattened `Nested` leaf is not pushed, since scalar element statistics cannot decide it. **ORC built its KeyCondition from the reader header,** which carries only the parent column, so the predicate degraded to `unknown`. ORC now passes `initKeyConditionOnce` a local copy extended with the tuple element paths the filter references; `FormatFilterInfo`, the Parquet call site and the reader header are untouched. Admission requires a named tuple at every level (unwrapping `Nullable`/`LowCardinality`/`Array`), which refuses Map `.keys`/`.values`: they use `SubstreamType::TupleElement` but have no per-element statistics. <details> <summary>Measurements (100k rows, one row group / stride per 10k)</summary> | Arm | master | this PR | |---|---|---| | ORC `WHERE tup.1 = 55555` | 200000 rows read | **20000** | | ORC `WHERE id = 55555` (control) | 20000 | 20000 | | Parquet `WHERE tup.1 = 55555` | 7 row groups / 0 pruned | **1 / 6** | | Parquet `WHERE id = 55555` (control) | 1 / 6 | 1 / 6 | Results identical in every arm. Refusal arms (Map `.keys`/`.values`, `.null`, `.size0`, unnamed tuple, `Array(Tuple)`, type-mismatch structure hint) return correct results with pruning off. Multi-level `tup.2.1` stays unpruned: correct, and a separate optimization. Regression sweep over `*functions_to_subcolumns*`, `*tuple_element*`, `*_parquet_*`, `*_orc_*` and the named pushdown tests, run on this build and on an unmodified master build for attribution: no regression attributable to this change. New tests are 50/50 green under randomized settings. </details> Also noticed, not touched here: reading a standalone dotted ORC tuple element with its inferred type returns column defaults, because `Nested::flatten` does not descend a `Nullable(Tuple)`. #109741 (open) rewrites that helper for the `Arrow` spelling.

signal.title: Add experimental Wallaby floating-point compression codec
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66467 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110613 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the experimental `Wallaby` lossless compression codec for `Float32` and `Float64` columns: it adaptively picks the cheapest of constant, decimal (Frame-of-Reference or zigzag-delta bit-packing, with PFOR-style patching and ULP-adjustment lanes), or XOR encoding per 1024-value block. Gated behind the `allow_experimental_codecs` setting. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) **Motivation.** This follows the evaluation of the `Chimp` codec proposal (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66467) and of the newer floating-point compression literature: `ALP` (SIGMOD 2024), `Elf` (VLDB 2023), `Camel` (SIGMOD 2025), `Kangaroo` (SIGMOD 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3802076, in production in Alibaba Lindorm since 2024), and the independent evaluation "Beyond Compression" (PVLDB 18(11), 2025). No single family dominates: integerization (`ALP`) wins on decimal-mappable data and decompression speed; the XOR family wins on non-decimal and mixed-precision data; run-length collapse wins on repetitive IoT data. `Wallaby` picks per 1024-value block, and its delta-packing of integerized values exploits time-series smoothness that neither `ALP` (plain Frame-of-Reference) nor the XOR codecs use. **Patent note.** The mantissa-erasure preprocessing shared by `Elf`, `Elf+`, `SElf*` and `Kangaroo` (erasing low mantissa bits derived from the decimal-place count and exponent) is covered by patent US 12,289,120 B2 (Chongqing University, granted 2025-04-29), including the decompression side. `Wallaby` deliberately does not implement it. All building blocks used here are prior art or openly licensed: `Gorilla` XOR (2015), windowed references with an explicit index (Chimp128, VLDB 2022), integerization with FOR bit-packing (`ALP`, MIT-licensed reference, already in ClickHouse as the shared `FFOR` helper), and delta/zigzag/run-length encoding. The encoder-side reference search is three O(1) hash probes, not Kangaroo's LZ-history algorithm; the on-disk format is original. **Decimal-scale chooser.** The decimal scale (`alpha`, now signed) is chosen per vector by measurement, not by a fixed rule: candidates are generated from four sources (the scales of 32 sampled values, with the sample grown up to 256 exactly when a stronger pruning bound would pay for itself; the trailing-decimal-zero structure of the quantized reference, which enumerates scales at which subsets of the vector become exact; the minimal scales of exception values, which discovers a high-precision minority the sample missed; and the exact scales behind tolerant votes, for when a voted scale fails on the rest of the vector), each candidate is evaluated against the full vector, and the smallest measured payload wins. Exceptions are bounded only by a size-based budget — a candidate is abandoned exactly when its exceptions alone already make it larger than the best encoding known for this vector, or when the running width of its packed lanes provably cannot come in under it. Pruning uses only provable bounds (counted sampled failures and failure carry-over from wider scales — never width extrapolation, which can prune true winners), so the chooser never skips a scale that could win. The scale that won the previous vector is evaluated first, and homogeneous vectors stay at a single full pass. **Lane capping, ULP-adjustment lanes, signed scales** (added after reading the pcodec, `ALP`, and FastLanes internals). The packed lane width can be capped below the widest value, exiling outliers into the existing exception list — PFOR-style patching, chosen in closed form from a width histogram for Frame-of-Reference and by an exact chain walk for the delta lanes. Values that integerize only up to a small distance are absorbed by a second bit-packed lane set of zigzag ULP adjustments instead of 10-byte raw exceptions (the idea behind pcodec's `FloatMult`): decimals disturbed by lossy arithmetic — a `Float32` round trip, a unit conversion — no longer force the vector to XOR. The scale is signed as in `ALP`'s `(e, f)` factorization: a negative scale divides by a power of ten, so integers ending in decimal zeros (cents, millisecond timestamps holding whole seconds) pack their cofactors, including magnitudes beyond the `Int64` domain. The XOR window search additionally probes the previous value's lookback distance, which interleaved series keep hitting. Per vector, the candidates compete on the cheaper of the exception list and the adjustment lanes, and only the winner takes one capping pass. These mechanisms are what moved sensors `temperature` −7 %, sensors `pressure` −3 %, weather `tempMax` −2.7 %, and the synthetic `smooth gauge` −11 % against the previous revision of the tables below. **Synthetic benchmarks** (this machine, `clickhouse local`, 10M `Float64` values per dataset, `max_threads = 1`, compressed size after `OPTIMIZE FINAL`; insert is the best of 3 runs, `SELECT` is `sum(x)`, mean of 5 runs; `PCO` is the pcodec Rust crate linked as a codec by #110613, compiled into the same binary, at its default level 8; smallest size and fastest insert / select per row in bold — times are in seconds, lower is better; dataset-specific, not a general claim. The `Chimp` numbers in the previous revision of this description were measured against an older encoder revision and are omitted; the qualitative picture for `Chimp` — robust on non-decimal data, slow The trade was made knowingly: the size wins above come from the same revisions, and the encoder keeps a running lane-width floor that abandons hopeless scans mid-vector and a double-buffered winner so no scale is quantized twice. **Comparison with PCodec.** `PCO` is the strongest competitor overall. On ratio it is the smallest floating-point codec on 9 of the 11 columns, and the standalone `pco` CLI compressing each column as one chunk does better still (e.g. mgbench `load_one` 36.7 MB, weather `precipitation` 32.2 MB): per-64-KiB-block operation costs pcodec 20-45 % of its ratio, since every block re-learns its tANS tables and delta state. Against `ALP`, `Wallaby` is smaller on all 11 columns — dramatically so where `ALP`'s Frame-of-Reference degenerates (hits `UserID` 155 MB vs 684 MB, hits `ResolutionWidth` 47 MB vs 142 MB, weather `precipitation` 72 MB vs 132 MB). A correction to earlier revisions of this description: in-engine `PCO` was previously reported as 10-70x slower. That measurement came from a local build affected by a build-system bug that compiles all vendored Rust code with `opt-level = 0` unless `-DSANITIZE=` is passed explicitly (a `contrib/corrosion-cmake` condition mistakes `SANITIZE=OFF` for an enabled sanitizer; CI is unaffected because it always passes the flag). The numbers above are from a corrected build; a separate fix for the build system is being prepared. **Where `Wallaby` is not the winner.** On columns dominated by entropy redundancy rather than numeric structure — the three mgbench columns, weather `precipitation`, hits `ResolutionWidth`/`UserID` — plain `ZSTD` and/or `PCO` produce smaller data. The interesting exception is `precipitation`, where `ALP, ZSTD` wins because `ALP`'s plain Frame-of-Reference lanes on zero-dominated data are almost pure zero bytes, which `ZSTD` collapses better than `Wallaby`'s already-compact XOR runs. Side observation from benchmarking (independent of this PR): for `Nullable` columns the null-map substream appears to be stored uncompressed (+1 byte per row for every codec, including `LZ4`/`ZSTD`) — visible as a constant +22 MB / +31.2 MB across all codecs on the mgbench / sensors columns. Worth a separate look. Correctness: bit-exact round trip is verified by the encoder for every value with a per-value raw-exception fallback (`NaN` payloads, infinities, denormals, signed zeros, arbitrary bit patterns are all preserved; verified on random bit patterns and on all real datasets by multiset checksums in tests; the sensors dataset contributes 9298 genuine `NaN` values). The decoder validates all lengths and bounds, so corrupt input causes an exception, not undefined behavior; a decompression fuzzer target is included. An adversarial review of the current revision additionally round-tripped ~15M hostile values (per-block scale flips, `NaN` payloads, subnormals, domain edges) bit-exactly on both float widths. signal.title: Fix vertical merge nested default corruption
signal.text: ### Summary --- Vertical merge gathers columns one at a time. When a column has `DEFAULT` that references another column which is absent from all source parts and has no `DEFAULT` itself – that dependency is already expired and won't be in the block during evaluateMissingDefaults. Expression engine substitutes a typeless empty value for it, the resulting column gets wrong outer array dimensions, and this corrupts shared Nested offsets when written to the merged part. This is challenge (1) from [#91127](https://github.com/germiBest/ClickHouse/issues/91127). Fix extends existing column expiration logic to transitively expire columns whose DEFAULT depends on already-expired column. Since these columns were never present in any source part, read path was already computing them on-the-fly with full column context available – so expiring them during merge changes nothing for the end user. Fixes [#86123](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/86123). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix silent data corruption during vertical merge when a Nested subcolumn added via ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN has a DEFAULT expression that depends on another missing column without a default. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Add SQLite input/output format
signal.text: ### Changelog category - New Feature ### Changelog entry - Added support for reading and writing data in the SQLite format. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) ### Description Adds the SQLite data format, which allows importing and exporting SQLite database files through ClickHouse formats and the `file` table function. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/33763 The format supports: - Reading from the first user SQLite table in the sqlite database, or a custom table name via `input_format_sqlite_table_name`. - Writing to the default SQLite table named table, or a custom table name via `output_format_sqlite_table_name`. - Schema inference from SQLite declared column types. - Projection pushdown for requested columns. - Complex ClickHouse types by storing their ClickHouse text representation in SQLite TEXT columns and deserializing them back when an explicit ClickHouse structure is provided. Example: ``` SELECT 1 AS id, 'hello' AS name INTO OUTFILE 'data.sqlite' FORMAT SQLite; SELECT * FROM file('data.sqlite', 'SQLite', 'id UInt64, name String'); ``` ### Implementation overview #### Input format - For input, SQLite format first tries to open a local regular file directly when seekable reads are allowed. - If the input is not a local regular file, the data is loaded into memory and opened with `sqlite3_deserialize`. - Rows are read from a prepared SQLite statement and converted into ClickHouse columns. #### Output format - For output, SQLite format writes directly to a local regular file when the output buffer exposes one. - Otherwise, it writes to an in-memory SQLite database first, then serializes it with `sqlite3_serialize` and writes the serialized database image to the output buffer. - Appending to an existing SQLite output file is not supported; users can explicitly truncate the target file with `engine_file_truncate_on_insert`. ### Not implemented yet - Non-local input and non-file output currently materialize the whole SQLite database in memory through `sqlite3_deserialize` / `sqlite3_serialize`, so very large SQLite files may hit memory limits. This is close to the current `Arrow` file data format (https://clickhouse.com/docs/interfaces/formats/Arrow) approach for non-seekable inputs, which also loads the file into memory before opening it as a random-access file. - Filter pushdown is not implemented. It needs careful handling because SQLite and ClickHouse type systems differ, so only partial pushdown may be feasible. The exact scope should be discussed separately before implementation. - Appending rows into an existing SQLite database file or an existing SQLite table is not supported. ### Documented behavior impact A review-driven change within this PR: a SQLite `NULL` read into an explicitly non-`Nullable` ClickHouse column through `ENGINE = SQLite`, the `sqlite` table function, or the `SQLite` database engine now raises the `CANNOT_INSERT_NULL_IN_ORDINARY_COLUMN` exception instead of silently substituting the column type default (which could turn a failing query into a successful one once predicate pushdown drops a `NULL` row remotely). - No documentation promised the old substitution behavior; schema inference is unaffected and maps SQLite columns to `Nullable`, so inferred-schema reads keep working. - The SQLite table engine is not supported in ClickHouse Cloud and requires a local file path, so no Cloud flow is affected. The `SQLite` input format keeps following `input_format_null_as_default`. - Migration: declare the column `Nullable` (the inference default), or exclude `NULL` values in a query-backed table. The behavior is documented in the `SQLite` table engine page in this PR.

signal.title: Add table schema to SQLInsert output
signal.text: Adds the `output_format_sql_insert_include_table_schema` setting for the `SQLInsert` output format. When enabled, `SQLInsert` prepends a `CREATE TABLE` statement derived from the query result schema, making the generated SQL directly replayable into an empty database. The table definition uses the result column names and types with `MergeTree` and `ORDER BY tuple()`. Source-table metadata such as keys, default expressions, codecs, TTLs, and indexes is not preserved. The setting is disabled by default and cannot be enabled together with `output_format_sql_insert_use_replace`. The change includes embedded documentation and stateless coverage for replaying the generated SQL, complex types, identifiers, empty results, batching, and incompatible settings. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/84736 ### Changelog category: - Improvement ### Changelog entry: The `SQLInsert` output format can now prepend a `CREATE TABLE` statement with result column names and types. Enable `output_format_sql_insert_include_table_schema` to produce a ClickHouse SQL script that recreates the table and loads the exported data.

signal.title: Rename `allow_experimental_adaptive_codec_selection` to `enable_adaptive_codec_selection`
signal.text: Renames the MergeTree setting `allow_experimental_adaptive_codec_selection` to `enable_adaptive_codec_selection`. The `allow_experimental_` prefix is the pre-tier way of gating a feature. The `EXPERIMENTAL` tier in the declaration already carries that information and is exposed as `tier` in `system.merge_tree_settings`, so the prefix duplicates it in the one place that is expensive to change later: the name. When the feature graduates, a prefixed name has to be renamed and the old spelling carried as an alias forever. That is why the tree already holds `allow_experimental_analyzer` -> `enable_analyzer`, `allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type` -> `enable_nullable_tuple_type` and `allow_experimental_database_iceberg` -> `allow_database_iceberg`. With the tier doing the gating, graduation becomes a one-word change. `enable_` matches the neighbouring MergeTree booleans (`enable_block_number_column`, `enable_block_offset_column`, `enable_mixed_granularity_parts`). **Why this can be a plain rename.** The setting was added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111834 and has not shipped in any release: its `SettingsChangesHistory` entry sits in the unreleased `26.8` block, which this PR updates in place. So there is no alias, no `MAKE_OBSOLETE` and no compatibility entry, and nothing for `compatibility` to revert. The tier stays `EXPERIMENTAL` and the default stays `false`; only the name changes. The autogenerated settings reference pages (`docs/reference/settings/merge-tree-settings/allow-experimental.mdx`, the manifest, the settings explorer and the legacy-route map) still spell the old name. They are generated from a binary's introspection tables by the nightly docs job (`ci/jobs/docs_autogen_nightly.py`), so they are deliberately not hand-edited here and the setting will move to its new group page on the next run. Hand-written prose in `docs/reference/statements/create/table.mdx` is updated. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111834 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required)

signal.title: Add clickhouse-proxy application mode
signal.text: Implements a new application mode in the `clickhouse` binary, named `proxy`. The proxy accepts connections over end-user ClickHouse protocols, finds the upstream backend based on configurable rules (hostname from TLS SNI or HTTP header, user name, database name, and — for HTTP — query type), and forwards the traffic to it. It is built on the `silk` fiber framework so that many concurrent connections are handled with low RAM usage. Start it with `clickhouse proxy --config-file proxy_config.xml`; a fully commented example config is in `programs/proxy/proxy_config.xml`, and the feature is documented at `docs/en/operations/clickhouse-proxy.md`. **What it does** - Protocol frontends for HTTP(S), native TCP, MySQL, PostgreSQL, transparent TLS-by-SNI, and opaque TCP streams. It handles only end-user protocols (not Keeper or inter-server replication). The user name and database are parsed from the first packets where the protocol allows it (HTTP headers/params/Basic auth, native `Hello`, PostgreSQL `StartupMessage`, HTTP query type). MySQL is server-speaks-first with in-band TLS, so it is forwarded transparently and routed by peer address or the default pool. - TLS routing options: terminate and re-encrypt (the proxy and each backend hold their own certificates), terminate only (unwrap: TLS to clients, plaintext to backends), and transparent (route by SNI without decrypting). Optional ACME certificate provisioning, as in `clickhouse-server`. - Multi-criteria routing rules matching host / user / database / query type / protocol, by exact value or regular expression; regexp captures can be substituted into a backend address template (e.g. route users `ch-<tenant>` to per-tenant backends). - Pools with pluggable load balancing (`random`, `round_robin`, `least_connections`, `lowest_latency`, `least_resources`) behind a common interface; a pool may list several backends for load balancing. - Session stickiness by `session_id` (from the HTTP URL) or by peer address, using a consistent (rendezvous) hash of the backends. - Backend health monitoring (connect latency, consecutive failures) and optional CPU/memory polling with per-backend credentials, feeding the `least_resources` strategy; a JSON status endpoint, `/ping`, and static pages are served by the proxy itself. - An abstract routing table exposing hooks (unknown route, no backends available, first time a user or database is seen) that run a shell command — for example to provision a backend on demand and wait for it to become available. Validated end to end against a live server: HTTP `/ping`, static pages, the status endpoint, GET/POST forwarding, the no-backend error paths, native protocol round-trips, and clean shutdown. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/silk/pull/120 (the `splice` operation this proxy relies on, sent to `silk` upstream) ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new `proxy` mode to the `clickhouse` binary: a lightweight, protocol-aware proxy that routes end-user connections (HTTP, native, MySQL, PostgreSQL, TLS-by-SNI, and raw TCP) to backend servers based on a configurable routing table, with TLS termination/passthrough, load balancing, health checks, and session stickiness. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

Since `show_remote_databases_in_system_tables` defaults to `true`, that database is visible in `system.tables`, `system.columns` and `system.completions`, so a concurrent query scanning those tables without a database filter connects to the unreachable host. The connection failure is logged on the scanning query's own thread, so it reaches that client's stderr, and `clickhouse-test` fails any test whose stderr is non-empty. The polluter stays green and an unrelated test goes red, which makes the failure unattributable from the victim's side. One master hit since the test landed on 2026-08-13: `00938_fix_rwlock_segfault_long` in `Stateless tests (arm_binary, parallel)`, whose whole body is an unfiltered `system.tables` and `system.columns` scan. [CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=5c5dd13e2760e7087bd9a7f5e6e6fa572a2b003f&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28arm_binary%2C%20parallel%29) I add `no-parallel` with a written justification, matching the sibling `04210_show_remote_databases_in_system_tables`, which documents this exact hazard and carries the tag for it. I checked the two alternatives first, and both are impossible rather than merely unattractive: the visibility setting is read from the scanning query's context, so the polluter cannot hide itself (verified: setting it to 0 on the scanner silences the log, setting anything on the creator cannot), and a blackholed address only turns an instant refusal into a connect timeout while still logging, which is why `04210` uses `192.0.2.1` and the tag. Test statements and the reference file are unchanged; the test runs in 0.23 s, so serializing it costs nothing.

signal.title: Fix serialization of Map-valued settings in access entities
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114591 (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a bug where an access entity carrying a `Map`-valued setting, such as a settings profile with `http_response_headers` or `additional_table_filters`, is stored in a form that ClickHouse cannot read back, leaving the entity permanently unloadable after a restart. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114591 `CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE p SETTINGS http_response_headers = '{...}'` succeeds, but the entity is stored as `http_response_headers = [('k', 'v')]`, which nothing can parse back. No error appears at `CREATE` time, so the entity is **permanently unloadable** after a restart: ``` stored: ATTACH SETTINGS PROFILE `p` SETTINGS http_response_headers = [('a', 'b')] CONST; after restart: Code: 62. Syntax error: failed at position 65 ([) ... Could not parse <path>/access/<uuid>.sql ``` The list rebuild drops it silently, reading it back throws, so `SELECT` from `system.settings_profile_elements` fails while it is present, as does `RESTORE` of a backup holding it. Root cause: the value is cast to the setting's native type, so a Map setting holds a `Map` Field, which `FieldVisitorToString` renders as an array of tuples; but `ParserSettingsProfileElement` reads values with a scalar-only `ParserLiteral` and cannot open a `[`. That spelling is rejected everywhere, `SET http_response_headers = [('a','b')]` included, so the write side is wrong. Fix: when a profile element's value, MIN or MAX is a `Map` and the setting is builtin, emit the setting's canonical text as a quoted string. Write side only, no grammar change. Custom settings are excluded because `castValueUtil` returns their value unchanged, so a string would come back a `String` rather than a `Map`. Covers `CREATE USER`/`ROLE`, `ALTER ... SETTINGS` and MIN/MAX, and transitively BACKUP/RESTORE and both storages. `SHOW CREATE` now prints a quoted string rather than `[('k', 'v')]`, intended since the new form is copy-pasteable. Entities already stored in the broken form are not repaired, as they were never parseable; recreate them. Downgrade is safe: a pre-fix binary reads the new form correctly, so no versioning is needed. New test `04902_access_entity_map_setting_round_trip`: 11 of its 16 arms fail on pristine master and pass here, covering empty, multi-key and hostile maps plus a two-process on-disk reload.

signal.title: RFC: Runtime filter transport in DQE
signal.text: Right now a join runtime filter is local to its fragment: the build side creates it and only the `__applyFilter` sites in the same fragment ever see it. So when the probe side is a fact table scan in another stage, we shuffle the whole scan output even though the filter would have killed most of it. I want to ship the filter instead: each build task sends its partial over the exchange layer, the probe-side fragments merge the partials and apply the union, and the pruning happens before the shuffle rather than after. A few things I consider non-negotiable: - fail open: rows pass unfiltered until the merged filter shows up, and a filter that never arrives (or half-arrives) can't change the result - only inclusion filters can travel, an exclusion filter built from a subset of the keys drops rows it shouldn't - wire cost stays bounded by the configured static filter size even when the cardinality estimates are garbage - don't ship at all unless the estimated build key set is small next to the receiving scan None of this is new. It's the Bloomjoin from R* ([Mackert & Lohman, VLDB 1986](https://dblp.org/rec/conf/vldb/MackertL86.html)): ship a hashed bit vector instead of doing a semi-join, in their measurements it beat everything else. The modern take is predicate transfer ([Yang et al., CIDR 2024](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2024/papers/p22-yang.pdf)), which extends the same trick to the whole join graph.

signal.title: Transport join runtime filters across distributed plan stages
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114901 A join runtime filter is currently local to its fragment: the build side creates it and only `__applyFilter` sites in that fragment see it, so a fact table scan in another stage crosses its shuffle exchange in full even if the filter would have removed most rows. If `distributed_plan_join_runtime_filters` is enabled, each build task now ships its partial filter through a bounded fan-in cascade of merge stages, and the final stage broadcasts the complete merged union to the probe-side fragments, which apply it before the shuffle. Everything fails open: rows pass unfiltered until the merged filter arrives, so a filter that never arrives (or half-arrives) can't change results. Only inclusion filters travel, a shipped filter never costs more on the wire than one of the configured static size, and filters are only shipped when the estimated build key set is small compared to the receiving scan. This replaces an earlier prototype where the initiator collected and merged the filters and probe dispatch was rescheduled around filter readiness; here the partials just ride the exchange layer like any other stream, with no new worker operations, no dispatch changes, and no measurable planning cost. New settings: `distributed_plan_join_runtime_filters` (experimental, default off) is the only user-facing one; with it off, plans, wire traffic and results are identical to master, with one sizing-behavior exception: the exact phase of every runtime filter (including local ones under `enable_join_runtime_filters`) is now bounded by its actual key bytes rather than the hash-table buffer size, which moves the exact-to-bloom degradation point—earlier for long string keys (their bytes were previously uncounted) and later for short keys (the buffer, transiently up to ~2 MB per stream at the default 10000-row cap, no longer counts against the byte budget). Results are unchanged either way. The serialized plan additionally gains `join_runtime_filter_exact_bytes_limit`, which carries a transported filter's exact-phase byte budget to the workers. On public ClickHouse the transported exact-phase row cap is taken from the scan's row estimate, not from column-statistics NDV. HyperLogLog undershoots distinct keys, so using NDV as the cap overflowed complete key sets into bloom filters. An unindexed plan-time filter is also treated as unknown for transport sizing, so it keeps the settings geometry instead of letting statistics override it. ### TPC-H SF1000 r7g.4xlarge, ap-south-2, shared io2 volume read-only on every node, 2 warmups + 3 timed runs per variant, medians. Execution time only (planning excluded; it is identical with the setting on and off). | query | 4 nodes | 8 nodes | 16 nodes | exchange saved (4/8/16) | |---|---|---|---|---| | q17 | −77.6% | −65.6% | −60.8% | 202.7 / 202.6 / 202.6 GiB | | q02 | −71.9% | −67.1% | −45.9% | 51.7 / 51.6 / 41.5 GiB | | q20 | −63.7% | −49.6% | −33.9% | 34.6 / 33.7 / 25.3 GiB | | q11 | −42.9% | −27.0% | −17.7% | 25.1 / 24.8 / 23.6 GiB | | q07 | −23.3% | −18.6% | −16.6% | 37.2 / 37.2 / 36.9 GiB | The other ten campaign queries are ties, with one exception: q16 regresses (+0.15 s at 8 nodes, +0.39 s at 16) because a filter that ends up pruning nothing still gets broadcast and the broadcast grows with node count. The admission heuristic should catch this; tracked in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114901. ### TPC-H SF100 on a real network From an earlier prototype, included because it is the measurement over an actual NIC: 4× m8g.4xlarge, 9.53 Gbps between nodes, 0.116 ms RTT, medians of 5. The mechanism differs but the filters, admission logic, and apply sites are the same. | query | single node (s) | dist 4N off (s) | dist 4N on (s) | speedup | |---|---|---|---|---| | q02 | 0.448 | 1.214 | 0.446 | 2.72x | | q03 | 1.585 | 1.498 | 1.075 | 1.39x | | q07 | 1.582 | 1.501 | 1.186 | 1.27x | | q10 | 2.024 | 1.853 | 1.606 | 1.15x | | q11 | 0.317 | 0.593 | 0.293 | 2.02x | | q12 | 1.156 | 0.830 | 0.615 | 1.35x | | q17 | 1.321 | 3.206 | 0.831 | 3.86x | (q04, q09, q13, q14, q16, q19, q20, q22 were flat there; q05/q08/q15/q18 excluded for environment reasons unrelated to the transport.) Plan shapes for the two headline queries, from the SF100 evidence runs: *q17 without the transport, both `lineitem` scans run in full:* *q17 with it, both scans collapse ~996x before their shuffles:* *q02 without the transport, both 80M-row `partsupp` arms feed the join unpruned:* *q02 with it, the union reaches both `partsupp` scans and the cascade collapses:* ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Join runtime filters now travel across distributed plan stages when `distributed_plan_join_runtime_filters` is enabled: build-side tasks ship partial filters over the exchange layer and probe-side scans apply the merged union before their shuffle exchange, dramatically reducing the number of rows crossing the network. All failure modes are fail-open and results never depend on the filters.

signal.title: Count each SSH key against `max_authentication_methods_per_user`
signal.text: The `max_authentication_methods_per_user` check counted each `ssh_key` method as one, regardless of how many keys it held. This meant the same set of keys could pass or fail the limit depending on syntax: `IDENTIFIED WITH ssh_key BY KEY k1 TYPE t1, KEY k2 TYPE t2` counted as one, whereas `IDENTIFIED WITH ssh_key BY KEY k1 TYPE t1, ssh_key BY KEY k2 TYPE t2` counted as two. Now each SSH key counts individually toward the limit, regardless of syntax. This applies to both `CREATE` and `ALTER` statements. From the possible options mentioned in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/70898, I went for the second one (accounting for all SSH keys when checking the limit). This is the least intrusive fix in both user experience (no syntax deprecation) and code changes (no need to refactor the parser). Refactoring the parser would be a bigger change code-wise, as each SSH key would need to emit a separate `ASTAuthenticationData`. Keeping the parser as-is also preserves the user-visible representation (`SHOW CREATE USER`). Existing users are unaffected and continue to work: the limit is only re-validated when the authentication data is created/changed. For testing, I opted for integration tests rather than stateless functional tests. `max_authentication_methods_per_user` is a server-level setting, not settable per session (only via server config), so a stateless test cannot lower it. Relying on the default value of 100 would be fragile. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/70898 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Each SSH key now counts individually toward the `max_authentication_methods_per_user` limit, so the limit applies consistently regardless of syntax. Previously, multiple keys in a single `ssh_key` method counted as one. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1445` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Reject a table reference in the IN operator of a constraint expression
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107424 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A constraint whose `IN` operator had a bare identifier on the right-hand side, such as `CONSTRAINT c CHECK a IN (b)`, silently rewrote it into a table reference `default.b` and persisted it. The resulting table rejected every `INSERT` with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`, and the server refused to start once the referenced column was dropped. Such a constraint is now rejected with `BAD_ARGUMENTS` when it is supplied by `CREATE TABLE`, a full-definition `ATTACH TABLE`, or `ALTER TABLE ... ADD/MODIFY CONSTRAINT`, and when it is copied by `CREATE TABLE ... AS` or `CLONE AS`. Existing tables keep loading. ### Description `AddDefaultDatabaseVisitor` turns an `IN` right-hand side into a table identifier. Correct in a SELECT, where `x IN t` is shorthand for `x IN (SELECT * FROM t)`, but wrong for a constraint, evaluated against the inserted row. The rewritten AST is persisted. Measured on master, for `CHECK a IN (b)` with `b` a column: `SHOW CREATE` reports a constraint the user never wrote (`IN (default.b)`), and every `INSERT` fails `Code: 47 UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`. Dropping that column makes the metadata unloadable, fatal at startup. Found on `Stress test (amd_msan)` in three unrelated PRs, as the fuzzer's operand-swapped mutation of `02841_not_ready_set_constraints`. This adds `checkConstraintExpressionIsValid`, mirroring #107424's key-expression check, applied only to user-supplied DDL. The recursion stops at subquery boundaries, so `IN <table>` inside a subquery keeps working. **Cases found in review.** `CREATE TABLE ... AS src` and `CLONE AS src` parse no declaration; they copy the source constraints, so a legacy source could seed the shape into a new table. Copied constraints go through the same gate. An `ALTER` command that stores nothing (`ADD ... IF NOT EXISTS` on an existing name, `MODIFY ... IF EXISTS` on a missing one) stays accepted as on master, judged against the commands preceding it in the same statement. **What this removes.** Where the identifier names an existing table the constraint did work, but only in the process that parsed the DDL: the load path never applies that visitor, so after a restart `INSERT` fails `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`. I reject it rather than keep a form that write-deads a table at the next restart. Tell me if you would rather keep it. Unlike #107424 I do not reject at load time: such metadata exists in the wild. Existing tables keep loading, stay ALTER-able including `DROP CONSTRAINT`, and Replicated databases still recover them.

signal.title: Let functions answer `canThrow` instead of deriving it from short-circuit suitability
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/55656 `IExecutableFunction::canThrow` decides whether the rows that a query does not reference have to be removed from `ColumnReplicated` arguments before a function is executed. It was derived from `isSuitableForShortCircuitArgumentsExecution`, with a `TODO` in `IFunctionAdaptors.h` asking for a dedicated interface. Those two properties answer different questions, and they disagree in both directions: - a function that is expensive but cannot throw is reported as throwing - this only loses an optimization; - a function that is cheap but can throw is reported as not throwing - this is not safe. Comparisons are the second case. `FunctionComparison` declares itself unsuitable for lazy execution because a comparison is cheap, so it was reported as never throwing, while a comparison does throw while it is executed: ```sql SELECT count() FROM numbers(3) WHERE toDate('2020-01-01') = 'garbage'; -- Code: 38. DB::Exception: Cannot parse date: value is too short: while converting 'garbage' to Date (CANNOT_PARSE_DATE) ``` This adds `IFunction::canThrow` so that a function describes the property on its own, and describes it for comparisons: whenever both sides are compared the way they are stored, or only the narrower side is widened - numbers, strings, `Date` with `Date32`, equal decimal, `DateTime64` and `Time64` scales, and equal types compared by `IColumn::compareAt` - a comparison cannot throw, which keeps the fast path for the overwhelming majority of queries. The cases that have to interpret one of the sides report that they can throw: a string parsed as a date or a tuple, a string validated against an enum, or different decimal scales brought to a common scale. `isNotDistinctFrom` is described the same way and additionally requires the two types to be equal, because it casts both sides to their common type first. `repeat` now says explicitly that it can throw - it throws `TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE` depending on the data of a single row. Its answer does not change (it is suitable for lazy execution, so the old approximation already reported `true`), but the property is now stated where it belongs instead of following from an unrelated one. The default implementation still falls back to the old approximation, so no function other than the comparisons changes its behaviour, and the `TODO` is narrowed to the remaining work: annotate more functions, then make the default the conservative `true`. Verified locally by compiling the affected translation units (`equals.cpp`, `less.cpp`, `isNotDistinctFrom.cpp`, `repeat.cpp`, `IFunction.cpp`) and by checking the added test against a build of `master`, where its results are the same - the compaction of unreferenced rows is invisible in the results, only in whether an exception can escape. The rest is left to CI. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required)

signal.title: [WIP] Byte stream split Codec
signal.text: ### Changelog category Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry Added experimental ByteStreamSplit codec for fixed-width columns. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) **Motivation:** : Floating-point and integer columns often have bytes at the same positional offset that are nearly identical across rows (e.g. the exponent byte of Float32 values in a narrow range). Grouping those bytes together can sometimes increases the compressibility of the data for general-purpose compressors. In tests on public GeoIP IPv6 datasets, this approach improved compression ratios by 2.43x over standard Zstd and 3.85x over LZ4. Similar gains were observed in UUIDv7 data, where BSS-LZ4 outperformed standard LZ4 by 1.94x. I also reproduced the https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PARQUET-1716, and it saw similar gains in scientific floating point datasets. Because the ipv6 was my target use case, I added specialization for w=16 bytes so the performance is acceptable. **Enabling:**: The codec is gated behind the experimental codecs setting: ```sql SET allow_experimental_codecs = 1; ``` **Parameters:**: ByteStreamSplit accepts one optional integer argument — the element byte width. When omitted, the width is inferred from the column data type. - No argument (default) — element width inferred from column type (e.g. 4 for Float32, 8 for Float64, 16 for UUID/IPv6) - Explicit integer (e.g. ByteStreamSplit(4)) — override the element width; useful with FixedString Supported types: Any fixed-size type with element width ≥ 2: Float32, Float64, Int16/32/64/128, UInt16/32/64/128, Date, DateTime, DateTime64, IPv4, IPv6, UUID, FixedString(N) for N ≥ 2 and N<=255 (for now) Need to see if FixedString(N) is worth it. **Example use:** ```sql SET allow_experimental_codecs = 1; CREATE TABLE example ( val_f32 Float32 CODEC(ByteStreamSplit, LZ4), val_f64 Float64 CODEC(ByteStreamSplit, ZSTD(1)), val_u128 UInt128 CODEC(ByteStreamSplit(16), LZ4), val_fs FixedString(8) CODEC(ByteStreamSplit(8)) ) ENGINE = MergeTree() ORDER BY val_f32; ``` ### Implementation - Registered under method byte 0x9d. - Maximum element width: 255 bytes. ### Testing - Tested using my Harness in the misc_script_folder and using in real dataset, need to run the clickhouse static test. - Benchmark Compression: [Google Sheet](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1h-Rcg6oXKD6pdf_GzaEe0YUvP41-K32B0idnsNAy-GU/edit?gid=0#gid=0) - Benchmark Speed: #### Specs - CPU: Intel i7-12500H (Alder Lake) - Data: 256–500 MiB, multiple rounds with inner iterations - Compiler: Clang -O2 #### Results Median (GB/s) | W | Ours Encode | Ours Decode | Arrow Encode | Arrow Decode | Speedup Encode | Speedup Decode | |-----|------------|------------|--------------|--------------|----------------|----------------| | 1(memcopy) | **19.4** | **19.9** | **19.4** | **19.9** | **1.0×** | **1.0×** | | 2 | 10.5 | 10.8 | 9.7 | 10.7 | 1.08× | 1.01× | | 4 | 10.4 | 10.8 | 10.0 | 10.9 | 1.04× | 0.99× | | 8 | 9.1 | 10.3 | 10.5 | 10.9 | 0.87× | 0.94× | | 16 | 7.4 | 10.2 | 4.6 | 4.7 | 1.61× | 2.17× | | 20 | 5.1 | 5.5 | 4.5 | 4.6 | 1.13× | 1.20× | | 32 | 4.9 | 5.4 | 3.7 | 4.1 | 1.32× | 1.32× | | 64 | 4.5 | 5.2 | 2.5 | 2.6 | 1.80× | 2.00× | | 128 | 4.5 | 4.6 | 2.4 | 2.4 | 1.88× | 1.92× | ***Arrow supports W > 255; ours would need VLA or dynamic allocation.***

signal.title: Re-land: make Ctrl+C terminate the output of a result set in the client promptly
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/22426 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106430 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107845 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107828 ### Description This re-lands #106430 ("Make Ctrl+C terminate the output of a result set in the client promptly"), which was reverted by #107845, and folds in the data-race fix from the (now closed) #107828 so the feature can land safely this time. Why it was reverted: `BuzzHouse (amd_tsan)` reported a ThreadSanitizer data race on master (STID 5296-4b74) on the client's persistent stdout buffer (`std_out`, an `AutoCanceledWriteBuffer<WriteBufferFromFileDescriptor>`). The interruptible-output feature installed a cancellation hook on `std_out` at the start of `processOrdinaryQuery` and cleared it via `SCOPE_EXIT({ std_out->setCancellationHook({}); })` at the end of the same scope. When the result set is written with parallel formatting, `ParallelFormattingOutputFormat` runs a background collector thread that writes through `std_out` and reads its `cancellation_hook` in `WriteBufferFromFileDescriptor::nextImpl`. On the normal end-of-stream path the collector is joined by `output_format->finalize` before the scope guard runs, so the clear is safe; but on paths that leave `processOrdinaryQuery` by an exception without first finalizing the output (a `NetException`, or a `LocalFormatError` rethrown from `receiveResult`), the scope guard cleared the hook while the collector thread was still alive and reading it — a data race on the `std::function`. The fix (from #107828): the hook is cleared in `resetOutput` right after `output_format.reset()`, which destroys the parallel formatter and joins its collector thread, so the mutation is single-threaded with respect to `std_out`'s hook. The hook is also re-pointed for the teardown flushes that follow: on normal completion the interrupt handler is still armed and is honored, so a fresh Ctrl+C keeps interrupting a flush to a slow or stuck stdout; on exception paths the handler is already stopped (its `cancelled` is then unconditionally true), so the genuine cancellation flag is used instead to avoid discarding already-produced output. `resetOutput` runs on every exit path and at the start of the next query, so `std_out` (which outlives a single query) never carries a stale hook into the next query. The pager and `INTO OUTFILE ... AND STDOUT` buffers are per-query and destroyed in `resetOutput` after the collector join, so they were never affected. The change is split into two commits: the first reapplies #106430 verbatim (a revert of the revert #107845); the second folds in the #107828 fix, confined to `src/Client/ClientBase.cpp`. The low-level `WriteBufferFromFileDescriptor` (used server-wide on a hot single-threaded write path) is unchanged by the fix. Revert that motivated this: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107845 TSAN report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=73e97deb9abbc3258e75d297aabfc3fbe7c3ca5e&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_tsan%29&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_tsan%29 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Pressing Ctrl+C in `clickhouse-client`/`clickhouse-local` now promptly stops printing a large result set, even when the output is being written to a slow or stuck destination such as a slow terminal. Previously the first Ctrl+C could appear to have no effect. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Stop exchange sinks when the consumer needs no more data
signal.text: A distributed-plan query with a satisfied `LIMIT` kept all upstream stages running to completion: an exchange sink consumed and dropped the rest of the stream after the consumer sent `NoMoreDataNeeded`, so the client received the result while the query kept running until cancelled. Now the sink closes its input instead, and the stop propagates backward through the stages the same way a local `LimitTransform` stops its producers. The in-memory exchange reader also detaches when its output port is closed, not only on cancellation. The new test covers a `LIMIT` in the middle of the plan: the stage that satisfies it finishes early and the stop crosses two exchange layers down to the scans. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A distributed plan query (`make_distributed_plan`) now stops its upstream stages when a `LIMIT` is satisfied, instead of computing the full result and discarding it. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: Fix ANY INNER JOIN with OR conditions depending on which table is built
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114354 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114676 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111645 `ANY INNER JOIN` returns one row per key, from both the left and the right table. With several `OR`-ed conditions in `ON`, the key of a condition was claimed through the used flag of the right row that the key is stored for — and one right row can be the stored row of a different key in each condition, so claiming it for one key silently retired the others. The result therefore depended on which side the hash table was built from. On the dataset from the issue, `t1 ANY JOIN t2` returned 3 rows and `t2 ANY JOIN t1` returned 6, and the same query returned 3 or 6 depending on `query_plan_join_swap_table`, which is a plan setting and must not change the result. `JoinUsedFlags` now keeps one flag array per condition, indexed by the cell of that condition's map, exactly as `per_offset_flags` does for a single condition, so the claim names the key of a condition rather than a right row. A left row visits every condition instead of stopping at the first match, so it may be joined once per condition whose key it claims — hence `ANY INNER JOIN` results are replicated now. The residual-condition path (`joinRightColumnsWithAdditionalFilter`) claims the same way, after applying the filter to the candidates of a key. The outcome is the union of the single-condition joins: a pair of rows matching through several conditions is joined once per condition, and the number of result rows no longer depends on the probe order, on the order the tables are written in, or on the plan. Deduplicating those pairs instead was measured to leave the row count dependent on which left row claims a key first, and so on the probe order — 39 runs out of 40 disagreed with the 40th at `max_threads = 8`. That semantics change moves two existing references, both for pairs that match through more than one condition: - `01660_join_or_inner`: `2 3 2 3` is returned twice, matching both `a2 = a3` and `b2 = b3`; - `03006_join_on_inequal_expression_fast_2`: `(1, 1, 1) INNER ANY JOIN (1, 1, 1) ON t1.a = t2.a AND (t1.b > 0 OR t2.b > 0)` returns its row twice, and in `ON t1.key = t2.key AND t1.a < t2.a OR t1.a = t2.a` one left row is now dropped because another left row with the same key claimed it, as single-condition `ANY INNER JOIN` already does. `SEMI`, `ANTI` and the `LEFT`/`RIGHT` forms of `ANY` are unaffected: their unit is the right row, which a per-row flag expresses exactly, and every branch added here is gated on `INNER` + `ANY`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `ANY INNER JOIN` with several `OR`-ed conditions in the `ON` section returning a different number of rows depending on which table the hash table is built from, that is on the order the tables are written in and on the `query_plan_join_swap_table` setting. Such a join now returns one row per key of every condition, from both tables.

signal.title: Fix Block structure mismatch when the split filter column name clashes with an input
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108142 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108210 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a logical error `Block structure mismatch in IntersectOrExceptStep stream: different number of columns` that could happen when the filter split optimization (`query_plan_split_filter`) ran on a `WHERE` whose filter column name is also an input column name. The optimization left an internal `__split_filter` column in the branch output header, which then diverged from the sibling branch of a set operation such as `INTERSECT` or `UNION`. ### Description `trySplitFilter` hand-rolled a workaround for the case where the filter column name is also an input name: it called `ActionsDAG::splitActionsForFilter` without `avoid_duplicate_inputs`, then renamed the first matching output of the first DAG half to the literal `__split_filter`. That rename landed on the pass-through input rather than the promoted computed node, and it used the removal verdict computed for the original name in the other half, so the inner `FilterStep` could keep the column. The outer `ExpressionStep` cannot drop it, because the second half's inputs still carry the original name and `ActionsDAG::updateHeader` passes through unmatched header columns. The synthetic name therefore reached the branch output header, and `IntersectOrExceptStep::checkHeaders` compared a 4-column header with the sibling's 3 columns. `ActionsDAG::split(nodes, /*mapping=*/ true, /*avoid_duplicate_inputs=*/ true)` already solves the same collision correctly: it renames the promoted node in the first half and repairs the second half by adding an input under the new name while rewriting the old node into an `ALIAS` onto it. This PR deletes the hand-rolled workaround, passes both flags inside `splitActionsForFilter` (it has a single caller, so the signature and `ActionsDAG.h` are unchanged), and takes the filter column name from `split_nodes_mapping`, the same idiom as `splitSingleAndFilter` in `FilterStep.cpp`. `__split_filter` no longer exists anywhere in the source. The rename only fires on a genuine collision, so plans without one are unchanged. Found by the AST fuzzer on an unrelated PR: `AST fuzzer (amd_msan)`, https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=63383&sha=7141227edb42247eb136d0a095b99491123deabe&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_msan%29 (STID 0993-315b). Same family as #108142 and #108210. This is a logical error, so it is an exception that is handled normally in release builds and an abort in debug and sanitizer builds. Minimal reproducer, which fails on master and passes with this change: ```sql SELECT x FROM (SELECT arrayJoin([materialize(1), NULL]) AS x GROUP BY NULL) WHERE NULL INTERSECT DISTINCT SELECT 1; ``` The same header leak also aborts with `UNION ALL` and `EXCEPT`. The new test `04628_split_filter_name_clash_header_leak` covers all three, and asserts both that the optimization fired and the branch output header column count, so it fails if the optimization is disabled and if the internal column reappears under any name. It also checks the result values of a second query whose filter column name is an input name and whose value is consumed downstream. Value equivalence against the unsplit (`query_plan_split_filter = 0`) plan was verified across a matrix of clash shapes. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Backported to: `26.7.4.21`, `26.6.3.40`, `26.5.7.44` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Handling `max_authentication_methods_per_user` setting for multiple ssh keys in user authentication
signal.text: The new setting `max_authentication_methods_per_user` was introduced in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/65277. It is possible to specify multiple SSH keys for user authentication as a single method: ```sql IDENTIFIED WITH ssh_key BY KEY 'public_key' TYPE 'ssh-rsa', KEY 'another_public_key' TYPE 'ssh-ed25519', KEY 'another_public_key' TYPE 'ssh-dsa' ``` The example above is treated as one authentication method, but in reality, it involves three separate keys. Using the new multi-authentication method syntax, it can be rewritten as: ```sql IDENTIFIED WITH ssh_key BY KEY 'public_key' TYPE 'ssh-rsa', ssh_key BY KEY 'another_public_key' TYPE 'ssh-ed25519', ssh_key BY KEY 'another_public_key' TYPE 'ssh-dsa' ``` While functionally equivalent, the second option considered as three separate authentication merhods. Question: Should this behavior remain as it is, or should there be adjustments to handle this scenario? Possible options include: 1. Introducing a breaking change that requires a new syntax (e.g., enforced use of the BY keyword). 2. When checking if the limit has exceeded, account for the list of ssh keys that can be used for authentication. 3. Refactoring the parser to treat the first syntax as multi-authentication rather than a single method with multiple keys. 4. Leaving the current behavior unchanged. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #111181 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1445` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Avoid repeated EXPLAIN ANALYZE clock lookups for staged processors
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Performance Improvement** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): - **Avoid repeated wall-clock registry lookups in **EXPLAIN ANALYZE** for multi-stage processors.** ### Why this matters - `StepWallClockRegistry::find()` is keyed by the query-plan step and processor group. - The cache pointer was stored, but the group stayed at its default value of `0`. - For non-default groups, such as aggregation finalization and join build/probe, the old code repeated the lookup for every task. - Normal query execution is unchanged because this registry is only used by **EXPLAIN ANALYZE**. ### Changes - **Store:** the group together with the clock pointer after lookup. - **Keep:** the existing retry behavior when no clock is found. - **Use:** the cached-clock alias consistently in the condition. ### Benchmark This is a focused microbenchmark of the cache lookup section, not end-to-end **EXPLAIN ANALYZE** latency. Setup: Apple arm64, Apple Clang `-O3`, stable group `1`, matching registry entry, 10,000,000 tasks, 9 rounds, median result. | Version | Registry lookups | Median time | Relative | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Before | 10,000,000 | 25.89 ms | 1.00x | | After | 1 | 3.21 ms | 8.07x faster | The lookup count is exact. Wall-clock time is machine-dependent. ### Validation - `git diff --check` - **Validation:** Focused cache lookup microbenchmark - **Validation:** Existing **EXPLAIN ANALYZE** coverage for aggregation and join stages
