signal.title: Support PromQL histogram_fraction for classic histograms
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **PromQL: support `histogram_fraction()` for classic histograms.** ### Description **What was missing** Prometheus supports `histogram_fraction(lower, upper, b)` for estimating the fraction of observations between two bounds. ClickHouse previously rejected this function in TimeSeries PromQL queries. **What this PR adds** - **Add:** support for classic Prometheus bucket series. - Reuses the existing classic histogram handling used by `histogram_quantile`. - Matches Prometheus behavior for interpolation and bucket edge cases. - Keeps different histogram metric names separate during aggregation. - Removes the input metric name from the result. Example: ```promql histogram_fraction(0.1, 0.5, http_request_duration_seconds_bucket) ``` ### Why this matters **This is used for real latency and SLO queries**, not only parser compatibility. - **Pyrra:** generates `histogram_fraction()` in native-histogram latency SLO rules. See the [query generator](https://github.com/pyrra-dev/pyrra/blob/main/slo/promql.go#L761-L784) and [example SLO config](https://github.com/pyrra-dev/pyrra/blob/main/examples/pyrra-connect-latency.yaml#L14-L20). - **Grafana SLO:** uses it in a [request-latency SLI query](https://grafana.com/docs/plugins/grafana-slo-app/latest/sli-examples/latency/). - **Grafana Mimir:** documents it for calculating the [fraction of requests in a latency range](https://grafana.com/docs/mimir/latest/visualize/native-histograms/). - **Prometheus:** uses it for [fraction and Apdex calculations](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/histograms/). Without this function, PromQL copied from these workflows fails in ClickHouse. ### Scope - **Supported:** classic `*_bucket` histogram series. - **Supported:** constant scalar lower and upper bounds. - **Not supported yet:** native histogram samples. - **Not supported yet:** non-constant bound expressions. Native histogram samples are not supported by the current TimeSeries Engine. This PR intentionally covers the classic bucket form first. ### References - [Prometheus histogram functions](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#histogram_fraction) - [Prometheus classic histogram implementation](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/quantile.go) ### Changes - **Function support:** add `histogram_fraction` to the TimeSeries function registry and support documentation. - **Execution:** add a Prometheus-compatible classic histogram fraction aggregate. - **Shared logic:** reuse the histogram SQL-building pipeline with `histogram_quantile`. - **Precision:** preserve Float64 bound literals for Float32 tables and exact cumulative-count differences for large UInt64 counts. ### Tests - **Interpolation:** normal buckets, `rate()` input, negative bucket bounds, and bounds inside buckets. - **Bucket edges:** exact boundaries, degenerate buckets, `+Inf`, `NaN`, malformed `le`, and out-of-range bounds. - **Grouping:** range queries with multiple histogram groups and `sum by (le)` aggregation. - **Input validation:** invalid argument types and non-constant bounds. - **Float32:** regression coverage for precision near an `le` boundary. - **UInt64:** regression coverage for one-count differences above `2^53`. - **Compliance:** add classic histogram fraction queries to the PromQL compliance cases. - **Checks:** `git diff --check` and Python syntax validation for the integration test files.
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Support PromQL @ start() and @ end() modifiers
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Improvement** ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **PromQL: support `@ start()` and `@ end()` timestamp modifiers.** ### Summary PromQL allows `start()` and `end()` as special values for the `@` modifier. They mean the fixed start and end of a range query. For an instant query, both resolve to the evaluation time. Without this support, valid PromQL such as `http_requests_total @ start()` and `rate(http_requests_total[5m] @ end())` cannot be used against ClickHouse. Fixed-`@` subqueries keep their complete inner time grid and remain step-invariant across the outer range query. Standalone `start()` and `end()` functions are not included. ### Why this matters This is standard PromQL surface used by major Prometheus-compatible systems: - VictoriaMetrics has executable range-query tests for both `time() @ start()` and `time() @ end()`. - Grafana Mimir, Thanos, and Cortex replace these modifiers with fixed timestamps before splitting range queries, including subqueries. - Elasticsearch includes `@ start()`, `@ end()`, and subquery forms in its valid PromQL grammar fixtures. These are public implementation and compatibility references, not a claim about private customer query volume. Supporting the syntax keeps dashboards and recording/alerting queries portable across Prometheus-compatible backends. References: - **[Prometheus Querying basics:** `@` modifier](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/basics/) - [VictoriaMetrics executable tests](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics/blob/master/app/vmselect/promql/exec_test.go#L1207-L1227) - [Grafana Mimir query splitting](https://github.com/grafana/mimir/blob/main/pkg/frontend/querymiddleware/split_and_cache.go#L2838-L2948) - [Thanos query splitting](https://github.com/thanos-io/thanos/blob/main/internal/cortex/querier/queryrange/split_by_interval.go#L593-L690) - [Cortex query splitting](https://github.com/cortexproject/cortex/blob/master/pkg/querier/tripperware/queryrange/split_by_interval.go#L1061-L1157) - [Elasticsearch valid PromQL grammar fixtures](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/esql/qa/testFixtures/src/main/resources/promql/grammar/queries-valid.promql#L1112-L1122) ### Changes - **Add:** `start()` and `end()` to the PromQL timestamp grammar. - **Preserve:** the symbolic modifier in the Prometheus query tree. - **Resolve:** the symbols against the outer query boundaries during evaluation. - **Keep:** offset and range-selector handling consistent with numeric `@` timestamps. - **Preserve:** the complete inner grid for fixed-`@` subqueries. ### Tests - **Coverage:** parser coverage for both symbols, modifier order, literals, and subqueries. - **Coverage:** instant and range query coverage, including a range selector under `@ end()`. - **Coverage:** `last_over_time()` coverage for symbolic and numeric `@` on subqueries. - **Comparison:** the new range-query cases with Prometheus through the existing integration helpers. - **Generated artifacts:** the ANTLR parser artifacts.
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Support quoted PromQL grouping labels
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Support quoted label names in PromQL grouping modifiers.** ### Summary Prometheus accepts quoted label names in grouping modifiers. ClickHouse previously only accepted identifier-style tokens there. Prometheus 3.x supports UTF-8 label names, and OpenTelemetry uses dotted resource attributes such as `service.name`, `deployment.environment`, and `k8s.namespace.name`. When a PromQL backend preserves these names, grouping queries need the quoted form. This comes up with OpenTelemetry-aware dashboards and backends that keep the original label names instead of converting dots to underscores. Examples: - `sum by ("service.name", "k8s.namespace.name") (http_requests_total)` - `max without ("deployment.environment") (http_request_duration_seconds)` - `http_requests_total + on ("service.name") group_left ("pod.name") target_info` - `http_requests_total / ignoring ("cluster.name") group_right ("instance.name") target_info` ### Changes - **Allow:** quoted strings in `by`, `without`, `on`, `ignoring`, `group_left`, and `group_right` lists. - **Unquote:** and validate the names before passing them to the PromQL tree. - Quote non-legacy names again when serializing the tree back to PromQL. - **Use:** PromQL-specific escaping for serialized strings, including control bytes. ### Tests - **Generated artifacts:** ANTLR output from the grammar. - **Coverage:** `gtest_PromQLParser` coverage. - **Coverage:** realistic quoted-label queries to `04131_prometheus_query_parser`. - **Coverage:** invalid empty quoted-label coverage. - **Coverage:** parse/serialization/parse round-trip coverage for an escaped NUL label. References: - [Prometheus UTF-8 in Prometheus](https://prometheus.io/docs/guides/utf8/) - [Using Prometheus as your OpenTelemetry backend](https://prometheus.io/docs/guides/opentelemetry/) - [Prometheus query language parser](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/tree/main/promql/parser)
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Accept signed PromQL @ timestamps
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Accept signed numeric timestamps in PromQL @ modifiers.** ### Summary PromQL allows an optional `+` or `-` sign before a numeric timestamp in an `@` modifier. ClickHouse previously accepted only unsigned timestamps. This change accepts signed timestamps and preserves negative values in the PromQL query tree. It also keeps negative evaluation times safe for TimeSeries tables with non-negative timestamp types. For `DateTime` and `UInt32` storage, selector ranges are clipped at the Unix epoch instead of allowing negative timestamps to wrap to a large positive value. `DateTime64` continues to support pre-epoch timestamps. Examples: - `http_requests_total @ -100` - `http_requests_total @ +3.3e1` - `http_requests_total @ 1700000000` ### Changes - **Allow:** an optional sign before numeric timestamps in the PromQL grammar. - **Preserve:** negative timestamps in the query tree. - Clip selector ranges to the supported timestamp range for `DateTime` and `UInt32` TimeSeries storage. - **Keep:** negative timestamps available for signed `DateTime64` storage. ### Tests - **Coverage:** parser coverage for negative timestamps. - **Coverage:** parser coverage for explicitly positive scientific timestamps. - **Coverage:** integration coverage for `UInt32`, `DateTime`, and `DateTime64` TimeSeries timestamp types. - **Coverage:** negative timestamps before the Unix epoch and positive timestamps whose lookback range crosses the epoch. - **Generated artifacts:** the ANTLR parser artifacts. References: - [Prometheus query basics](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/basics/)
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Preserve 64-bit row counts in PostgreSQL CommandComplete
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Preserve PostgreSQL protocol row counts above the signed 32-bit range.** ### Description - The PostgreSQL handler tracks affected rows as `UInt64`. - `CommandComplete` narrowed the count to `Int32`, so counts above 2147483647 could be reported as negative. - **Keep:** the count as `UInt64` through command-tag formatting. ### Tests - **Coverage:** a byte-level unit test for serializing `UInt64::max()`. - **Cases:** git diff --check`
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Reject overlapping PromQL on and grouping labels
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Reject PromQL binary expressions that use the same label in both `on(...)` and `group_left(...)` or `group_right(...)`.** ### Why this matters The label lists have different jobs in PromQL vector matching: - `on(job)` makes `job` part of the match key. - `group_left(job)` or `group_right(job)` copies `job` from the "one" side into the result. Using the same label for both is redundant because an `on(...)` match already requires the values to be equal. Prometheus rejects it during parsing: ```promql foo + on(job) group_left(job) bar ``` ```text label "job" must not occur in ON and GROUP clause at once ``` The exception for `ignoring(...)` is intentional. A label excluded from the match key can still be copied from the "one" side into the result, so this remains valid: ```promql foo + ignoring(job) group_left(job) bar ``` This behavior has been part of Prometheus vector matching since [prometheus/prometheus#1571](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/1571), merged in 2016. It is also stated in the current [vector matching documentation](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/operators/#many-to-one-and-one-to-many-vector-matches) and enforced in the [Prometheus parser](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/parse.go#L788-L794). ClickHouse previously parsed the invalid forms and only kept the two label lists separately. ### Description - **Check:** the intersection after parsing the matching and group label lists. - **Apply:** the check to both `group_left` and `group_right`. - **Match:** the Prometheus error message. - **Keep:** overlapping `ignoring(...)` expressions valid. - **Add:** focused parser coverage for the invalid and valid forms. ### Tests - **Coverage:** PromQL parser tests for `group_left`, `group_right`, distinct labels, and the `ignoring(...)` exception. - **Cases:** git diff --check`
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: PromQL: Use native 64-bit division for common TimeSeries bucket indexing
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Performance Improvement** ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Use native 64-bit division for common `timeSeries*ToGrid` bucket indexing while preserving overflow-safe behavior for extreme timestamp ranges.** ### Description `bucketIndexForTimestamp` is called for every sample added to a `timeSeries*ToGrid` aggregate. It currently promotes the timestamp offset to `Int128` before division and modulo, even when the offset fits in `Int64`. This puts wide integer division on the common per-sample path. The change keeps the existing overflow-safe behavior while avoiding wide division when it is not needed: - **Calculate:** `timestamp - start_timestamp` with `common::subOverflow`. - **Use:** native `Int64` division and modulo when the subtraction succeeds. - Fall back to the existing `Int128` calculation when the subtraction overflows. - **Keep:** split-point and final bucket-index arithmetic in `Int128`. The fallback is important for grids spanning the signed 64-bit boundary, such as `start = INT64_MIN` with a positive timestamp. Normal PromQL query ranges take the native path, while those extreme inputs keep the current wide arithmetic. #### Performance Isolated benchmark of the changed arithmetic: | | Before | After | |---|---:|---:| | Time per sample | 7.958 ns | 1.819 ns | | Throughput | 125.652 M samples/s | 549.696 M samples/s | This is a **4.38x speedup** for the bucket-index arithmetic, not an expected full-query speedup. The performance test includes a bucketing-heavy query that assigns 4 million samples to two grid buckets per series. This keeps finalization small while retaining 4 million calls to the changed code. #### Validation - The native and wide implementations produced identical results across 5,000,486 boundary and fixed-seed random inputs. - The existing `04106_timeseries_bucket_count_overflow` regression exercises the overflow fallback with `start = INT64_MIN`, `step = INT64_MAX`, and positive samples. - A new case in the same regression covers the native path with `timestamp - start_timestamp = INT64_MAX` and verifies that the sample reaches the expected bucket.
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Use compensated summation for PromQL sum
signal.text: ### Description PromQL `sum` currently uses the regular `sumForEach` aggregate, while Prometheus uses compensated summation for floating-point samples. For example, summing ten series with the value `0.1` produces `0.9999999999999999` with ordinary sequential accumulation, while Prometheus returns exactly `1`. This adds a dedicated `sumPrometheus` aggregate and lowers PromQL `sum` to `sumPrometheusForEach`. It follows Prometheus's compensated addition for samples, including its handling of infinities. A separate aggregate is needed because the existing `sumKahan` behavior is not equivalent for these cases. The aggregate state stores the running sum and correction so partial states can still be combined by ClickHouse's parallel and distributed aggregation. As with other floating-point aggregates, merging independently accumulated states can produce a different result from Prometheus's serial evaluation for order-sensitive inputs. Exact bit-for-bit reproduction would require preserving the original sample order across partial states. The goal here is to improve PromQL sum accuracy while keeping normal ClickHouse aggregation behavior. The integration tests cover fractional values, merged aggregate states, repeated same-sign infinities, and opposite-sign infinities, and compare the PromQL results with Prometheus. ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Use compensated summation for PromQL `sum` aggregation to reduce floating-point errors.**
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Fix PromQL stddev and stdvar for large finite values
signal.text: ### Description PromQL `stddev` and `stdvar` were using the numerically unstable ClickHouse variance aggregates. With two equal samples of `1e155`, squaring the values overflows and the result becomes `NaN`, even though the expected population variance is `0`. This switches the PromQL lowering to `stddevPopStableForEach` and `varPopStableForEach`. I also added integration coverage for both operators that compares the results with Prometheus. ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Fix PromQL `stddev` and `stdvar` returning `NaN` for large finite values whose variance is representable.**
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Fix mixed-case PromQL aggregation operators
signal.text: ### Description PromQL keywords are case-insensitive, and the grammar already accepts mixed-case aggregation operators. However, the parser kept the original spelling in the query tree, so expressions such as `SuM(up)` reached lowercase-only lowering dispatch and failed as unsupported. This change normalizes aggregation operator names when building the query tree. The normalization is limited to aggregation expressions, so metric names such as bare `SUM` and case-sensitive function names keep their original spelling. Parser coverage includes mixed-case `sum`, mixed-case `topk` with grouping, and preservation of the bare `SUM` metric name. ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **PromQL aggregation operators now accept mixed letter casing, matching Prometheus.**
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Fix PromQL DateTime64 offset scaling
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Fix PromQL offset queries for TimeSeries tables with DateTime64 timestamps.** ### Description The DateTime64 path in applyOffset currently rounds the timestamp scale with std::max(..., 9). Since DateTime64 supports scales up to 9, this always selects scale 9. As a result, PromQL offset queries use a nanosecond interval even for millisecond or microsecond timestamps. For example, a fractional offset query can fail with ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT. Use std::min to cap the rounded scale at 9. This keeps second, millisecond, microsecond, and nanosecond offsets on the matching interval function. The integration coverage adds a fractional offset query and runs it with both the default millisecond and microsecond timestamp layouts. ### Tests - **Checks:** --check - **Checks:** -m py_compile tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_different_table_engines.py - **Checks:** ./promql/parser
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Fix PromQL changes for consecutive NaNs
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **PromQL: do not count consecutive NaN samples as changes.** ### Description PromQL changes() compares consecutive samples in a range vector. The ClickHouse implementation used curr != prev, which treats NaN -> NaN as a change because NaN is not equal to itself. Prometheus explicitly treats consecutive NaN samples as unchanged. The time-series summary predicate now follows Prometheus for changes(), while the resets() path remains unchanged. The regression test uses changes(vector(NaN)[80:10]) and expects zero changes. Prometheus documents changes() [here](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#changes), and its implementation [explicitly excludes the NaN -> NaN case](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/functions.go#L2464-L2468). ### Tests - **Checks:** --check - **Checks:** -m py_compile tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Fix negative subquery timestamp alignment in PromQL
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Align negative PromQL subquery timestamps to the preceding step.** ### Description alignTimestampWithStep currently uses the signed C++ remainder directly. For a negative timestamp that is not divisible by the step, this rounds toward zero instead of down to the previous step. When a subquery offset makes its effective timestamp negative, the evaluation grid can therefore move forward by one step. This change normalizes negative remainders before subtracting them, so timestamps are aligned to the greatest step boundary not greater than the input. ### Tests - PromQL subquery regression using `vector(time())[40s:20s] offset 31s` at outer timestamp 10, which exercises effective timestamps below the Unix epoch. - **Checks:** -m py_compile tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py - **Checks:** --check
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Parse PromQL octal numeric literals
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Parse PromQL legacy octal numeric literals with Prometheus-compatible semantics.** ### Summary Prometheus parses integer literals with base 0 before falling back to floating-point parsing. As a result, `0755` and `-0755` are parsed as `493` and `-493`, while values such as `08`, `0759`, `0755.0`, and `0755e1` still use decimal parsing. ClickHouse's PromQL parser previously used decimal parsing for all non-hexadecimal, non-duration numbers, so `0755` was parsed as `755`. This change adds a narrow octal pre-pass for integer-shaped literals. Invalid octal digits, floating-point forms, and integer overflow continue through the existing decimal parser. The behavior follows the Prometheus parser: - [Prometheus number parsing](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/parse.go#L650-L660) - [Prometheus octal parser tests](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/parse_test.go#L109-L136) ### Tests Added parser coverage for: - **Cases:** 0755` and `-0755` - **Cases:** 0_755` - Decimal fallback cases `08`, `0759`, `0755.0`, and `0755e1`
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Reject zero-length PromQL ranges
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Reject zero-length PromQL ranges and explicit zero subquery steps, round positive selector ranges up to the table timestamp precision, and reject unrepresentable explicit subquery steps.** ### Summary Prometheus rejects zero-length range selectors and explicit zero subquery steps. ClickHouse previously accepted them because the parser only checked the duration syntax. The parser now rejects zero and negative range or explicit step values. Positive selector ranges that are finer than the table timestamp precision are rounded up to the next representable tick, while positive explicit subquery steps that are not representable at that precision are rejected. Omitted steps such as `up[5m:]` and positive unit durations such as `up[1ms]` remain valid. Duration-unit exactness is calculated from the original millisecond remainder, so large whole-second durations are not misclassified when a higher-precision representation would overflow. ### Tests Added parser coverage for zero and negative ranges, zero and unrepresentable steps, positive unit and decimal ranges, scientific notation, large durations, ceiling overflow, and omitted steps.
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Accept PromQL line comments at EOF
signal.text: ### Description PromQL line comments currently require a newline, so valid queries with a trailing comment at EOF, such as `up # trailing comment`, are rejected by ClickHouse. Prometheus consumes line comments through CR, LF, or EOF and skips comment tokens before parsing the expression. This change matches that behavior, regenerates the checked-in ANTLR lexer artifacts, and adds coverage for EOF, LF, CRLF, adjacent comments, and comment-only input. Upstream references: - [Prometheus lexer](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/lex.go#L874-L882) - [Prometheus line-ending handling](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/lex.go#L1123-L1125) - [Prometheus parser comment handling](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/parse.go#L2817-L2855) - [Prometheus comment-only query test](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/parse_test.go#L3206-L3220) ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Accept PromQL line comments that end at EOF.**
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Fix PostgreSQL startup payload bounds check
signal.text: ### Description `StartupMessage::deserialize` tracked the remaining declared payload in `ps`, but checked the unchanged `payload_size` after reading each parameter pair. The check therefore could never reject parameter data that extended beyond the declared startup-message payload. The unbounded null-terminated reads could also consume subsequent stream bytes before detecting the mismatch. Parse startup parameters through a `LimitReadBuffer` restricted to the declared payload, validate message lengths before subtraction, require the final zero terminator, and normalize only EOF and boundary failures to `UNKNOWN_PACKET_FROM_CLIENT` while preserving unrelated read errors. Regression tests cover valid parameters, a valid empty parameter section, invalid lengths and terminators, parameters truncated inside both a name and a value, exact stream-boundary preservation, and preservation of unrelated exception codes. ### Documented behavior impact No documented flow changes. This only rejects malformed PostgreSQL startup messages whose parameter data exceeds their declared payload size. Valid PostgreSQL clients require no migration, and no corresponding behavior is documented in either the ClickHouse repository or the current documentation repository. ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Reject malformed PostgreSQL startup messages whose parameter data exceeds the declared payload size.**
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Fix PromQL sgn() for NaN and negative zero
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **PromQL: preserve NaN and negative zero in sgn().** ### Description Prometheus sgn() returns -1 when the sample is less than zero, 1 when it is greater than zero, and the original sample otherwise. The current ClickHouse lowering maps sgn() directly to sign(). For NaN, ClickHouse sign() returns 1, and for negative zero it returns an ordinary zero. The PromQL lowering now mirrors Prometheus with multiIf(x < 0, -1, x > 0, 1, x). The generic ClickHouse sign() function is unchanged. Prometheus documents sgn() [here](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#sgn), and its implementation [returns the original value in the default branch](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/functions.go#L1889-L1900). The regression tests cover sgn(vector(NaN)) and sgn(vector(-0)). ### Tests - **Checks:** --check - **Checks:** -m py_compile tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py
signal.author: fallintoplace

signal.title: Docs: add `NOSIGN` to public `s3` documentation queries
signal.text: Update anonymous public S3 documentation examples to pass `NOSIGN` explicitly following the ClickHouse 26.7 server credential behavior change. This prevents public reads from attempting to use server-managed credentials. The audit also found and repairs two stale public paths: the LAION guide now uses the surviving 10-million-row shard, and the S3 brace-expansion example references the four files that currently exist. Authenticated, requester-pays, write, placeholder, and Foursquare examples are intentionally outside this PR. Related: https://linear.app/clickhouse/issue/DOC-945/update-public-s3-docs-examples-to-use-nosign ### Changelog category (leave one): - Documentation (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Updated public S3 documentation examples to use `NOSIGN` and repaired stale public dataset paths.

signal.title: Docs: Replace `Native` format Mermaid diagrams with static SVGs
signal.text: Replace the seven client-rendered Mermaid diagrams in the `Native` format specification with optimized, lazy-loaded static SVGs. It also adds an Interfaces navigation group for the companion `Native Protocol` and `Native Format` specifications so both pages are discoverable from the reference sidebar. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Documentation (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Not for changelog.

signal.title: Fix flaky test_long_disconnection_stops_backup: allow transient UNKNOWN_TABLE
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108459 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Description Residual flakiness after #108459 (which fixed `test_shutdown_cancels_backup` and part of `test_long_disconnection_stops_backup`). `test_long_disconnection_stops_backup` still fails intermittently with: ``` AssertionError: assert ('UNKNOWN_TABLE' in [] or 'UNKNOWN_TABLE' in ['FAILED_TO_SYNC_BACKUP_OR_RESTORE', 'KEEPER_EXCEPTION', 'SOCKET_TIMEOUT', 'CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA', 'NETWORK_ERROR', 'TABLE_IS_READ_ONLY', 'NO_REPLICA_HAS_PART']) ``` raised by `NoTrashChecker.__exit__` (test_cancel_backup.py:375), which asserts every error observed in `system.errors` during the scenario is in `expect_errors` or `allow_errors`. Under a long ZooKeeper disconnection a replica can briefly observe `UNKNOWN_TABLE` during backup teardown. This is a benign transient in the same error family as the entries already tolerated for this scenario, so the checker wrongly rejects it as unexpected. Fix: add `UNKNOWN_TABLE` to `allow_errors` for this scenario, mirroring how `NO_REPLICA_HAS_PART` was added to this same list in commit e55610d4100 (#96961). The meaningful assertions are unchanged: the `"Lost connection"` check, the `3 < elapsed < 45` timing bound, and the `BACKUP_FAILED` status check.

signal.title: Array subscript operator supports array of integers as index.
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108095 The array subscript operator now accepts an array of integers as the index, so `arr[indexes]` gathers the elements at all of those positions at once. It is equivalent to `arrayMap(i -> arr[i], indexes)`, including the result type, the handling of negative indexes and the value produced for an out-of-range position, but it has its own implementation: a constant source array is not materialized per row, and numeric element types are gathered through the `PODArray` directly. ```sql SELECT [10, 20, 30, 40][[2, 4, 1]]; -- [20,40,10] SELECT [10, 20, 30][[1, 5, -1]]; -- [10,0,30] SELECT arrayElementOrNull([10, 20, 30], [1, 5]); -- [10,NULL] SELECT [10, 20, 30][[1, NULL, 2]]; -- [10,NULL,20] ``` The positions may be nullable, and a `NULL` position produces `NULL`, just as for a scalar index. The main use case is a lookup table: a constant dictionary array indexed by a per-row array of positions. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The array subscript operator supports an array of integers as the index: `arr[indexes]` returns the elements at all of the given positions, equivalently to `arrayMap(i -> arr[i], indexes)`.

signal.title: Preserve unchanged TOAST values in MaterializedPostgreSQL
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/83517 Preserve PostgreSQL columns encoded as unchanged TOAST references in `MaterializedPostgreSQL` replication instead of replacing them with default values. The consumer resolves the previous value from an earlier row in the same replication buffer when possible. Otherwise, it reads the current row from the nested `ReplacingMergeTree` by replica identity, batching key lookups to avoid a query per value. The old replica identity tuple is used when an update changes the key. An unchanged TOAST value in a replica identity column is rejected because the replication message does not contain a value that could identify the row. The integration test covers a regular update, multiple updates of the same row in one PostgreSQL transaction, and a replica identity change. The user-facing documentation is updated for both `MaterializedPostgreSQL` engines. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `MaterializedPostgreSQL` now preserves unchanged PostgreSQL `TOAST` values during updates instead of replacing them with default values.

signal.title: Fix startup hang when `max_thread_pool_size` is too small
signal.text: Setting `max_thread_pool_size` to a value that is too small made `clickhouse-server` hang forever at startup instead of reporting the problem. A `ThreadFromGlobalPool` created while all the threads of the global thread pool are already taken by other such jobs was silently put into the pool's queue instead of getting a thread. The queue is much larger than the number of threads by default (`thread_pool_queue_size` is 10000 against `max_thread_pool_size`), so scheduling succeeded, but nothing ever picked the job up, because the threads are held by jobs that never return. Its creator got a seemingly running thread whose function was never called, and any code that then waited for that thread to make progress hung forever. An idle server permanently occupies about 200 threads of the pool for the workers of the background pools and of the background schedule pools, and for the flush threads of the system logs, so a `max_thread_pool_size` below that ran out of threads while starting up: * With `max_thread_pool_size` of 128 the starved job was the loader worker of the `system` database, and startup hung forever right after `Wait load job 'startup Atomic database system'`. * With 100 it hung in the constructor of the merge/mutate background executor instead. * Values between roughly 130 and 200 appeared to start, but silently left some background threads unstarted - for example the flush threads of the system logs, so those tables never received any data. Jobs that occupy their worker for the whole lifetime of that worker are now scheduled through `ThreadPoolImpl::scheduleThreadOrThrow`, which hands them one of the `max_threads` slots at scheduling time and throws `CANNOT_SCHEDULE_TASK` naming `max_thread_pool_size` when there is none left, rather than queueing a thread that can never start. Two components started threads in their constructor and stopped them only in their destructor, so the resulting exception left those threads running while the destructor of the member thread pool blocked forever joining them. Both now stop their workers before letting the exception out, following the pattern `CacheDictionaryUpdateQueue` already uses: * `MergeTreeBackgroundExecutor` - this was the second hang above. Its `increaseThreadsAndMaxTasksCount` now starts the additional workers on a best-effort basis, so a configuration reload does not fail when the pool is saturated, and it reports the number of workers that actually started. * `BackgroundSchedulePool` - its handler used to `LOG_FATAL` and `abort`, turning a misconfiguration into signal 6 and a crash report. It now logs the same hint and rethrows, so the server exits cleanly. Note that the hint in that handler ("Please make sure max_thread_pool_size is considerably bigger than background_schedule_pool_size") was previously unreachable, because saturating the global pool never produced `CANNOT_SCHEDULE_TASK`. **Behaviour change.** Values of `max_thread_pool_size` that cannot hold the permanent threads of the server now make it refuse to start with a clear error naming the setting, where some of them used to start in a silently degraded state. This looks like the intended contract: `max_thread_pool_size` is documented as the maximum number of threads in the pool, and the documentation of `thread_pool_queue_size` already recommends keeping it equal to `max_thread_pool_size`, which makes saturation an error today. The requirement is now documented on the setting itself. No test configuration is affected: `tests/casa_del_dolor/properties.py` randomises `max_thread_pool_size` only down to 700. Tested by starting a server with values of 16, 32, 64, 100, 128 and 160 (all fail with the error, no `abort`, no crash report) and 192, 256 and the default (all start normally), plus a check for slot accounting leaks under concurrent load with `max_thread_pool_size` of 400. The full `unit_tests_dbms` suite passes, including `FunctionsStress`. The pre-existing `ThreadPool.GlobalFull1` and `ThreadPool.GlobalFull2` tests did not catch this because they give the global pool a queue as small as its thread count, which makes saturation fail on queue fullness instead. The new `ThreadPool.GlobalFullLargeQueue` covers the shape of the real pool, and the `test_thread_pool_size_too_small` integration test asserts that the server terminates with the error rather than hanging. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a hang at server startup when `max_thread_pool_size` was set too small to hold the threads that the server occupies permanently. Such a configuration is now reported with an error naming the setting, instead of hanging forever or starting with some background threads missing.

signal.title: Parquet: map TIME logical type to Time64
signal.text: The native Parquet reader currently maps both `logical.TIMESTAMP` and `logical.TIME` (and the deprecated converted types `TIMESTAMP_MILLIS`/`TIMESTAMP_MICROS`/`TIME_MILLIS`/`TIME_MICROS`) to `DataTypeDateTime64`. That was fine before ClickHouse 25.6, when there was no time-of-day type, but it now produces the Parquet analogue of #104038: when the target column is `Time64` and `session_timezone` is non-UTC, the `DateTime64 -> Time64` cast (PR #90310) shifts the value by the timezone — silent data corruption for a value that has no date/timezone to begin with. This PR splits the schema-converter branch so that: - `logical.TIME` / `TIME_MILLIS` / `TIME_MICROS` → `DataTypeTime64(scale)` (timezone-unaware). - `logical.TIMESTAMP` → `DataTypeDateTime64(scale, timezone)` (unchanged). It also extends `is_output_type_decimal` to recognize `Time64` so min/max stats stay enabled when the output column is `Time64`, and removes the stale comment that claimed ClickHouse has no time-of-day type. While covering explicit type hints in the test (`SELECT * FROM file(..., 'Parquet', 't Time')`), I hit a second pre-existing gap from 25.6: `Time64 -> Time` was never registered as a cast — it threw `CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE` because `IsDataTypeNumber<DataTypeTime>` is `false` (it inherits `DataTypeNumberBase<Int32>`, not `DataTypeNumber<Int32>`). Before this PR the path went `DateTime64 -> Time` and returned a wrong, timezone-shifted value; after the Parquet fix it would have thrown. The second commit adds an inline `Time64 -> Time` branch in `ConvertImpl` that divides by the scale multiplier — no timezone offset, because both Time64 and Time are timezone-unaware seconds-of-day. A new stateless test `04277_parquet_time_of_day` covers: - Schema-less inference (Parquet `time32[ms]`/`time64[us]`/`time64[ns]` → `Nullable(Time64(3/6/9))`; `TIMESTAMP` stays `Nullable(DateTime64(6, 'UTC'))`). - Import into `Time64(scale)` columns under `session_timezone = 'Asia/Shanghai'` (values must not shift). - Explicit type hints under non-UTC session: `Time64(3)` / `Time` / `DateTime64(3, 'UTC')` / `Int64`. Review follow-up: making `Time64 -> DateTime` legal also exposed that `ToDateTimeMonotonicity` treated `Time64` sources as monotonic, while the cast wraps negative time-of-day values with the default `date_time_overflow_behavior = 'ignore'` (`-00:00:01` -> `2106-02-07 06:28:15`), i.e. it drops at zero. `toDateTime` now reports non-monotonic for `Time`/`Time64` sources; the regression test `04828_time64_to_datetime_not_monotonic` shows that without the guard the key condition prunes every granule and range/point queries over a `Time64` key silently return empty results. The Parquet docs (`docs/reference/formats/Parquet/Parquet.mdx`) are updated for the new `TIME` -> `Time64` mapping. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix Parquet `time32`/`time64` columns being read as `DateTime64` and then silently shifted by `session_timezone` when inserted into a `Time64` target column. Parquet `TIME` logical types now map directly to `Time64`, and a previously-missing `Time64 -> Time` cast is added. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Add mutation completion time `finish_time` to `system.mutations`
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/89216 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105255 Adds a `finish_time` column to `system.mutations` reporting when a mutation was completed; `0` means the mutation is not finished yet or its completion time is unknown. This is a rework of #105255 that avoids any new persistent state: no mutation-file format changes and no new Keeper znodes, so there is no upgrade path, no cleanup changes, and no retry/idempotency concerns. For non-replicated `MergeTree` tables the value is tracked in memory (like `latest_fail_time`) and stamped only when the completion is observed by the event that caused it: the commit of the last mutated part, or the creation of a mutation that has no parts to process. Mutations whose completion moment was not observed (entries loaded at startup, parts removed by `DROP PARTITION`) report `0` instead of a fabricated timestamp. For `ReplicatedMergeTree` tables the value is per-replica and equals the modification time of the replica's `mutation_pointer` znode — the write that marks mutations done on the replica. After the replica state is reloaded (e.g. server restart), the completion time of the mutation the pointer points at is restored from the znode `mtime`; older completed mutations report `0`. A cluster-wide completion time can be obtained with `max(finish_time)` grouped by `mutation_id` across replicas. Note for the CH Inc sync: `SharedMergeTree` constructs `MergeTreeMutationStatus` positionally and will need a follow-up to populate `finish_time`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a `finish_time` column to `system.mutations` that records when a mutation was completed. Unfinished mutations and mutations whose completion time is unknown report zero. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: Add server setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread`
signal.text: Each thread accumulates up to `max_untracked_memory` (4 MiB by default) of allocations before reporting them to the server-wide `MemoryTracker`. With many threads, this unreported memory can sum to a large amount, causing the server's tracked memory usage to under-count actual consumption and leading to OOM. This PR introduces a server-level setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread` (default 4 MiB) and speculatively charges this amount to the server-wide `MemoryTracker` for each worker thread of a `PipelineExecutor`, including query, merge, and mutation pipelines. The global tracked memory becomes a tighter upper bound on actual consumption. The reservation is charged on the server-wide (total) tracker only — deliberately not through the query's tracker chain. Query-level accounting feeds heuristics that compare memory deltas against byte thresholds (conversion of aggregation hash tables to two-level via `group_by_two_level_threshold_bytes`, spill-to-disk decisions), and phantom reservations of `num_threads * 4 MiB` trip those thresholds immediately: an earlier revision of this PR that charged the query tracker showed consistent slowdowns of GROUP BY queries in performance tests for exactly this reason. With the server-wide-only reservation, query-level and user-level accounting (`max_memory_usage`, `memory_usage` in `system.processes`) are unaffected. The speculative reservation uses the throwing path of the memory tracker, so when it would exceed the server memory limit the corresponding job is treated as failed with `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — the same behavior as if the job itself had exceeded the limit. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new server setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread` (default 4 MiB) which speculatively reserves this amount on the server-wide `MemoryTracker` for each worker thread of a `PipelineExecutor`, including query, merge, and mutation pipelines. It compensates for the up to `max_untracked_memory` of unreported allocations per thread, making server-wide tracked memory a tighter upper bound on actual consumption and reducing the risk of OOM with many concurrent pipeline workers. Query-level and user-level memory accounting are not affected. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <details> <summary>Modify your CI run</summary> **NOTE:** If your merge the PR with modified CI you **MUST KNOW** what you are doing **NOTE:** Checked options will be applied if set before CI RunConfig/PrepareRunConfig step #### Include tests (required builds will be added automatically): - signal.title: Apply read in order with ORDER BY for plan-based parallel replicas
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114723 Plan-based parallel replicas (`parallel_replicas_plan_based`) splits the plan at the reading step into a `UNION` of a local read and a fragment shipped to the replicas. The split marker was lifted through `Expression`/`Filter`/`Aggregating`/`Union`/`Join`, but not through `SortingStep`, so for a plain `ORDER BY` the sort stayed on the initiator above the union and neither the local half nor the shipped fragment contained a `Sorting` above the read. `ReadFromMergeTree::requestReadingInOrder` was therefore never called on either side and both announced `CoordinationMode::Default`: results were correct, but the read-in-order optimization was lost compared to classic parallel replicas, which uses `ReadPoolParallelReplicasInOrder` for the same query. The split now lifts through `SortingStep` the same way it already does through `AggregatingStep`: a full sort is cloned into the fragment and the initiator keeps a `MergingSorted` sort above the union. Each side then re-derives read-in-order from the same sort description and they agree on `WithOrder` / `ReverseOrder` - `ReverseOrder` was not reachable under plan-based parallel replicas before. Since `SortingStep::serialize` drops the limit, a top-N is restated as an explicit `LimitStep` inside the fragment, as `tryMakeDistributedSorting` already does; it is skipped when an enclosing `LIMIT` has `alwaysReadTillEnd`, so `exact_rows_before_limit` stays exact. This also fixes a pre-existing failure on the same path: `tryOptimizeTopK` injects an internal `__topKFilter` function that is not registered in `FunctionFactory`. It was suppressed for `make_distributed_plan` but not for plan-based parallel replicas, so `SELECT ... ORDER BY <non-primary-key> LIMIT n` failed on the replica with `Unknown function __topKFilter`. A read that carries Top-K is now excluded from the shipped fragment (`mergeTreeReadCanBeShipped`), so such a query stays local and keeps its Top-K filtering instead of being distributed. Suppressing Top-K up front instead was rejected: enabling `parallel_replicas_plan_based` does not by itself mean the plan gets shipped, so that would silently lose Top-K for queries that end up running locally anyway. Verified locally against a three-replica cluster: `ReadType: InOrder` / `InReverseOrder` and `ReadPoolParallelReplicasInOrder` are reached, the coordinator logs `WithOrder` and `ReverseOrder`, and results stay identical to non-parallel execution for `ORDER BY` with `LIMIT`, deep `OFFSET`, filters, `WITH TIES`, `LIMIT BY`, `exact_rows_before_limit` and a full-sorting merge join. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Apply the read-in-order optimization to `ORDER BY` queries when `parallel_replicas_plan_based` is enabled: the sort is now shipped to the replicas and merged on the initiator, so each replica reads in the sorting key order. Also fixes `Unknown function __topKFilter` for `ORDER BY` on a non-primary-key column with this setting enabled.

signal.title: fix: error message for ALTER DROP COLUMN of a key column
signal.text: <!-- PR title: Fix error message for ALTER DROP COLUMN of a column used in a key expression --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/71776 Related follow-up issues: #114481, #114181 `ALTER DROP COLUMN` and `ALTER CLEAR COLUMN` behaved inconsistently on a column that belongs to `ORDER BY`, `PRIMARY KEY` or `PARTITION BY` An `ALTER` is validated by building the new table schema first and inspecting it afterwards. Once the column is gone the sorting key cannot be resolved, so building the schema fails before the check that knows the real reason. That check is now done first, on the current schema, where the key columns are already known. It understands all the ways a key can refer to a column: the column itself, a column inside a key expression, a subcolumn (`ORDER BY a.x` for `a Tuple(...)`) and a whole nested group dropped by its common prefix Examples: 1. Basic ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a UInt64, b UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a; ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN a; -- before: Code: 47. Missing columns: 'a' while processing: 'a' ... (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) -- after: Code: 524. Trying to ALTER DROP key a column which is a part of key expression. (ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN) ``` 2. Dropping a column that is used only in a TTL expression now also reports which TTL expression it breaks Note: `ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN` would be wrong here. Dropping a column used in a `TTL` is not always forbidden - `ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN d, MODIFY TTL a + INTERVAL 1 DAY` is valid and passes. And this is a wrapper not a check: the same step returns `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` for `MODIFY COLUMN d Array(UInt8)`, which `ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN` would mislabel ```sql CREATE TABLE t (d Date, a UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a TTL d + INTERVAL 1 DAY; ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN d; -- before: Code: 47. Missing columns: 'd' ... (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) -- after: Code: 47. Cannot apply ALTER because it breaks the TTL of the table: Missing columns: 'd' ... (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) ``` 3. For a key column the command is rejected whatever the partition is, so the old error only sent the user to fix something that would not help ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a UInt64, b UInt64, c UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree PARTITION BY b ORDER BY a; ALTER TABLE t CLEAR COLUMN a IN PARTITION 'nonsense'; -- before: Code: 53. Cannot convert string 'nonsense' to type UInt64. (TYPE_MISMATCH) -- after: Code: 524. Trying to ALTER CLEAR key a column ... (ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN) ``` 4. With `share_nested_offsets` enabled, a name that is not a column of the table denotes the whole nested group `<name>.*`, and `DROP`/`CLEAR` of the group is now rejected the same way when any column of the group is used in a key. Before, this was worse than a confusing message: the checks compare names exactly and did not see the group, so `DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS n` destroyed the group's data with a mutation that then failed halfway and `CLEAR COLUMN n` on a non-empty table left a mutation that can never finish (a key column cannot be rewritten) in `system.mutations` until `KILL MUTATION` ```sql CREATE TABLE t (`n.a` UInt64, `n.b` UInt64, x UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY `n.a`; ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN n; -- before: Code: 47. Missing columns: 'n.a' while processing: '`n.a`' ... (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) -- after: Code: 524. Trying to ALTER DROP whole Nested group n whose columns (`n.a`) are part of key expression. (ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN) ALTER TABLE t CLEAR COLUMN n; -- before: accepted, data of `n.a` and `n.b` is zeroed and the mutation stays in system.mutations forever -- after: Code: 524. Trying to ALTER CLEAR whole Nested group n whose columns (`n.a`) are part of key expression. (ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN) ``` Groups with no key columns inside are dropped as before, and with `share_nested_offsets = 0` the name does not denote the group and the check does not apply. The remaining group/exact-name mismatches (silent data destruction for groups without key columns, dependent views, races with background mutations) predate this PR and are reported separately with reproductions ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN` of a column that is used in the sorting, primary or partition key now fails with `ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN` and an explanation, the same as `ALTER TABLE ... CLEAR COLUMN` does. Previously it failed with a confusing `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER: Missing columns` error coming from the recalculation of the key expressions. The same applies to dropping or clearing a whole `Nested` group by its common prefix when a column of the group is used in a key; previously that could silently destroy the group's data or leave a mutation that never finishes. Dropping a column that is used only in a `TTL` expression now also reports which TTL expression it breaks

signal.title: Iceberg writer declares `timestamp` (without zone) in metadata but writes Parquet with `isAdjustedToUTC=true` — CH-written tables with DateTime are unreadable by pyiceberg
signal.text: **Describe what's wrong** When ClickHouse writes an Iceberg table containing a `DateTime` or `DateTime64` column, the table metadata and the data files contradict each other: - the Iceberg schema declares the column as `timestamp` — which the [spec](https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#primitive-types) defines as *microsecond precision **without** timezone*, and whose required [Parquet mapping](https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#parquet) is `timestamp(isAdjustedToUTC=false, unit=MICROS)`; - the Parquet data files are written with `isAdjustedToUTC=true` (`timestamp[us, tz=UTC]`). Spec-following readers refuse the combination. pyiceberg 0.10.0 fails the scan of every ClickHouse-written Iceberg table that contains a timestamp column: ``` ValueError: Unsupported schema projection from timestamp[us, tz=UTC] to timestamp[us] ``` Either consistent choice would fix interoperability: declare `timestamptz` in the Iceberg schema (arguably the right mapping for `DateTime`, which is epoch-based instant semantics), or write the Parquet files with `isAdjustedToUTC=false`. ClickHouse's own reader accepts its own output, so the bug is invisible in ClickHouse-only round-trips. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on master 26.8.1.1375, on every write. Same behavior for `DateTime` and `DateTime64(6)`. **How to reproduce** ```bash clickhouse local --path . --query " CREATE TABLE t (k Int64, ts DateTime) ENGINE = IcebergLocal('\$PWD/ice/', 'Parquet') SETTINGS allow_insert_into_iceberg = 1; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, toDateTime('2026-01-01 00:00:00') + number * 3600 FROM numbers(50) SETTINGS allow_insert_into_iceberg = 1; " grep -ho '"type" : "timestamp[^"]*"' ice/metadata/*.json | sort -u python3 - <<'PY' import glob import pyarrow.parquet as pq from pyiceberg.table import StaticTable print(pq.read_schema(sorted(glob.glob('ice/data/**/*.parquet', recursive=True))[0]).field('ts').type) t = StaticTable.from_metadata(sorted(glob.glob('ice/metadata/*.metadata.json'))[-1]) t.scan().to_arrow() PY ``` **Expected behavior** Metadata and data files agree — either `timestamptz` + `isAdjustedToUTC=true`, or `timestamp` + `isAdjustedToUTC=false` — and external readers can scan the table. **Actual behavior** ``` "type" : "timestamp" timestamp[us, tz=UTC] ValueError: Unsupported schema projection from timestamp[us, tz=UTC] to timestamp[us] ``` Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114848 (the same writer also serializes day/hour partition transform names non-canonically; both were found probing writer output against external readers). Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).
signal.author: zlareb1

signal.title: Iceberg writer serializes day/hour partition transforms as non-canonical `days`/`hours`, breaking external readers (pyiceberg: UnknownTransform)
signal.text: **Describe what's wrong** The Iceberg writer serializes the `day` and `hour` partition transforms under the non-canonical plural names `days` / `hours` in the table metadata. The [Iceberg spec](https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#partition-transforms) defines the transform names as `year`, `month`, `day`, `hour` (singular), and that is what other writers emit. Spec-following readers do not recognize the plural forms: pyiceberg 0.10.0 parses them as `UnknownTransform(transform='days')`, so a ClickHouse-written time-partitioned Iceberg table silently loses its partition information (and with it partition pruning) in external readers. The writer is also internally inconsistent: the *sort order* serialization path maps the same functions to the canonical singular names (`{"toRelativeDayNum", "day"}, {"toRelativeHourNum", "hour"}` in `parseFunction`, `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Iceberg/Utils.cpp`), while the *partition spec* path emits the plural (`getPartitionField` writes `"days"` / `"hours"`, same file). `year` and `month` are emitted correctly in both paths. ClickHouse's own reader is lenient (`parseTransformAndArgument` accepts `day`, `date`, `days`, `dates`, …), so the bug is invisible in ClickHouse-only round-trips — it only breaks interoperability, which is the main reason to write Iceberg metadata in the first place. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on master 26.8.1.1375, on every write. **How to reproduce** ```bash clickhouse local --path . --query " CREATE TABLE t (k Int64, ts DateTime) ENGINE = IcebergLocal('\$PWD/ice/', 'Parquet') PARTITION BY (toRelativeDayNum(ts)) SETTINGS allow_insert_into_iceberg = 1; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, toDateTime('2026-01-01 00:00:00') + number * 3600 FROM numbers(100) SETTINGS allow_insert_into_iceberg = 1; " grep -ho '"transform" : "[^"]*"' ice/metadata/*.json | sort -u ``` **Expected behavior** ``` "transform" : "day" ``` **Actual behavior** ``` "transform" : "days" ``` And through pyiceberg 0.10.0: ```python from pyiceberg.table import StaticTable t = StaticTable.from_metadata('ice/metadata/<latest>.metadata.json') print([repr(f.transform) for f in t.spec().fields]) # ["UnknownTransform(transform='days')"] ``` `PARTITION BY (toRelativeHourNum(ts))` produces `"transform" : "hours"` with the same result. `toYearNumSinceEpoch` / `toMonthNumSinceEpoch` correctly produce `year` / `month`. Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).
signal.author: zlareb1

signal.title: S3Queue `after_processing='move'` silently destroys a consumed file on a basename collision (default `move_preserve_path=false`)
signal.text: ### Company or project name _(quality/durability testing)_ ### Describe what's wrong With `after_processing = 'move'` and an `after_processing_move_prefix` set, S3Queue relocates each consumed object to `<move_prefix>/<basename>`, because `after_processing_move_preserve_path` defaults to `false`. When two consumed objects share a basename under different source prefixes — e.g. `data/a/part.csv` and `data/b/part.csv`, both matched by a glob like `data/*/part.csv` — they both resolve to the **same** destination key `<move_prefix>/part.csv`. The move is a per-object copy-then-delete (`ObjectStorageQueuePostProcessor::moveWithinBucket`): `copyObject(src -> dst)` followed by `removeObjectIfExists(src)`. So the second object's `copyObject` **overwrites** the first at the destination, and both source objects are then deleted. An S3 overwrite is not an error, so no exception is raised, nothing is logged, and `ObjectStorageQueueMovedObjects` counts both moves as successful. Net effect: one consumed file's content is permanently destroyed — gone from the source, overwritten at the destination — while the queue reports both files moved. The `move` action exists specifically to *retain* consumed files (audit, replay, or relocating them out of the ingest prefix), so this silently violates the very guarantee the feature provides, and it happens with the default settings. Same-basename objects across prefixes are common in practice (e.g. partitioned exports `date=2026-01-01/part.csv`, `date=2026-01-02/part.csv`). ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce - ClickHouse version 26.8 (also present in current master). - Object storage layout — two files that share the basename `part.csv` under different prefixes, with distinct content: - `s3://<bucket>/data/a/part.csv` → rows `0..9` - `s3://<bucket>/data/b/part.csv` → rows `100..109` ```sql CREATE TABLE dst (id UInt64, val UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; CREATE TABLE q (id UInt64, val UInt64) ENGINE = S3Queue('https://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/data/*/part.csv', '<key>', '<secret>', 'CSV') SETTINGS mode = 'unordered', keeper_path = '/clickhouse/s3q_move_demo', after_processing = 'move', after_processing_move_prefix = 'archive'; -- after_processing_move_preserve_path defaults to false CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv TO dst AS SELECT id, val FROM q; ``` After both files are consumed: ```sql SELECT count(), uniqExact(id) FROM dst; -- 20, 20 → both files were ingested/acked ``` List the bucket: ``` archive/part.csv <- ONE object (only one file's content survives) data/a/part.csv, data/b/part.csv <- both GONE (deleted after the move) ``` One consumed file's bytes are destroyed. Setting `after_processing_move_preserve_path = 1` avoids it — the archive then keeps both `archive/data/a/part.csv` and `archive/data/b/part.csv`. ### Expected behavior Every object retained by `after_processing = 'move'` should survive exactly once. A destination-key collision under the default `after_processing_move_preserve_path = false` should not silently overwrite-and-delete a consumed file. Reasonable options: default `preserve_path` to `true`, fail the move loudly on a collision, or skip an existing destination — but not destroy data without any error or log line. ### Error message and/or stacktrace None — the loss is silent. `ObjectStorageQueueMovedObjects` reports both objects moved even though only one survives at the destination. ### Additional context Related to the `after_processing = 'delete'` silent-leftover behaviour in #114801 and the re-ingestion duplication in #114421; this is the `move`-leg sibling, but here the consequence is data loss (a destroyed file) rather than leftover or duplicated objects. Source (current master): `applyMovePrefixIfPresent` builds the destination as `move_prefix / fileName(remote_path)` when `preserve_path` is false, and `moveWithinBucket` does `copyObject` then `removeObjectIfExists` per object, swallowing per-object failures — in `src/Storages/ObjectStorageQueue/ObjectStorageQueuePostProcessor.cpp`.
signal.author: zlareb1

signal.title: `OPTIMIZE TABLE` on DeltaLake/Paimon/Hudi object-storage tables silently succeeds as a no-op instead of throwing `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`
signal.text: **Describe the unexpected behaviour** `OPTIMIZE TABLE` on an object-storage table whose lake type does not implement compaction — `DeltaLakeLocal`/`DeltaLake`, `Paimon*`, `Hudi`, and plain object-storage engines — returns Ok and does nothing: no files rewritten, no new `_delta_log` commit, no error, nothing in the log. Every other engine that does not support OPTIMIZE throws `Code: 48. Method optimize is not supported by storage <name>` (`Memory`, `Join`, `Distributed`, ...), and Iceberg — the one lake type that does implement compaction — validates its gate loudly (`Code: 36. ... Enable 'allow_experimental_iceberg_compaction' setting to call optimize for iceberg tables`). So within the same `StorageObjectStorage` class, `OPTIMIZE TABLE iceberg_table` either compacts or tells you why not, while `OPTIMIZE TABLE delta_table` silently succeeds as a no-op — a user running it reasonably assumes compaction happened. **How to reproduce** Master `26.8.1.1375`, via `clickhouse local` (the Delta log is bootstrapped by hand with the same pattern as the `04628_delta_lake_partition_special_values` stateless test, because ClickHouse cannot initialize a Delta transaction log itself): ```bash mkdir -p delta/_delta_log cat > delta/_delta_log/00000000000000000000.json <<'EOF' {"protocol":{"minReaderVersion":1,"minWriterVersion":2}} {"metaData":{"id":"optimize-noop-repro","format":{"provider":"parquet","options":{}},"schemaString":"{\"type\":\"struct\",\"fields\":[{\"name\":\"k\",\"type\":\"long\",\"nullable\":true,\"metadata\":{}},{\"name\":\"v\",\"type\":\"long\",\"nullable\":true,\"metadata\":{}}]}","partitionColumns":[],"configuration":{},"createdTime":1700000000000}} EOF for i in 1 2 3; do clickhouse local -q "INSERT INTO FUNCTION deltaLakeLocal('$PWD/delta') SELECT number + $i*100 AS k, number AS v FROM numbers(10) SETTINGS allow_experimental_delta_lake_writes = 1" done ls delta/*.parquet | wc -l # 3 ls delta/_delta_log/*.json | wc -l # 4 clickhouse local -q "CREATE TABLE td ENGINE = DeltaLakeLocal('$PWD/delta'); OPTIMIZE TABLE td; SELECT 'OPTIMIZE returned Ok'" ls delta/*.parquet | wc -l # still 3 — nothing happened ls delta/_delta_log/*.json | wc -l # still 4 — no commit was written ``` The contrast on the same binary: ```sql CREATE TABLE tm (x UInt8) ENGINE = Memory; OPTIMIZE TABLE tm; -- Code: 48. DB::Exception: Method optimize is not supported by storage Memory. (NOT_IMPLEMENTED) ``` ```sql -- Iceberg (the one lake with OPTIMIZE support) refuses loudly without its gate: OPTIMIZE TABLE iceberg_table; -- Code: 36. DB::Exception: Enable 'allow_experimental_iceberg_compaction' setting to call optimize for iceberg tables. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) ``` **Mechanism** The base `IStorage::optimize` throws `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` (`src/Storages/IStorage.cpp:261`), which is what makes every non-supporting engine loud. `StorageObjectStorage::optimize` (`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorage.cpp:727`) overrides it to `return configuration->optimize(...)`, whose default implementations return `false` (`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorageConfiguration.h:285`, `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/IDataLakeMetadata.h:138`) — and `InterpreterOptimizeQuery::execute` discards the returned `bool` (`src/Interpreters/InterpreterOptimizeQuery.cpp`, the `table->optimize(...)` call). So the "nothing was optimized" signal exists but is dropped. The override was introduced with the Iceberg compaction work (`IcebergMetadata::optimize` is the only lake implementation), and the silent success for the other lake types looks like collateral rather than a decision. **Expected behavior** When `configuration->optimize` returns `false`, `StorageObjectStorage::optimize` should throw like the `IStorage` default (`NOT_IMPLEMENTED`, or a hint in the Iceberg gate style), so `OPTIMIZE TABLE` never reports success while doing nothing. Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).
signal.author: zlareb1

signal.title: Parallelize single-level to two-level conversion in Aggregator::prepareVariantsToMerge
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114640 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107490 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/pull/1360 When some per-thread aggregation states convert themselves to two-level mid-scan, `Aggregator::prepareVariantsToMerge` converts all the remaining single-level variants **sequentially on one thread**. Initializing a two-level variant allocates and zeroes 256 bucket tables, and there is one variant per query thread, so on machines with many cores this serial loop dominates short aggregation queries. This regime became reachable after #107490: the accurate aggregation memory accounting makes `group_by_two_level_threshold_bytes` (default 50 MB) engage for queries with **few groups but heavy states** (e.g. `uniqExact` over ~300 groups, where the states sum to hundreds of MB while the hash tables stay tiny). Previously the query-tracker delta under-reported such memory (each thread batches up to `max_untracked_memory` before propagating), so the threshold effectively never fired for this shape. Once it fires mid-scan, only the variants that happen to execute a block after the crossing convert themselves (measured: ~25 of 192 on ClickBench Q11), and the merge preparation then serially converts the remaining ~170. Effect on ClickBench (`c7a.metal-48xl`, 192 cores), hot runs, bisected and measured via manual ClickBench dispatches (evidence and result files in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/pull/1360): | build | Q10 | Q11 | |---|---|---| | master `c79b0d9227e` (4 min before #107490) | 0.133 | 0.092 | | master `32129f76fca` (4 min after #107490) | 0.297 | 0.165 | | master 07-11 (`ab8535b3ab0`) | 0.391 | 0.213 | | master 07-11 + `group_by_two_level_threshold_bytes=0` | 0.093 | 0.102 | | pre-#107490 + `group_by_two_level_threshold=1` (uniform early conversion) | 0.132 | 0.095 | The last two rows show the cost is specifically the serial merge-prep conversion after a mid-scan flip: disabling the bytes trigger recovers fully, and uniform early conversion (which happens in parallel, each thread converting its own variant during the scan) is also fast. The daily ClickBench dashboard shows the same regression on both `c7a.metal-48xl` and `c8g.metal-48xl` (192 physical cores) since 2026-07-19, and not on machines with 96 or fewer physical cores. The fix converts the remaining single-level variants in parallel on the aggregator thread pool, following the existing `ThreadPoolCallbackRunnerLocal` pattern used elsewhere in the file. Converting distinct variants concurrently is safe: `AggregatedDataVariants::convertToTwoLevel` touches only the variant's own members. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Parallelize the single-level to two-level conversion of per-thread aggregation states before merging. This fixes a 2-3x regression of short `GROUP BY` queries with heavy aggregate states (e.g. `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)`, ClickBench Q10/Q11) on machines with very many cores, introduced in 26.7 development builds when the aggregation memory accounting was made accurate. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)
